On Wednesday afternoon, while the wages were being paid out to several hundred workers at Mr. Fürstenberg's zinc factory, there sprang up „out of the bare skin“ (i.e. out of nowhere) a Communist „deputy“, who began an anti-state speech.
The police station (commissariat) was notified of this; the commissioner soon arrived and dispersed the crowd.
When the speaker left, the workers „honoured“ him with blows.
Agreement between Jewish and Polish craftsmen

As we have already written, the elections to the Chamber of Crafts in the Kielce voivodeship will take place on 17 June (czerwiec) of this year.
In the Kielce voivodeship there will be 5 electoral centres. The main electoral district of the Będzin and Zawiercie counties (powiats) will be located in the premises of the Będzin starosty.
The main electoral commission will sit in Kielce at Orla 4.
Candidates in the electoral districts must be submitted by the 21st of this month.
In connection with the elections, an agreement has been reached between Jewish and Polish craftsmen in the following way:
Of the 24 mandates of the whole voivodeship, Jewish craftsmen will receive 9 mandates and Christian craftsmen 15 mandates.
From the Będzin and Zawiercie counties 4 representatives will be elected, and negotiations are being conducted between the local Jewish and Christian craftsmen's organizations regarding the number [each side gets].
Rape of a 6-year-old girl

At Zagórska 10 lives a Christian woman, a widow, with her 6-year-old girl. Into the Christian woman's home came the 26-year-old Zygmuntowicz, who made her an indecent proposal.
The Christian woman, afraid of the „guest“, ran over to a neighbour, leaving her 6-year-old girl in the home.
Then the human beast threw himself on the child and raped her.
A few days later the child developed pains, and Dr. Barlicki, who was called in, established that the child had been infected with a venereal disease.
The human beast has been put in the local prison.
The „activity“ of the merchants' organizations

Some time ago a district council was founded, in which the Jewish merchants' organizations in Zagłębie are represented.
The council was created, but to this day it has not yet happened that a quorum came to a meeting.
The same fate also befell the meeting that was supposed to take place last Sunday.
Sosnowiec — General Meeting of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association

(Sh.) Only recently a general meeting of the Merchants' and Industrialists' Association took place, and we already have to record yet another fresh general meeting with an „original“ agenda: election of a board. It gives the impression that the matter is not the existence of one of the most important merchant institutions in Sosnowiec, but a children's game. Today one man is offended, tomorrow another — and the thought prompts no particularly cheerful reflections. In any case — it is high time to end this dangerous game and take up more useful work.
———
On Sunday evening, under the chairmanship of Mr. Lubelski, a general meeting took place, which was called because the board elected at the meeting held only recently had resigned. The reason was that some members of the „Old Guard“, not being satisfied with the outcome of the elections, lodged a protest questioning[?] the validity of the elections. With sharp speeches against the tactics of the opposition that had formed, Messrs. Kabak, Safer and Tencer spoke on behalf of the board, condemning the action of the opposition, since it is after all an accepted custom that the minority always submits to the majority. The speakers also spoke out against the system of voting by proxy: the point is that a large number of members do not come to the meeting and send their proxies to vote in their name. All these arguments (very correct, by the way) from Messrs. Kac, Tencer and others helped little, however, and it was adopted by a majority of votes that the proxies are valid. Thus the opposition won, and a board was elected of the following persons: Kwiatek, Kabak, Rejger, Rajcher, Judenherc, Kac and Safer. Deputies: G. Abramczyk, Fürstenberg and Binder.
The kehilla board has resigned

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.]
On Sunday the kehilla board held a meeting at which the answer of the starosta was discussed, namely that the kehilla council is the legal body in matters of the kehilla.
Because of this, the majority of the board, proceeding from the standpoint that "they have no say", resigned.
In connection with the resignation, the secretary of the gmina [Jewish community], Mr. Lewenhof, conferred with the starosta on the matter, and the starosta declared that he would shortly give notice regarding the resignation of the board, but that in the meantime they should carry on as until now.
Former Sejm deputy Baczyński sentenced to 5 years of hard prison

[Sosnowiec — court; communists.]
In the local district court, in a packed hall, the trial took place of the communist deputy Baczyński, whom the Sejm had handed over to the court.
The indictment states that Baczyński went to Russia illegally, where he agitated against Poland, and conducted communist agitation in the Zagłębie district.
After the defence speech of advocate Duracz of Warsaw, the accused was given the last word; instead of asking for a milder punishment, he delivered a communist speech to the audience.
The court took the floor away from him and pronounced the following verdict:
Baczyński is sentenced to 5 years of hard prison and to the loss of rights. Baczyński listened to the verdict calmly.
A murder in a robbery attack

[Sosnowiec — crime.]
In the night from Friday to Saturday bandits got into the office of the firm "Ulen" with the aim of robbing the cash box.
The watchman was in the office at the time. When the bandits saw the watchman, they struck him on the head with a piece of iron and killed him.
On reaching the cash box, the bandits found nothing there...

A horrible murder
At Szopena 70 a drunken Christian, a well-known brawler, came to a friend of his and began making a row.
When the landlady tried to remove the drunk from the flat, he pulled out a bayonet, with which he killed the woman.

Olkusz
The kehilla's matzah oven closed
For 2 years only one baker baked matzah in Olkusz. Because of this matzah ran short every year, and the poorer strata suffered most from it. On the initiative of Mr. Abraham Kerner and other communal workers a kehilla oven was set up in the beth-midrash courtyard, where the kehilla baked matzah, and everything went as usual. This year someone "tipped off" the sanitary commission that the matzah oven did not comply with the sanitary regulations, and the commission closed the oven. The other bakers took advantage of this and raised the price of matzah...

From the Small Traders' Association in Sosnowiec. / The Shekel campaign has begun in Będzin

[Sosnowiec — small traders and peddlers; letter to the editor.]
(A letter to the editor).
In connection with the articles, letters and notices in "N. Unzer Tog" ["N. Our Day"] about the so-called "revolution" in the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association — we kindly ask you to give space in your esteemed paper to the following statement:
At the general meeting of the peddlers' section of the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association, our board undertook, a few months ago, a campaign to obtain the necessary permits (visas) for the peddlers and traders in Upper Silesia. After a series of interventions with the central authorities in Warsaw and in Katowice, and thanks also to the tireless and energetic work of the leadership of our organisation, the said campaign was brought to a successful conclusion, and dozens of Jewish families were saved from hunger, want and suffering.
Unfortunately, irresponsible persons forced their way into the ranks of the peddlers who, owing to the binding procedure whereby visas are granted at the discretion of the competent administrative authority in Katowice, could not obtain visas. These very persons dared to organise a smear campaign against the board of our association, from which, incidentally, the integrity of the small traders' organisation as such has suffered, and this in turn has had a negative effect on the most pressing needs of the local small traders themselves.
The disputes and intrigues blown up[?] in public have caused, first and foremost, that at this year's expert sessions of the assessment commissions for turnover tax at the "Urząd Skarbowy" [tax office] the just demands of the small traders were not considered to the desired extent, and in some cases our representatives were not admitted to the sessions at all.
Because of the threat to the existence of the association, the board saw itself compelled to adopt the strictest measures against the disrupters and agitators, expelling (in accordance with para. 12 of the statutes) a certain number of members — for whom, however, an open way back[?] into the organisation has been left, if they pay in their overdue monthly membership dues. It should be stressed here, incidentally, that of the total number of those expelled barely 40% are peddlers and the remaining approx. 60% small traders.
However, in order to settle all the incidents radically and restore the equilibrium of the organisation, it was resolved, with the participation of the director of the Central Union of Small Traders in Poland, Mr. S. Burka, at the last extraordinary board meeting of Tuesday the 16th of this month:
1) to organise the peddlers in a separate autonomous section within the Small Traders' Association;
2) to hand over all disputes concerning the expelled members to the association's court of honour;
3) to convene a general meeting of the peddlers' section on the 28th of this month, at which, among other things, 4 candidates for the main board of the association will be elected; and
4) to convene a general members' meeting on Sunday the 5th of May, to which all members will be admitted with voting rights who have paid their overdue dues at least up to the 1st of February ["luty"] of this year.
Allow us also to express our annoyance and indignation towards the gentlemen of "N. Unzer Tog", who indirectly contributed to intensifying the chaos among the small-trader masses by giving considerable space in the columns of their so-called newspaper to tendentious notices and the like, without first informing themselves about the actual state of affairs in the leadership of the association.

Dąbrowa — A Theft That Failed.

Into the drapery (manufaktura) shop of Mr Y. Unger came an elegantly dressed Christian woman and asked to be shown silk fabric. While she was bargaining over the price, 2 more Christian women came into the shop and asked for woollen fabric.
The first customer bought a quarter of a metre of silk and paid. But as she was leaving the shop, the wool customers handed her a piece of silk, which she hid lightning-fast under her coat, and [and] went out.
Outside, "as the devil would have it" [printed "maase shokhn"], the piece of silk unrolled and thus[?] trailed after her along the pavement. A Jewish woman passing by noticed it and, suspecting it had something to do with a theft, went into Unger's shop and reported it there.
Unger's son at once ran after her and caught up with her in Fabryczna Street. But the cunning swindler had packed the piece of silk into a travelling bag and put up fierce resistance. Meanwhile a crowd gathered in the street, more robbed merchants soon came forward, and finally the girl was led off to the police station, where it was established that she is an accomplice of a well-practised gang of thieves now "touring" Zagłębie.
Various other stolen goods were also seized from the thief.

A Few Words

About the Passover issue of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung".

In the course of the 18-year existence of our paper we have been the opposite of those papers that announce to their readers a new contributor, or dwell on whatever article is going to be printed. We hold [in any case?] that it is better to give directly than to promise that one will give.

This time we are making an exception, because it is worth devoting more attention to our Passover issue, which will in every respect surpass all the holiday issues so far and will surely be a surprise for our esteemed readers.

In the large and rich Passover issue of our paper, which appears on the eve of Passover, readers will find, besides the rich news material, also a series of articles and feuilletons. Mrs. Nete[?] Ratner offers a study of the work of the convert Ruth Lazarus, "The Book of the Jewish Woman", in which she describes the tasks of the Jewish woman with regard to her traditions.

The well-known writer Mrs. Roza Jakubowicz, born in Będzin, has also sent us a sketch entitled "The Last Way[?]". In this sketch the readers will be led into a not-forgotten world...

Good news will also be the report that, after a break of several months, the beloved feuilletonist Mr. Oberżanek has agreed to be our regular contributor. For the Passover issue Mr. Oberżanek has sent a splendid political satire entitled "I Reform[?] My Kingdom"...

This issue will contain a detailed study of the newly published novel about Zagłębie, written by the most important Polish novelist, Bandrowski. The study was written by a young Jewish-Polish poet who is already renowned in the Polish literary world.

The popular painter Moshe Appelbaum has dedicated to the issue an article entitled "Plastic Art among Jews". In an instructive form the author develops the role of the plastic arts among Jews.

Besides various other articles and feuilletons, a new Jewish novel, "The Seduced[?]", based on historical facts, begins to appear; it reads very suspensefully and arouses enormous interest in the reader.

What Is Going On with Our Talmud Torah? (Does the institution belong to the community, or is it a private little shop?)

We have in Będzin a Talmud Torah that will not let itself be touched, and one may not touch it. Hardly does anyone come near it, and the heavens open; at once there is shouting and drum-beating that the "sinners" [poshim] want to uproot Jewishness, that they defile the sacred. So we do not touch this sacred thing, which keeps on sinking, and its state grows ever sadder, ever more dreadful.
It seemed to them, the administrators of the Talmud Torah, that one may not touch the mould that has grown up, which with them has turned into a kind of holiness, and we said to ourselves: may it do them good, let them delight in what is dear and precious to them...
It turns out, however, that all this is done for appearances only, and there, on the one hand, they tear at each other for all the world is worth, and on the other hand the finances are far from flourishing ["poygldige"[?]]. It is an old rule: where there is no livelihood, there is no domestic peace either. Who knows, perhaps the quarrels arise precisely because the finances are limping?
And indeed, can an institution exist that has to wait for some rich man in town, God forbid, to depart this world, so that it can send the "charity saves from death" [tsedoko tatsil mimoves] children to the funeral? Is it a business to keep teachers [melamdim] for children if they will not earn it? People remember that there is a Talmud Torah with ragged, worn-out children only when we see them, God forbid, at a rich man's funeral. Otherwise one could live for years and not remember that Będzin has a Talmud Torah.
And this is an educational establishment, that is to say a people's institution, which is supposed to educate poor children. Ah, whoever looks at the condition of these little children, and at the conditions they are kept in at the Talmud Torah! But all this is still not enough. The teachers, although they take the most minimal salaries ["pensions"], almost pennies [groszy], do not get even these pennies paid on time, so that it is impossible to understand how these people support themselves. And this at a time when people were told: introduce a little order, make the institution into a public establishment, as a people's institution should be, and then efforts will be made to draw up a large budget, and the town will cover the money for the budget; but to this the dictators of the Talmud Torah could not agree — what, are we to let people look into our bowl? — and they said to themselves: "neither your honey nor your sting." Don't be my uncle and don't sew me any shoes.
And[?] now one hears something else again: that autocracy exists in all its size and strength even in matters of religion. So last week's chronicle tells us that the gabbai has abolished ["skasirt"] the minyan, which has existed for 40 years already, in order to carry out an act of revenge against a worshipper. This surely has nothing to do with education, "free elements", "sinners" — so how could the administration allow it? And who knows — everything there is veiled; perhaps there is no administration at all, perhaps a single individual does what and how he pleases and nobody may interfere there; otherwise people would not have let things come to lawlessness and desecration of God's name [hillul hashem], and that we "sinners" should have to come and preach morals to them.
It is surely out of the question that a Talmud Torah can maintain itself on such foundations. As soon as the town learns of the lawlessness and dictatorship that reign there, it will stop taking any interest in the institution altogether, and how then will the upkeep of the institution be able to continue? Whoever pays wants at least to know whether his guilder [gulden] is used for the proper purpose; otherwise even the small number of members who pay — incidentally[?] only pennies — will stop paying, and then the situation will be menacing, catastrophic. And however it may be, however sad the management may be, one must not forget that in the end there is no other such educational establishment — to whom will the poor children turn then? Who will teach them Ivri [Hebrew reading]?
It goes without saying that it is sad to have to speak in such a tone about a people's educational establishment, but what can one do when we see[?] ourselves fallen so low, when the poor child is abandoned and nobody is interested in raising an outcry that Będzin must have a Talmud Torah as it should be! That Będzin cannot be content with what we have, and that we call it a Talmud Torah only to discharge our duty.
Either — or: either it is a Talmud Torah, and then it must be maintained, and it must be maintained by the whole town; if not — if this is not an institution that deserves confidence — then let it be known that we have no Talmud Torah in Będzin, and that one must be created anew.
More than once householders [baalebatim] have declared that they want a Talmud Torah that will know how to educate children and not discharge its duty by sending them to funerals in order to bring income into the till — which is a desecration of God's name and an insult, a crime and a humiliation.
It would therefore be high time to know whether the existing institution is willing to submit to public control so as to make of it a [?] ["leyt"]; if not, let us at least know that in Będzin we have no Talmud Torah, only an institution that nobody may touch and for which, in this case, nobody is responsible.
— That is what is worth knowing.
R. Let.
Greetings from Home from Eretz Israel

Eretz Israel is already blessed with the good fortune of celebrations and attractions. Only just after the Purim parades ["manifestations"], people are already preparing for the huge Eretz Israel exhibition, which opened on 8 April in Tel Aviv. This "Taarucha" [exhibition], which represents Jewish production and serves as propaganda for "Totzeret Ha'aretz" [produce of the Land], is held under the patronage of the municipality, the Zionist Executive and the High Commissioner, Sir [John] Chancellor. As the local Hebrew newspapers report, thousands of merchants and tourists are coming to the exhibition, among them a few hundred from Poland. The first "emissary" of the Polish industrialists to the exhibition, Mr. Oskar Kahn [Kan] of Łódź, has been staying here for several weeks already and intends to found several textile ["manufaktur"] factories in Eretz Israel. In general one feels here in Eretz Israel an improvement in economic life, and of the recent unemployment there is no trace whatever.
I pass on further the greetings from home of the Zagłębie Jews in Eretz Israel. Mr. Motl Tenenbaum, who went to Eretz Israel with his wife 5 years ago as halutzim [pioneers], is a government official and has been working for several years on the railway at Lod. He lives very nicely and comfortably; he is an active labour activist in "Poalei Rakevet" [the railway workers' union] and holds an office in the council of the railway workers.
From Tel Aviv I went by car to "Herzliya", where I visited Mr. Anszel Lenczner, a former citizen of Będzin, who lived on Czeladzka[?] street and had a small butter business. Here Mr. L. has a "Beit Okhel la-Poalim" [workers' eating-house]; he is very content and does not want to hear or know any more about the Diaspora. His children work at Rutenberg's power station, earn a lot of money, and he has much naches from them. Mr. L. is now building himself a "tzrif" [hut], that is, a little house of boards and tin, to which he wants to move his restaurant. He also owns a plot of land, on which he has planted an orange grove [pardes].
From "Herzliya" I set off on foot to Magdiel, about 10 kilometres, through the colony of "Ra'anana" and the workers' settlement [moshav ovdim] "Ein Hai". The road from "Herzliya" to Magdiel, on which I met only Arabs, who greeted me with the Hebrew "Shalom", is a very hard one, and for several hours I crawled in the greatest heat through deep hot sands until I finally arrived in Magdiel at sunset.
In Magdiel I met Mr. Issachar Liwer of Będzin, who has been transformed from a merchant into a "peasant" in the full sense of the word. Mr. L., who shows me great hospitality, takes me around the colony and shows me his live and dead stock. The "meshek" [farm] is truly a splendid one and is valued at 1.500 pounds. He owns 50 dunams of land, on which he has an orange grove and "plaha" (extensive farming). 2 years ago he built himself a little house with several rooms and conveniences. He has a few cows and much poultry. Mr. L. received from "Keren Hayesod" a long-term loan of several hundred pounds. For Passover his wife and children are coming to him from Zawiercie, and they will remain citizens of Eretz Israel.
Tel Aviv. M. Hampel.
Spring at Work

[Feuilleton — literary sketch: spring.] (Feuilleton)
By "Lebedikn" ["Der Lebediker" — "the lively one"; a pen name].
With me, spring always comes with a great urge to walk, to wander and to roam about just like that.
In the days of spring I am too lazy to think and to wrinkle my brow.
Something drives me out into the street.
I simply feel like frolicking about the streets and alleys, bridges and empty stretches...
I love to watch how spring works at its workshop...
How it does its magic work, how it bewitches and acts on people's gait, how it kindles the blood with youthful mischief, how it plays with sunbeams, throws them onto hearts, heads and faces...
How it scatters smiles by the millions.
Where does it get so much? — Such riches!
I love to stand in the sun and listen to the song of the earth, which is warming up its chilled winter blood.
The earth sings, and it seems to you that you hear her voice as it comes and [from; printed "and"] the deepest depth with such freshness and youth.
The song of the earth in spring is the greatest song of all songs.
I love to stroll through the revived streets and snatch up conversations and words.
I catch them with half an ear, caught and not caught...
It is such a fine[?] game.
You realise that on a spring day the world does not talk, it just chatters away like a young couple in love.
I love to watch, in the spring days, enamoured [couples?] and heads [sic; a word seems dropped].
There is nobody dearer than they in spring.
They are bride and groom and the witnesses themselves...
They are spring itself.
I stroll and renew myself.
I feel like feeling for myself the tremor of love that passes over the world on a fine spring day,
that makes young shoulders and hearts quiver for ever and ever.
And now I go and catch a train and ride.
And oh, how new and young the wheels clatter today!
They run one after the other like boys playing with girls; it seems to me I hear lust in their noise...
One wheel wants to catch the other, as if saying: run, run, and I'll catch you!
But the loveliest thing in spring is the young girl.
The young girl skips along like a doe.
Every young girl is a young doe.
The feet — so slender! The gait — so singing! The necks[?] — so tower-like!
And what about the men?
Spring acts on them too,
you feel in every man the power of spring, his will to live, his capacity for relationships, to begin the world anew...
And here I go and actually talk to myself.
What about? — I don't know.
And what difference does it make? In the days of spring one may talk nonsense.
Spring is the babble of youth.
How beautiful the days of spring are!
The sun comes out in the sky like a freshly printed newspaper, fresh with news and sensations.
"The Sun in the Sky" is the oldest newspaper with the largest circulation.
One feels like grabbing a sun like a fresh newspaper and running with it like a newsboy, shouting and calling: People, buy sun! Buy sun!
And now I actually feel like running into a shop and asking them to give me a penknife.
The finest penknife — over here! I'm a little boy and I want to play!
Maybe even stick it into the ground?
Hit or miss? — Still the finest game.
Or now I go off to the bridge.
The bridge trembles with spring air; I admire the gold spread out below in the river.
The world has so much gold! The world is still richer than Ford and Rockefeller put together.
Spread out your hands and scoop up gold!
Open your eyes and delight in the brightness.
Enjoy, enjoy freely!
I get drunk on sun and gold.
I take hold of the iron railings ["porentshes", Polish poręcze] of the bridge.
They are warm like the hands of a beloved.
I embrace them with joy.
How good it is in spring.
It is so pleasant to watch how winter goes away, melts like ice, and without resentment.
As it seems to me, winter does not mind at all that it yields its place to spring.
It leaves with a light heart.
And you walk, stroll, get tangled among people[?] and sunbeams, and now you actually feel like stopping a young girl, a total stranger, a singing and a dancing one.
You suddenly feel so lonely being alone on such a holiday, you must share your joy with someone:
— Girl, come with me!
— Where to?
— To the end of the world!
— Ha! Ha! Ha! — Where is the end of the world?
— Right there, where the sun laughs!
And you want to believe that the girl will not refuse you.
Why should she?
And you go together, skipping along so young and fresh and spring-like.
And you laugh and you buy balloons.
And you lift the balloons.
And the balloons lift you.
And you fly and play like children, without care or purpose.
And now you grow tired, you run out beyond the town, sit down on a rock, take each other by the hand and look into each other's eyes. And in both of you is mirrored the great holiday of spring, the eternally young, eternally renewed, merrily erotic holiday of nature.
Blessed be spring with all its colours and hues!

Former Będzin Rabbi, Rabbi Yekutiel Zalman Graubart, on the Agunot Tragedy in Poland.

[Agunot — a former Będzin rabbi; New York / Poland.]
In the New York newspaper "Der Tog" Rabbi Yekutiel Graubart has published a longer article in which he discusses at length the tragedy of the agunot [“chained” wives] in Poland.
Because of the importance of the matter we give some tragic extracts from the article.
Rabbi Graubart writes:
The World War ended long ago. But the war's painful after-effects are still not over. In Central Europe, where thousands of Jewish families were torn to pieces and scattered over the seven seas, one notices a special wound in the Jewish organism, which seems about to become incurable if speedy, urgent help does not come.
I mean the tragedy of the agunot in Poland.
The misfortune of the thousands of separated Jewish families that still cannot be reunited can in no way be compared to the tragedy of those Jewish daughters who have not only been struck by misfortune, but also terribly betrayed and abandoned forever by their life partners. Left with small children, helpless and unprotected, they are robbed of the possibility of finding their vanished husbands so that these should at least free them by a get [bill of divorce], allowing them to start life anew. They are perishing of hunger, and in their loneliness and want they feel all the horror of the war, although the World War has been over for ten years now.
Their husbands are in America, where they hide from the authorities and from rabbinic inquiries. And not all of them can be prosecuted by law even when they are reached, because in most cases their marriages were not legally performed [i.e. religious marriages without civil registration].
Besides the latter, thousands also went missing in Russia, where they were killed in the war, died as prisoners of war and as hostages ["zakładniki"].
Their agunot are living widows, and their situation is far sadder than that of widows, who can still hope for a new home and a new life, whereas they remain in darkness and are condemned to a life of desolation.
At the last conference of the Agudat HaRabbanim [Union of Rabbis] in Poland a central bureau was founded, which has collected sufficient material and documents concerning the missing husbands, and the bureau has made contact with the whole world in order to rescue the unfortunate women.
It is [printed "עס ביז", misprint for "עס איז"] worth mentioning here a few facts to show how great the tangle of the aguna problem is, and the predicament in which the persons concerned find themselves. Each fact is only one of many similar facts that characterise the many-sidedness of the tragedy, and together they set before us a horrifying picture of scattered and dispersed Jewish life in exile.
A certain G., who as early as 1902 left his wife in Poland and went off to Chicago, was traced only a while ago and was summoned by the Polish consul there at his wife's demand. He claimed that he had already divorced her in Warsaw before a certain rabbi whose name he had forgotten. The Warsaw rabbinate investigated the matter and established that this is not true, and now they demand a get from him.
Remarkable, too, is the following case: in a certain town in Poland an aguna, seeing no way of finding her vanished husband, who had gone to America, went and married another man. The [new] husband's family, discovering that she is a married woman, did everything possible to separate the couple until she obtains a get. Now the local rabbi asks that efforts be made to obtain a get from her husband, explaining at the same time the tragic situation of the unfortunate woman.
Another fact: a certain man was taken into the army in Poland as early as 1912, where he left his wife behind. Since the outbreak of the war the wife had heard nothing of him. Some time ago rumours began to spread that he had fallen in the war, and his wife came to Warsaw so that the rabbinate would look into the matter. Through an official taking of testimony it was possible to confirm the rumours — that such a man by the same name had been killed in Russia and buried there. It seemed that the Warsaw rabbinate would, on the basis of that testimony, issue the woman a heter [permission to remarry]. But how astonished the rabbinate was when it suddenly received word that at the very time when the vanished man's wife already considered him [printed "איב", probably for "אים"] dead, a landsman [fellow townsman] of his — according to the letter that arrived — had met him strolling quite leisurely in the street in New York...
Not for nothing did our sages compare releasing a lonely Jewish woman to rebuilding a Jewish ruin ("Whoever releases one aguna, it is as if he rebuilt one of the ruins of Jerusalem"). They strove to ease the law in releasing agunot; with regard to recognising various kinds of testimony, recognition by sight, identifying marks, and even government documents and records, they gave the authorities grounds to release the wives of missing husbands.
Now the question arises: will our Jewish organisations, which concentrate the active forces, grasp the seriousness of this burning question?
Will our communal workers, who have great merits in all other fields of public activity, give [printed "נעבן", probably for "געבן"] the right answer to the great emissary of the Jewish people of many millions, Rabbi Eliyahu Lipschitz, the rabbi of Grójec [?], who has come here armed with all the necessary documents and material, to create the means for the planned work?
Will Jewish public opinion know how to appreciate the moral side of the tragedy, which threatens to strike a certain part of our Jewish daughters in Poland with immoral degeneration?
We believe that American Jewry, which helped so wonderfully in the distress of the World War, will surely not remain indifferent when the still-existing horrifying remnants [?] of those war times do not cease devouring the last strength of living victims.
The Rebbe's Son (30)

[Serialized historical novel — "The Rebbe's Son" by Yakov Zimmerman, instalment 30; from the time of the Chmielnicki massacres (1648–49).]
A historical Jewish novel by Yakov Zimmerman [Jakub Cymerman].

The two girls, too — Blumele, Isaac the baker's daughter, and Sarah, Chaim the coachman's daughter, the two inseparable friends — were among those assembled. Their patience, too, was put to a very hard test, but for the time being their efforts had no effect whatever. Still none of the soldiers coming home had been seen.

But all through that time nobody stood idle [printed "leyder", apparently for "leydik"]. People kept talking and talking, and the main topic of the whole long day was the Jewish heroes of Kraków, who had distinguished themselves so greatly, and to whom alone was owed the great victory and the defeat of Chmielnicki's robber bands.

The greater part of all the talk was about Dudl, the handsome and heroic son of the Rabbi of Kraków, the "Tosafot Yom-Tov". Shimon did not tire all day of telling, and telling over again and again, of the great deeds of heroism that Dudl had shown yesterday on the battlefield, and that it was to him, and to him alone, and to the courage he had put into the hearts of his comrades, the Jewish soldiers of Kraków, that it was owed that the victory had been so great and so complete; had it not been for him, who knows how the battle would have turned out and — let us not open our mouths to Satan! — the murderers, the robber bands, would have won...

Among the circles of people who stood constantly around Shimon and never tired of hearing his stories were also the two girls, Blumele and Sarah. Among other men they would certainly not have had the boldness to join in, but since Shimon was the leader of the whole circle here, they felt at home and allowed themselves to linger. But while nearly every one of the men standing around could not contain his curiosity, and they kept bombarding Shimon with their questions and queries, which he kept answering with a smile on his lips, the two girls stood the whole time with flaming cheeks, just as if they were mute, and did not utter a single word. Only the gleam of their eyes showed the strength of the feelings that stirred their hearts...

— — — — —

Suddenly a great shout was heard from the end of the street, not far from the gate; the joy suddenly swelled, and everyone kept calling and shouting!
— They are coming! They are here!

Who the lucky one was [printed "gliklíber"] who spotted the riders, nobody knows even to this day... Shimon, however, always held to his own, even years later, that he had been the first, and nobody wanted to argue with him over it — he could get very angry about it — and deny it to him...

Soon the first riders appeared in the street. The voices and shouts of joy reached the heart of heaven, almost up to the sky. People did not stop shouting and greeting the heroes returning home.

At the head of the whole procession rode the old Prince Wiśniowiecki, on his left side his son, the young prince, and on his right side Dudl, the son of the Rabbi of Kraków, the "Tosafot Yom-Tov".

By Isaac the baker's little house the procession of riders halted; the old prince waved his hand as a sign that he wished to say something.

As if by magic the great crowd fell silent all at once, so silent that in every corner of the street one could hear the prince's words.

— Friends, Jews of Kraków — the prince began in his mighty voice — my messenger Shimon already told you last night about the great victory we won over Chmielnicki and his robber bands, and that almost all of it is owed to the great heroism of our Dudl, the son of your beloved rabbi. I wish now to confirm here before you all that all this is true, and that he alone saved the whole situation, and we, who were already so close to being the losers, became the victors through his heroic courage.

What I said after the battle was won before my whole army, I repeat here today once again before all of you: young David is as dear, precious and rooted in my heart as my own son; and to show him my love, esteem, gratitude and recognition, I present him with my great estate of Dmitrowa [?], with all the manor farms (folwarks) that belong to it, and I ask him to accept this gift from me!...

Dudl even wanted to wave it away with his hand and say something — that the gift was too great for his small merits and that he was therefore unable to accept it — but in that very second the old prince made a movement with his horse, rode up close to Dudl, embraced him with both arms and kissed him on the face. This came upon Dudl so quickly and so expectedly [sic; printed "ervartet", evidently for "umervartet", unexpectedly] that he could no longer speak at all or protest against the great gift the prince had just given him. He could not get out a word; only tears, hot tears of joy, kept running down his cheeks.

When Dudl came to himself, he saw that not far from him stood his father, the Rabbi of Kraków. He leapt from the horse, embraced his father and kissed him.

But when he saw that not far off stood Blumele, the dear girl to whom his heart was so drawn and whom he had not been able to forget for a single minute even in the stormiest war, he could no longer control and restrain himself; he ran up to her, embraced her and kissed her.

— Blumele! — was the only word he could now get out.

— Dudl! — was her answer, and forgetting where they were and paying no heed to the great crowd of people around them, she pressed herself tightly to him and wept bitterly..

The voices again reached the heart of heaven; everyone present shouted and strained their throats for great joy. With their jubilant cries they wanted to show their approval and consent to the extraordinary match that had just been concluded here, so suddenly and unexpectedly, before all their eyes...

And Isaac son of Yekele ["Ayzik Yekeles"]?...

His joy now knew no bounds at all. With his own eyes he had seen that his dream had not been an empty one, idle words!

He ran about like a madman for great joy. "Esther!" — he kept calling — "you see, half of the dream has already come true, and the same will surely happen with the other half!.."

(Conclusion follows).

What's Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Around the Dispute between the Cantor and the Choir Conductor

[Będzin — Kehilla.]
(Slogan line above the page head: "By buying a shekel you help build our national home in the Land of Israel.")
What's happening in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 9 Nisan 5689 — 19 April 1929.)
Będzin
Around the dispute between the cantor and the conductor.
On Sunday a meeting took place of members of the kehilla board and council, who considered the dispute prevailing between the cantor Mr. Żwaczycz[?] and the conductor Mr. Kalmus.
It was resolved that Mr. Kalmus shall give a written undertaking that he will accept the regulations which the board will present to him, and also[?] that Mr. Kalmus shall not demand a compensation sum in case he has to leave his post as conductor.
Threatening with Knives...

[Będzin — Beit midrash.]
There is no peace among the gabbaim of the town beit midrash. It has gone so far that the gabbai Mr. Salomonowicz received a threatening letter with the following content:
"In the name of our organisation we warn you and caution you not to come into the beit midrash, because an attempt has been prepared against you — to stab you with knives."
Mr. S. handed the letter over to the police.
Tea for Philanthropic Institutions.

[Zagłębie — Charity.]
As every year, the well-known tea firm "W. Wissotzky" has sent us 4 kilos of tea for us to distribute among the philanthropic institutions in Zagłębie.
We pointed out to the local representative that we cannot give such a small portion of tea to all the institutions, and the representative accordingly turned to the above-mentioned firm, asking them to increase their donation.
Since the holiday is already near, we are distributing the tea according to this allotment: for "Linat ha-Cholim" three quarters of a kilo; the orphans' ochronka (children's home) three quarters of a kilo; "Beit La-Em" half a kilo; the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec 1 kilo; the women's society in Dąbrowa half a kilo; "Dobroczynność" (charity society) in Zawiercie half a kilo.
The institutions listed are requested to collect the tea at our editorial office.
Conscription of the 1908 Class.

[Będzin — Military.]
On 2[?] May the conscription (pobór) of those born in 1908 begins. To each of those liable for conscription the magistrate sends a summons stating when he must report, and those who do not receive such summonses must report at the magistrate, military department, second floor.
On 2 and 4 May those with deferments (odroczenia) from the years 1906 and 1907 and part of 1908 must report.
The conscription will last until 16 May.
The magistrate asks us to draw the attention of young men who are not permanent local residents and are not on the local conscription lists that they must report in their places of birth.
Excursions to the National Exhibition in Poznań.

[Będzin — Municipality.]
The town administration has taken the initiative to organise excursions to the National Exhibition in Poznań. Professional, economic and social institutions are to take part in the excursions.
For this purpose a meeting will take place this Sabbath, to which representatives of the above-mentioned organisations have been invited, who will have to decide how the excursions are to be organised.
Saved from Death

[Będzin — Accident.]
On Wednesday in the daytime a young Christian tried to jump onto the tram while it was going at full speed on Małachowskiego[?] Street.
The Christian received a strong blow, from which he fell down right by the tram line. A few minutes later he got up. From the fall his face was covered in blood.
The Price of Matzah Has Risen

[Będzin — Passover / Cost of living.]
In the last days of the week the price of matzah rose by 30 groszy per kilo. Instead of 1.50 [złoty] the price has gone up to 1.80 per kilo.
The rise comes about because the bakers, seeing that no matzah is being brought in from the nearby small towns, have raised the price.
Wholesale Merchants Must Submit Applications Regarding the 1 Percent

[Będzin — Taxes and trade.]
The Merchants' Association asks us to draw the attention of the wholesale merchants: those who wish to benefit from the 1 percent turnover tax must, after receiving the assessment notices (nakazy), submit applications to that effect at the Urząd Skarbowy (Tax Office).
Water-supply plan being carried out

[Będzin — municipality; water supply.] These days the town administration [of Będzin] held a meeting at which the tender for awarding the work on the water-supply system throughout the whole town was drawn up. The tender will be published in the next few days.
Injured by the tram
[Będzin — tram accident.] On Kościuszki Street the tram struck Mr. Shloyme (Szlama) Gutman on his left hand. The latter went to the municipal hospital, where he is under treatment.
Suicide

[Będzin — suicide.] On Tuesday night the 42-year-old Żak, a resident of Warpie [a quarter of Będzin][?], hanged himself on the door. When the members of the household saw it, the suicide was already dead.
Sosnowiec — Suicide attempt of a young Jewish man

[Sosnowiec — attempted suicide.] In the night from Friday to Saturday (Shabbat) the 28-year-old Ch. Weinblum from „Pradle“[?] shot himself with the intention of committing suicide.
The bullet struck him in the lungs, in a place where it is impossible to perform an operation. The would-be suicide is lying in the local Jewish hospital [in Sosnowiec].
The suicide happened on romantic grounds. Mr. Ch. had for about a year been matched to Miss Y., whom he considered his bride.
But a day before the suicide, when Ch. asked for the consent of the young lady's mother, the latter refused him and advised him „to knock this foolishness out of his head“.
In despair at this answer, Ch. went up to the hotel „Wiktoria“ and wanted to put an end to his life.
A new Jewish bank

[Sosnowiec — economy; Jewish credit institution.] Last week a new Jewish credit institution was opened here [in Sosnowiec] under the name „Sosnowiec Mutual Credit Institution“.
At the head of the institution are Messrs. Leybish Zenrel[?], Shimon Mendel Tabiasz, Feivel Estri, L. Szwajcer, Simcha Estreicher, M. Zederman, Sh. Mencer, Y. Szwarcbaum and others.
Heavy sentences for trading in railway tickets

[Sosnowiec — court; railways.] On Monday the trial began in the local district court [in Sosnowiec] against several Jewish women and men who had been arrested on 5 May 1927 at Wolbrom station for carrying passengers on the Kielce—Strzemieszyce line „na gapę“ [Polish slang: without tickets].
In the dock sat: Rivka Ratner, Zisl Ratner, Pinchas Ratner, Pinchas Boym, Sheyndl Boym, Yekl Raskowski and 8 railway officials.
36 tickets were also found on those arrested.
To the trial, which lasted until Wednesday evening, 60 witnesses were summoned, who supported the charges against the Jews.
After the speech of the prosecutor, who demanded punishment for all the accused, the court withdrew for deliberation and then delivered the following verdict:
the 19-year-old Rivka Ratner is sentenced to a year in prison, the 20-year-old P. Ratner to 6 months in prison, the 24-year-old Zisl Ratner to 3 months; the 17-year-old P. Boym to 4 months and Rakowski — 3 months.
On the basis of the amnesty the sentences are reduced by half.
The remaining accused were fully acquitted.
Not for the League, only for his own pocket..

[Sosnowiec — court; embezzlement.] The well-known engineer Borkowski[?], who at one time committed abuses in the labour exchange office, sat again these days in the dock at the district court [in Sosnowiec].
This time he was accused that, while chairman of the „League of Seas and Rivers“ [Liga Morska i Rzeczna], he had collected the money at various private schools and collections, to the sum of a thousand złoty.
The „Seas“ chairman was sentenced to 8 months in prison.
Demands of the mine workers

[Zagłębie — miners; labour.] On Sunday a large meeting took place of the workers in the Zagłębie coal mines. At the meeting the question was presented of intervening with the Minister of Labour so that he should annul the agreement between the workers and the industrialists, who had added from 2 to 6 per cent (to wages), while soon afterwards they raised the price of coal by 10 per cent.
After hearing the report of the lawyer Pawlek[?] it was resolved: 1) working time in the mines must last no more than 8 hours; 2) the workers must receive ready-prepared lamps for work; 3) to raise the coal allowance (deputat); 4) to pay holiday time according to the normal wage; and 5) the agreement shall apply to all industrial enterprises.
City council sessions postponed because of the eve of the holiday

[Sosnowiec (?) — City council.] Yesterday and today, Friday, sessions of the local city council were to have taken place. The Jewish councillors therefore applied to the chairman of the city council asking that, because of the days before the holiday, the sessions be postponed. The request was taken into account, and the sessions will take place on the 27th and 28th of this month.
—o—
Vilna Troupe performs on Chol Hamoed Pesach in Sosnowiec.
[Sosnowiec — Theatre.] On Monday of Chol Hamoed Pesach the Vilna Ensemble [Vilna Troupe], headed by the artists Nechama, Karish, Kash, Shriftzetser, Malvina[?] Rafael, Litvina[?], Gradner and others, will give only 1 guest performance at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre, in Leo Fall's great musical operetta "The Rose of Stambul". The troupe has already proven itself here in its brilliant production of "The Golem", and there is no doubt whatsoever that we are dealing with a first-class theatre in the full sense of the word. The troupe has decided to present itself in our region with its excellent operetta forces in one of the richest European musical creations by the German composer Leo Fall.
—o—
Hersh Lipshitz, of blessed memory.
[Sosnowiec — Obituary.] On Wednesday the news caused mourning in the town that one of the town's notables, the long-time resident and grain merchant Hersh Lipshitz, had died suddenly. In the course of his life the deceased earned the greatest sympathy among all the inhabitants of the town, without distinction of nationality. When the Polish courts were established he was elected the first justice of the peace in Sosnowiec. The deceased was also a charitable man and took part in all public campaigns.
—o—
He "inspected" the letters to military men.
[Sosnowiec — Post office; crime.] The official at the Sosnowiec post office, Wojciechowski, who was employed sorting letters, had for a long time been "inspecting" the registered-value letters.
During the search of Wojciechowski's flat dozens of letters were found, as well as many postage stamps the official had removed from letters.
He committed the largest number of thefts on value letters sent to military men.
The official has been handed over to the investigation office.
—o—
Soap and oil merchants will have to take an exam.
[Poland — Trade; regulations.] An ordinance is soon to be issued under which all those who trade, wholesale or retail, in oil [petroleum], soap, paints and all kinds of chemical products will have to take professional examinations.
The examinations will take place in 3 series in the presence of representatives of the authorities, the chambers of commerce and delegates of the organisations concerned,

People's or Private Institutions?

[Economy — Jewish banks; opinion piece.]
(What is the purpose of the cooperative [„געז.“, probably “social/cooperative”] people's banks? Do they really fulfil their tasks towards the people?)
A Jew complains [?] to me: You keep writing that we. The public has no sense of responsibility towards the masses, that we — you say, [unclear word] — do not care that [—] social institutions be set up at the proper level, that everyone should benefit from them, that those who need support should be supported; and truly we understand that you are right, when you point out to us that as soon as we understand the responsibility of society and for society. We know — says the Jew — that every healthy people must know the necessity of its social institutions.
Unfortunately this is not understood among us; unfortunately people do not know how properly to socialise the institutions that are created among us on social foundations. True, people do not know how to set them up properly, and what is more, they also do not know how to maintain them. So this is how it is: neither does the public support them, nor do the leaders, those at the helm, make them such that they bring benefit to the community, that they really be institutions exclusively for the whole of the population.
So the one depends on the other: neither does the public see to it that we should first of all have rock-solid institutions which we could be proud of, that we possess such and could boast of them; and on the other hand, when we already do have such, the leaders of the institutions unfortunately do not show proper understanding of the matter.
True, first of all one must have well-established social institutions, and only then can one see whether they serve the benefit of the general mass of the population.
It goes without saying that we need first and foremost healthy and well-established institutions, but one cannot agree that we have none at all. We do have such, and if they are well established and do not bring the proper benefit, this proves that their leaders do not fulfil their tasks properly.
We have at least one single corner of Jewish life where the institutions prosper well — we mean our banks. We have several Jewish banks in every town and all of them develop well, all of them stand at the proper material level, and I do not at all agree with my fellow writers who have more than once stated in this very place that it is becoming dangerous when too many banks are founded, when these banks begin to be turned into little shops. No, on the contrary, let them become popular, let them penetrate every stratum of the population and let them learn the trade; the more they try, the more they will learn.
And therefore we must welcome the newly founded bank, and we need only wish that it understand, in the full sense of the word, its tasks, its obligations towards the community.
Until now, unfortunately, the leaders of our financial institutions do not understand this, for although we have well-established banks, they do not serve all strata of the population exclusively.
People here tell, after all, that while various members cannot get their customers' bills discounted for a few hundred złoty, others come in their place and get heavy thousands discounted.
So there are privileged persons whom the institutions serve and who make use of them properly, even beyond their means, while others cannot get even their minimal number of bills discounted.
One must not forget that those who get the larger sums in the Jewish banks have access everywhere and can arrange their position [?] so that even if they [?] are discounted only a half or a quarter [?], it is no harm either, because they have access everywhere and do not depend on this or that bank; whereas when the small man is not given his few hundred złoty, he is crushed, he cannot turn to others, and when "his" bank throws his few bills back at him, he is left hanging in the air and does not know what world he is in.
So the protection [favouritism] system exists in our banking institutions in its full size and breadth. One has to know how to talk to the director of this or that bank, one has to know how to get on with the council and with the board, and then one can attain the level of unlimited credit.
Can we call these institutions social? Are these banks for the community, for society, for the people? At best one can call them protection banks for a select few, for certain categories of people, at whose service they stand at any time and for whom [?] huge operations are made, while the average man of the people has almost no access there; for the fact that one grants [unclear words: "berlen or shterlen"] a hundred-złoty note now and then for form's sake, to show that the door is not shut to them, does not yet mean that the bank serves their interests, that it fulfils its needs.
Our banks are created and maintained by all strata of the population, and therefore they must serve the population exclusively, and all sorts of protection systems and various side considerations must be removed there. That is what does not stand on a healthy basis, that is what cannot be called honest conduct.
If we want our financial institutions to be called people's banks in the true sense — of the people — and really to be such, then first of all the protection system must be removed, which unfortunately has forced its way without exception into all our banking institutions.
That is what one must remember and guard well on every occasion.
Dr. Papuri [?].
The First Days of Passover

[Będzin — Passover in town; local feuilleton.] The days of the first days of Passover were cold, both outside and indoors. The cold began right from the eve of Passover, when the blood of the poor froze as they paid — thanks to the prohibitions — 1 gulden and 80 groszy for a kilo of "pletslekh" [flat cakes; apparently matzah]. The gentlemen meat suppliers, too, added 20 gr. to a kilo of meat. The surcharge — so people say — was made in honour of the holiday, but connoisseurs, the fine noses, interpret it thus: that the 20 groszy [?] were taken because certain butchers had paid a sum of 200 zł. so that they would be permitted to bring meat from Mysłowice.
———
Warmth [?] and a festive mood prevailed at the Seders in the orphans' shelter ("ochronka"); there, on the third floor of Zmigród's house, 40 boys celebrated the Seders like true "princes".
Year in, year out, the board of "Dobroczynność" [?], having no means to provide for the unfortunate children, distributed them among benefactors in town. This year, on the initiative of the "orphans' mother", Mrs. Cesia [Tsisha] Szajn, the "traditional shame" was lifted from the children — or rather only from the boys, since the orphan girls spent the holiday among strangers...
The tables laid with every good thing received the children in their holiday clothes, who recited the Haggadah with great "enthusiasm" and supported the Shulchan Aruch [the "set table"] even more.
The children allowed themselves extra cups, and at every cup wished each other that next year, as free men, they would already be freed from the cramped quarters on the third floor and find themselves in the new building that is being built for them...
———
In the cultural field there was a truly terrible crisis. Dr. Kruk's lecture "The Crisis in European Culture" had a "bombastic" [?] effect on the listeners, and a "crisis" began to reign in the hall. Especially in the gallery, which brought it about that the lecture was interrupted for a while..;
———
The "Muze", which has lately become so popular thanks to "At Night in the Old Marketplace", wanted to honour the poet Yitskhok Leybush Peretz and in honour of his 14th yahrzeit arranged an "academy" [commemorative evening].
The organizers, wanting [?] it to be "round and pointed", also arranged a dance evening as a "dessert". It is really a blockhead's question: what connection does honouring Peretz have with the Charleston?
— The result: the academy and the "kosher" [?] ball turned into a dance of the dead...

The Cup-Gift for the Jewish Teams in Zagłębie. First Conference of "Hakoah"—"Maccabi"—"Kraft"

[Zagłębie — sport; the paper's initiative.] On Sunday, in the apartment of the editor Mr. Szpigelman, the first conference took place on how to organize the so-called "puchar" [cup], which the editorial board of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" has decided to give to the best Jewish team ("drużyna") in Zagłębie.
Taking part in the conference were the representatives P. Barenblat and M. Felsner ("Hakoah"), M. Lancman [?] and Szywek [?] ("Maccabi"), and Sh. Rozenblum ("Kraft" Będzin).
To the question of several delegates, for what purpose the editorial board had taken the initiative upon itself, Mr. Lewkowicz explained on behalf of the editorial board that, in deciding to give a gift to a Jewish team, the editorial board had not the slightest intention [?] of bringing itself or the paper any material benefit whatsoever; the initiative was taken solely in order to abolish the feelings of enmity and to uproot the prevailing antagonism that has taken root in the ranks of the Jewish teams in Zagłębie, and in particular between the teams "Maccabi"—"Hakoah".
The explanation was received by the delegates with great satisfaction, and they welcomed the initiative of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", which strives to unite the Jewish teams into one great force that will represent them to the outside world.
After a short debate concerning the regulations, the proposal of Mr. Szymek was adopted that, since an error in the date had occurred in the first invitations, a second conference be called. For Sunday, 5 May, to which all the other teams in Zagłębie are also to be invited.
The conference will take place at 6 in the afternoon, and we ask all teams that receive invitations to delegate their representatives, who are to take part in the final decisions.
From Sport

[Sosnowiec and Dąbrowa — sport; football.] "Hakoah" 1—"Maccabi" 1 3:0 (1:0).
Maccabi won an undeserved victory over the technically better Hakoah in the friendly match played on Thursday, the 1st day of Passover, on the "Ruch" ground in Sosnowiec. The course of the game was even; though at moments "Hakoah" had the upper hand, "Hakoah" nevertheless did not manage to exploit very fine moments.
Already in the 3rd minute "Maccabi" (Lefik) shoots the first goal. The "Hakoah" attack begins, but without success. And the first half ends 1:0 for Maccabi.
In the second half Hakoah has more of the play and attacks the Maccabi goal continuously. But the "Pomac" [nickname, apparently the goalkeeper] and the Maccabi defence answer, beating off every ball. Still Maccabi manages in the 31st minute to shoot the second goal and immediately afterwards the 3rd goal. The rest of the time belongs entirely to Hakoah, but when Hakoah's attack comes up to the opponents' goal they cannot find their bearings, and so the result remains unchanged until the end of the game.
Best on the field: for Hakoah — Szywek, Gutman. For Maccabi — Lefik, Szmidt, Prachtowsz [?]. Referee Mr. Karzybucki — good.
Hakoah 2—Maccabi 2 1:0.

Strzemieszyce

[Strzemieszyce — taxes; accident; cooperative.] Strzemieszyce.
A victim of the excessive tax assessment.
The latest assessment of the turnover tax has put the local Jewish merchants in a desperate position. Turnover was raised by 40, 50 and in individual cases even by 600 per cent compared with last year. The tragic case of the manager and co-owner of the firm „J. Glikstein & Co.“ — Joel Glikstein — can serve as an illustration. For the year 1927 the said firm was assessed at 150 thousand zł., and for the year 1928[?] at two million zł., i.e. to pay 55 thousand zł. Mr Glikstein was hoping that the Main Commission would reduce the tax for him, but how astonished he was when on Tuesday, 23 April, right after receiving the „nakaz płatniczy“ [payment order], the Będzin[?] tax office sent out a bailiff, who placed a distraint on all the merchandise, giving as the reason „so that the firm should not liquidate the business and evade paying the tax“... While the merchandise was being distrained Mr Glikstein suffered a heart attack, and two days later he died.
The deceased was torn from the world in the bloom of life, at the age of 32, and leaves a wife and four children. The entire Jewish population, among whom the deceased was much beloved, took part in the funeral.
D. R—c.
