The orphans' home

(How is the construction going? On whom does it depend that the work be completed?)
For the first time — so we read last week in the newspaper — the children of the Jewish ochronka [children's home] in Będzin held the Passover seder by themselves, and they wished themselves that next year, a year from today, they would be masters of their own home and sit at their own tables in the great halls of the orphans' home that is now being built for their sake.
The children somehow remembered that something is being done for them; they evidently sensed instinctively that they are on the way to becoming free people, and by holding the seder they began to carry out the rehearsal...
Unfortunately there is still plenty of work before the building is roofed and before the structure is properly completed. True, it had been reckoned that at the present moment things would stand considerably further along than they do in reality. Nevertheless, that one has fallen behind is not so bad either, for the building committee still has enough good will and capacity for work to realize as quickly as possible the holy ideal which these people approached with so much sanctity and reverence.
And as we hear from the initiators, they are indeed setting to work immediately after the holiday; the finance commission is energetically starting a fund-raising campaign, which is to make it possible to finish the construction of the building as quickly as possible.
To complete the "orphans' home" one undoubtedly needs large enough sums of money, which in the present economic situation is not among the easy things. And it is all the less easy because the average Jewish citizen, the one who does not know all the various communal undertakings, does not know to whom one may entrust larger sums and to whom smaller ones, for whom small coins are handsome donations and which ones cannot make do even with larger sums.
For in recent years institutions and associations have begun to swim in from all sides; they have begun to multiply like fish in water, so that great public ideals have been exchanged for petty party shops, where everyone wants to bear the title of "president" and expects people to sing his praises, and one is to thank the other to the point of making himself ridiculous.
These very ceremonies have brought disharmony and demoralization into the public ranks, and the ordinary Jew [lit. "the Jew of the whole year"] no longer knows what is less and what is more important, whom one must trust and whom one must treat with disgust and scorn, which entrusted moneys are used properly so that the desired goal is achieved, and where one needs ancestral merit and connections... This very sinking to so low a level has degraded the prestige of society in general, and something of the trust once placed in an institution has been lost. The public no longer has the respect and reverence for public undertakings that it once had, before every minyan of people took it upon itself to supply us with party shops.
And therefore it is no easy thing to come and go and campaign for any institution whatsoever; it is hard to say that this or that institution deserves to be supported heart and soul, because it is not easy for the public to sort things out. Of course, for important institutions all this is a tremendous obstacle; the public cannot properly distinguish the need, or better said the necessity, of one institution as against another.
"Dobroczynność" [charity] now does great things; building a "children's home" for orphan children already counts as something grandiose, so that there is no need [lit. "it is not important"] to come to our Jews and tell them how necessary and useful such a building is for the poor, helpless orphan boys and girls, who will leave the damp cellar rooms where the sun never reaches and will find themselves in modern, elegantly built, hygienic halls. It will be an honour for Jewish Będzin when the building is fully completed, and when we merely look at the building we will think to ourselves: blessed be those who realized the plan, blessed be those who engaged in it and carried out the beautiful ideal.
On the building committee are the most respected people of the town, in whom everyone has the fullest trust — not only from today but for a number of years — and whose names give us the fullest guarantee not only that the idea will be properly realized but that every grosz will be spent on the needed purpose.
And if these people come to us and ask that we come to their aid in order to realize what was not long ago a fantasy, we must receive them with reverence and give the donation not as a donation but as a debt.
Let no one who is at all able to give forget that everyone is obliged to help build this beautiful building; everyone must lend a hand there, and all must help lay brick upon brick — only then will Jewish Będzin be sure that it has paid its debt to society.
On 17 June [czerwiec] it will be a year since the foundation was laid; let us come to the aid of the people who sacrifice their time and money, their patience and rest, so that by that day the building may be completed. Let the roof be covered by the anniversary, and that will give the building committee the courage to continue the beautiful and holy work.
Let us show them that we have passed the first examination.
R. Let [probably R. Les].
Short Feuilleton: To the High Windows

[Short feuilleton — satire.] The newspapers bring a strange sensation.
For the natural catastrophes, which have multiplied so much lately, none other than the press is to blame.
To me this is a tremendous novelty.
That the seventh kingdom [the press] is the strongest and that I am indeed the mighty king — that I have known for a long time. What do I mean, known? I see it with my own eyes, I touch it with my own hands!
Here, for example, I merely wrote that the measurements were taking as long as a Jewish woman measuring the "field" [the cemetery]: and the "urząd" [the office, authority] immediately took fright and soon redid everything as last year..
I merely hinted that it is not fair for the magistrate [city council] to be on bad terms with Yiddish; and at once they assigned 200 gulden to publish the magistrate's notices in Yiddish.
What more need I add here? Do you not know yourselves how esteemed and respected the press-man is [among][?] you all? When I walk in the street at night, I never meet a policeman; they have all scattered before me! If I walk by day with a speck of dust on my clothes, a fireman will at once jump up and wash the dust off with the "yatshke" [?]! Wherever I enter — the kehilla, the magistrate, or just a social gathering — people at once begin to whisper so quietly, with such respect, exactly as before a real emperor!
In short, no one doubts my unlimited rule in THIS world; but that I should have a say in the next world too, in the Kingdom of Heaven too — that I never expected!
And that's not all! It is I who bring the catastrophes — the earthquakes, the heavy rains, the hurricanes, the volcanic eruptions — all of it me!
Very well! Then I will now really take charge of the upper "pozhandkes" [?; probably Polish porządki — arrangements]. I will no longer guess [?] the weather ["pogodes", Polish pogoda] by the holy calendar, but rather prove in a leading article that tomorrow there must be fine weather, because my wife is going to Zakopane. I will command that instead of all the social catastrophes there come one catastrophe and clear the air once and for all. I will order that it rain from heaven not "błotes" [mud], but "złotes" [złotys].
And if I am not obeyed, I will "put them up on the page" [expose them in the paper].
Gabbaim and petty gabbaim, you may rest easy now! The seventh kingdom will no longer audit your cash-boxes nor poke with lanterns into your dark souls. It has more important matters now — it has reached the high windows.
Argus.
The Manchester of Zagłębie.

(Impressions from a visit to Zawiercie) — by Ben Amoz.
When the train pulls into the Zawiercie station, you stroll through the large, bright halls of the local railway station and set off along a good, asphalt-paved road planted with tall, full-grown trees, and a pleasant avenue for walkers — and you get the impression that you are in a well-ordered small town in Western Europe. But your delight does not last long. As soon as you approach the town and reach the first level crossing [przejazd], you are reminded of the small-town rich man who polishes his boots in front while the back part is covered in mud...
I got the same impression later, when my companion and I set out across Jewish Zawiercie to look over its communal and philanthropic institutions.
Our first visit was to the Gmina [the Jewish community board], which is, after all, "the highest authority in the little town". And to tell the truth, I had imagined it far worse. Knowing the kehilla muddle[?] in the Zagłębie towns, I was firmly convinced that the Jewish community in Zawiercie was surely even worse than a "house of the dead". But on crossing the threshold of the kehilla offices and seeing the closed window-doors that prevent one from catching a glimpse into the "Holy of Holies" room where "the chosen of the people" sit, I was reminded of the high-handed dozors [dozór — the community's supervisory board] of old, who held power firmly in their grip, and that the Zawiercie dozors are not yet as ___[?] as the dozors of Będzin or Sosnowiec...
Among the Zawiercie dozors the old "regime" still smoulders; not just offhandedly will one speak a few words with you — you must first pass an examination (through the secretary) as to who you are and the purpose of your visit; but simply walking into the Gmina and wishing to hold a conversation with a dozor without ceremonies — God forbid!..
— What does your activity consist of?
— We follow the old system, — I am answered. — The Jewish Gmina deals with all matters that fall within its competence. In winter several hundred children are clothed, we look after the Talmud Torah; here you see people coming and going — they come to pay for "kimcha [de-Pischa]"; without a slip from the Gmina the bakers do not sell any matzah; we have also seen to it that the price of matzah should not be a free-for-all — what can be done, is done.
Hearing this short report, a plan was born in my mind: it might perhaps be useful to make such an exchange — to pack the "democratic" Gminas of Będzin-Sosnowiec off to Zawiercie, and to engage the Zawiercie dozors here...
— How do you like the plan?..
———
Next door to the kehilla house is the "Talmud Torah". On entering the filthy premises where "the children of the poor, from whom Torah shall go forth" are found, I recalled the apt rendering of the late Rabbi of Będzin, the great Rabbi R' Yissachar Berish, of blessed memory, who rendered the words "How awesome is this place" as "how frightful this place looks".
In rooms whose walls bear witness that a painter's hand has not worked on them for many years sit two melamdim [teachers], with pale, gloomy faces, working in full for a wage of forty gulden [złoty] a week. The pay [lit. "pension"] is covered from two sources — 20 gulden a week is given by the Gmina, and the other 20 — by the town.
In each "class" some 40—50 souls mill about, wrapped in rags, from which peep out[?] emaciated faces, covered only by skin — these are the most unfortunate little Shloimes and Moishes, for whom the "fine" Jews, those who sit over the Torah, "care"...
— Does anyone take an interest in the institution?
— Who would take an interest in us? — The "Agudah" and the "Mizrachi" have their own "little shops", and especially now that the dispute over the rabbinate question has been liquidated — so whose worry is it that the Talmud Torah teachers go hungry and that the building too is in such a low state..
The answer was no news to me; the Talmud Torahs in Będzin and Sosnowiec are also almost on the same level...
———
From the "practical" kehilla institutions we go to the institution that holds a very honoured place among "the things that have no measure" — that is, the "Gemilut Chassadim" [interest-free loan] fund.
In a side lane, behind the town, an ordinary Jew ["a weekday Jew"], a certain Mr. Stopnicki[?], has built a small shul, and in this small shul the free-loan fund is located at the same time.
The shul, which is called "Ahavat Shalom", is a one-storey building, built in a stylish manner, and its outward appearance makes a good impression.
Inside, in the shul itself, there are three sections: the eastern wall, which is naturally occupied by the Holy Ark, the cantor's lectern, the "Shiviti" tablets and the like. On the north is the "women's gallery", which is divided off by a linen partition, a kind of "Spanish screen", and the western part is occupied from end to end by the entire apparatus of the fund and other matters that have rather to do with matter, pure materialism...
On the western wall hangs a large board on which are written in large letters the names of those who have undertaken to provide the "third meal" [shalosh seudos] in the course of the whole year 5689... i.e. from Sabbath of Parshat Bereshit to Ha'azinu.
After the "third meal" list hang several calendars of various firms, among them a calendar of the best playing-card firm...
The state of the fund is satisfactory. The number of monthly members [printed "chorsh-"] is growing, and even more the number of those in need of loans. In the short time the fund has existed it has made a name for itself in the whole town, and as soon as a Zawiercie Jew feels like boasting of something, he first of all mentions the "Gemilut Chessed" fund, the tender child wrapped in the lap of the tender mother "Ahavat Shalom"...
———
— What does national and communal life look like in your town?
— "Sadna de-ar'a chad hu" — my companion explains to me — "the whole world is one town"; with us in Zawiercie it is no better and also no worse than elsewhere. The parties are putting on a collective bluff, the older generation is sunk in day-to-day worries, sighing and groaning under the heavy, unbearable tax burden, and the youth — dances!
Only the girls look for a "purpose" in life, and they "find" it abroad... It is no longer the fashion to convert — what for? It is more "practical" "to make a life just so", and what will be later "is not grandma's worry"...
— True words. Everywhere one hears the same little song. Yes, "the whole world is one town"...
The Seduced Girl. (3)

[Literature — serial novel, instalment 3.] By Dr. A. Weisman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts).
For readers who have not read the beginning of this interesting Jewish novel we give the following exact [?] summary:
Mania, a young and very beautiful girl, the daughter of pious Jewish parents, runs away with her beloved Ludwig, the son of a Christian feldsher (barber-surgeon), on the night of Yom Kippur. On the way Mania tries several times to jump down from the britzka (carriage) and flee back to her parents, but the Christian Ludwig does not let her.
On Yom Kippur morning, when Mania's parents and the whole shtetl learn of the misfortune, darkness descends. Chana, Mania's mother, cries to her husband Reb Zelig to take a cart and drive off to search for Mania. The rabbi and the dayanim permit it, and Reb Zelig and his wife drive away amid terrible wailing from the whole shtetl.
The Jews of K. lived through a hard Yom Kippur. Everyone's heart was torn with pain. Only Madame Sherman, the rich lady of K., and her daughter Klara lived to see revenge on Mania, because she is a beauty — and Klara is not. Mrs. Sherman and her daughter stand in the synagogue courtyard and talk ironically about Mania's misfortune. Suddenly a cry is heard — water! Someone is fainting!
The men rushed to the women's synagogue, thinking that surely someone was fainting there.
Meanwhile a couple of young men were talking things over in front of the synagogue.
— So early still, and the women are already fainting from the fast!
— Well, what a people! If I were a rabbi I would forbid women to go to synagogue on Yom Kippur. Let them fast at home and not make a commotion in the synagogues every Yom Kippur. The greatest misfortune could come about through them.
— The whole world isn't enough for you — a young woman retorts — you even begrudge us praying in synagogue once a year.
— Who needs you here in synagogue? — the young man gets angry — only at home are you a useful thing!
— If today weren't Yom Kippur, I'd tell you something — the young woman answered, wagging her finger at him and smiling coquettishly as she did so.
When the fainted person was sprinkled with water, it was seen to be Aharon Weizman's son Chaim.
— Shame, Chaim — his acquaintances scolded him — you're a real woman after all, fainting from fasting right at the very start [?]!
Leaning on the two men who were leading him, Chaim could barely drag his feet, and with his blue, shining eyes he looked wearily at the crowd and murmured something quietly. At once Madame Sherman appeared with her Klara, both wringing their hands.
— Chaim! It's actually Chaim! Oh, how pale he is! Bring him in to my place — it's far to his home; he'll rest in my garden! — said Madame Sherman.
— How deathly pale he is! — cried Klara, and tears appeared in her eyes.
Madame Sherman and Klara, together with the men, held him up like some precious thing.
Various opinions were heard among the crowd.
— So what? A person isn't made of iron! Even a young man, and still he couldn't go on fasting — weak generations!
Two young women, praying in synagogue on Yom Kippur for the first time, whispered into each other's ears.
— What a pity for Chaim, the poor thing loved her so much.. I've known it for a long time.. for a long time, Basya!
— I heard — Basya whispered back into the first woman's ear — heard it from my Berish [?], my husband, who is an old friend of Chaim's, that Chaim wanted to become engaged to her one of these days, to Manyechka. I beg you, don't say a word about it to anyone; my husband asked me not to tell anyone, do you hear, Shprintzele?
— Oh, what a golden couple that would have been! — Shprintze murmured.
— Apparently not destined — such a misfortune! — Basya whispered.
Both women looked after Chaim as he was led away accompanied by Madame Sherman and her Klara.
— Just look how they tremble so over Chaim; maybe you know what kind of... relative Chaim is to them?
— May I know as little of a bad dream! Oy, what a world today! Oy — what a world!
The cantor was already singing. The women snatched up their machzorim and vanished into the synagogue among the women. The square became empty of people; everyone was in the synagogue, and in the street one heard only the singing of the cantors with the cries and prayers of the worshippers. — — — — — — —
Chapter Four.
Madame Sherman and Klara led Chaim up onto the veranda, which stands deep in the garden, enclosed by a high wooden fence. Here it was quiet and calm. Everything was secluded from the street, from the noise of the town and the bustle of people. In the very large garden, made up of trees and various plantings, stood the Shermans' one-storey house, steeped in greenery.
Chaim half lay in an armchair with a deathly pale face. Madame Sherman and Klara did not step away from him and gave him a glass of tea with wine; after Chaim had taken a couple of sips of the wine he came to. In a weak voice he slowly began to speak.
— Thank you for your kindness! — said Chaim. — I thought I would never get up again, I felt so unwell all of a sudden.
— What then? Are we to let you, in such a state, drag yourself in such a state [sic, repeated in print] home to the edge of town? We won't let you go from here until you have fully recovered. We'll prepare a room for you.
— I don't know how to thank you. Only, if I feel better, I'll ask you to take me home towards evening.
— Oh, no! That we won't allow. You lie here quietly. I must run to the synagogue. Rest, and you, Klarechka, don't step away from him for a minute until I come back from praying.
Klara remained alone on the veranda with Chaim. She sat beside him and looked at his blue eyes, which suited his pale face of today so beautifully. Her face showed so much kindness, devotion and love for Chaim that he noticed it and said to her:
— How good you are to me, Klara!
A happy ray shone on her face. In her dimmed eyes a happy little fire appeared. For the first time in her life she felt so happy. For the first time she found herself so close, so intimate with Chaim; now she felt his breath, she heard so close the beating of his heart, which was so dear to her. Without words she sat beside him; she devoured him with her eyes. He began to half doze; Klara wanted to hold her own breath so as not to disturb his rest, and she thought:
— Now perhaps I'll be able to draw him closer to me!
Klara had long known that Chaim loved Mania, and that he would not give her up for anyone. She knew that Mania was more beautiful, younger and with more virtues, which could please any young man — let alone Chaim — more than she could; but Mania was gone now, she had run away, and run away very disgracefully. It was unlikely she would come back, and even if she were found and brought home, she would no longer be the Mania of before whom everyone had loved so much.
— Mania is gone now — Klara thought — her beauty, all her virtues, I will replace for Chaim with my kindness and devotion to him. Chaim is mine, he will have to be mine, I won't give him away to anyone.
Chaim dozed and breathed lightly. Klara noticed a sweet smile begin to play on his pale lips.
— How handsome he is! How splendidly that sweet smile adorns his handsome face! He is dreaming of something beautiful, something happy!
Klara could not look her fill at his face. Unable to restrain herself and without giving herself any account of it, she did not herself notice how her body bent towards Chaim and gave him a light kiss on the forehead.
She drew back in fright. Chaim too started up and looked around, like someone who has only just lived through a dream.
— How do you feel, Chaim? — she asked.
— The sleep has refreshed me a little, but I wish I hadn't woken up; it was so good, I saw Mania, I talked with her and she was so good, so good to me.
Klara turned pale and could not utter a word.
— Oh, how sad she looked. I am suffering very much, Klara; her running away has killed me. When I learned of the misfortune I thought I would not survive it, that I would drop dead on the spot. I wanted to be so happy — and suddenly such a misfortune.
— One mustn't take it so much to heart, Chaim; one must be able to bear everything, one can't die after someone. It will pass; you must forget her, and if you can't, you will forget with time. You are still so young; Mania isn't worth your suffering so over her. If she had loved you, she would not have dared do such a thing.
(To be continued).
They Met

[Short story — a literary sketch ("A Picture").]
By Yitskhok Blum.

At a meeting, after many years, a former pupil and her one-time teacher happened to run into each other. It was not easy for them to recognise one another, so much had they both changed.
And once they had recognised each other, they looked at one another in astonishment. He, Mr. Finkel, could hardly believe that this was she, his former pupil, whom he remembered as a young, pretty girl of about eighteen — thin, pale, little developed both physically and mentally.
Now there stood before him a fully developed woman, beautiful and proud. Her spiritual elevation flashed from her wonderful woman's eyes, and in her whole bearing one could see the great progress she had made over time in every respect.
And she, Frida, could hardly imagine that this ageing man, whose hair was already almost entirely grey, was her former teacher, whom in her youth she had so idolised and so loved in secret.
And not she alone: almost all his pupils who studied with him at that time, she knows, were in love with him.
And how could one not fall in love with him then, when he, their teacher, was a handsome, wonderful man — and unmarried besides.
True, even then he was no longer so young, about thirty-five, but his looks, his clever eyes, his fine head of black curly hair, his intelligence, his ideal human traits captured the hearts of almost all his young pupils.
Frida looked up to him as a higher being, in whose teaching there was an idea, a deeper feeling, an ideal of life.
She was in love with him more than all his other pupils, perhaps because she thought she had less hope than all the others, since she was a simple working girl — true, with a great longing to learn, but with so little knowledge. How could she even think of letting him feel how strongly she was in love with him? She would never have dared.
So she buried her love in her heart, suffered in silence, and tormented and tortured herself in her love-ache...
Years have passed since then.
The hard luck that had pursued Frida as a girl left her. She married a young man whom she had known from her school years, who later qualified as a doctor [printed "raktar", misprint for "doktar"], and life was very good to her.
Only after her wedding did Frida begin to study anew, for she had more time, opportunities and means. She learned a great deal and in time became an educated woman, with knowledge and learning and with a fine [?] and lofty understanding of everything that makes life beautiful and sublime...
———
She stood and looked at her former teacher, who had changed so greatly, and did not know how to begin speaking to him; she waited for him to begin.
"How time changes... I hardly recognised you," he said at last, after a long while, looking at her in astonishment. "How long is it since you were my pupil? So young and childlike, and today..."
"And today already an old Jewish woman...," she remarked jokingly.
"Oh no, I mean the opposite..."
"Thank you. And how are you?" she asked with great courtesy and interest.
"Well... how should it go... one works and makes a living..."
The answer grated in Frida's ears and struck her heart... "One works and makes a living!" What sort of answer is that? she thought. That is the very same answer every simple worker gives. She still remembers that answer from her own working years as a girl.
And she had wanted so much to talk with her former, educated teacher now. Surely she would not have told him even now about her old feeling for him, but to talk with him about beautiful and lofty matters would have given her great happiness and joy.
And suddenly such an ordinary answer... "One works and makes a living"... as if his whole life now consisted of "making a living" and his mind were occupied with no other questions but the question of bread...
She did not know what else to talk to him about. She stood silently, thinking what had become of him, and wondering what had happened to him over the years that he had become such a materialist; what had happened in his life that had so changed both his appearance and his state of mind?
A middle-aged woman, not a pretty one, with an angry face, suddenly came up to him and said to him in an unfriendly tone:
"David, why have you stopped here to argue? It's late already. Time to go home!"
His face twitched like that of someone who feels a sudden pain, and casting a lost glance at his former pupil, without introducing her to his wife, he silently pressed her hand and, stooped, swaying a little, shuffled off at his wife's side...
Now Frida understood for herself...
And she gazed after him with regretful, pitying looks...

The Palestine Workers' Fund and the Histadrut / "Der Kooperator"

(On the occasion of Mr. Ben-Zvi's visit to Zagłębie.)
"Zionism cannot be realised in any other way than through the Jewish working class" — this very idea, which as recently as 23 years ago was regarded, both among the broad Jewish working masses and in general Zionist circles, as dangerous heresy (apikorsus), has finally been acknowledged by the entire organised working class of Eretz Israel. And not only in Eretz Israel. All the parties and non-party bodies that group themselves everywhere, in Europe as in America, around working Eretz Israel must acknowledge that without the working class and its self-activity the Jewish national home remains a mirage.
The first concrete practical result of this "credo" (ani maamin) was — the founding of an economic apparatus for workers' activity in Eretz Israel. Today, when we have in Eretz Israel a Workers' Bank with a founding capital of one hundred thousand pounds and a whole series of other constructive workers' cooperatives (Hamashbir, Solel Boneh, Nir, Kupat Holim, Va'adat HaTarbut), it is very hard to grasp what the founding of such a first institution meant in its time; but 19 years ago, in December 1909, when the representatives of the then one and only socialist union, "Poalei Zion", decided for the first time to found the Palestine Workers' Fund, it was an unheard-of novelty in the history of the Jewish workers' movement, one without any precedent whatsoever. The Palestine Workers' Fund expressed the unity of the will of the Jewish worker on a world scale — for the upbuilding of Eretz Israel.
A scant 6 years later, in Elul 5672, the Labour Bureau (Lishkat Avoda) was actually founded as an executive office to carry out all the work of the Fund.
The Pal. Work. Fund was already in its day intended to serve as a tool of work and of struggle in the hands of the entire Jewish working class in Eretz Israel, and also as a weapon in the hands of the worldwide Jewish workers' movement for Eretz Israel.
As long, however, as the Jewish working class of the country was not united and bound together in one class organisation, the connection between the P.A.F. (KPAI) and the country's working class was an indirect one. The programme and the forms of activity of the P.A.F. used to be decided at the conferences of the party that had created the Fund. The situation changed fundamentally, however, as soon as the Histadrut came into being.
Already 9 years ago, at the founding convention of the Histadrut in Haifa, declarations were made by Ahdut HaAvoda and by the board of the Pal. Work. Fund that they were ready to hand over to the Histadrut as such their place and their rights in the Fund. This proposal, however, required the consent of the Histadrut on the one side and of Poalei Zion abroad on the other. It therefore took a long time until a provisional modus was created. In the end, with the members' agreement, the decision was carried through that the property of the Palestine Workers' Fund should pass into the possession of the Histadrut and that the P.A.F. should be registered as a subsidiary company of Hevrat HaOvdim, like all other Histadrut institutions. The board of the KPAI (P.A.F.), however, is to be composed in such a way that, besides the Histadrut, all other parties and bodies connected with working Eretz Israel are also represented on it.
The P.A.F. is thus today the central initiative and investment fund of the Histadrut. It must serve as initiator and founder of new cooperatives, both industrial and agricultural. Here one may consider, for example, a series of projects for cooperatives that would process and preserve agricultural produce (for local consumption and for export), as well as projects for smaller cooperatives serving the local consumer. Many such urgent proposals, however, cannot be put into practice solely because of a lack of means. And not only that: most of the existing cooperatives cannot grow precisely for the same reason.
In order for the P.A.F. to be able to fulfil its role as initiator of new, and as a support for the old, already existing cooperative institutions, its means must be increased and a minimum of regular income must be secured for it.
Secondly, on the agenda are questions of longer-term investments for our larger and smaller enterprises, especially in the form of tools and work implements, huts and cabins for housing, means of transport, etc. (The "masn" [sic; probably "fund"] for tools must continue to remain a part of the Pal. Work. Fund.) But also in the form of money credit. The function of long-term credit, however, no bank can or may fulfil, according to its statutes. The Workers' Bank is no exception in this respect. Thirdly — easing the worker's life by founding workers' neighbourhoods and garden cities, workers' housing, water installations for workers' neighbourhoods, etc., which can be paid off only over many years. Fourthly — setting up workers' clubs and labour centres [in] all the most important centres of work, urban and rural, throughout the country.
I have not set myself the task here of actually exhausting the entire scope of the work programme. I only wanted to point out here some of its most important functions.
To what I have said I would like to add the following:
The last economic crisis was not the first in the new Yishuv. It was, however, the hardest, for 2 reasons: first, it dragged on longer than the previous crises, and second, we had no significant funds of our own with which to combat it or to mitigate it. Our purely constructive funds are adapted to their regular work and cannot fulfil the function of the P.A.F. In this respect the situation was worse even than in wartime. At that time the P.A.F. was the central economic aid institution in the hands of the workers; a united committee of all workers' parties and of the non-party agricultural and urban organisations had a certain say in its management, and the Fund carried out an important mission in the sense of constructive aid.
Many works were carried out by the P.A.F. during the war which served as the beginning of all of today's Histadrut institutions, such as the agricultural kvutzot of Upper Galilee; the roads at Zikhron and on the Carmel, the house-building in Haifa soon after the war, and the like. Had the P.A.F. had free means, it could, through its initiative and in many respects, have eased the crisis through constructive aid, and moved other, richer institutions to do so too. It is therefore the direct duty of all comrades and friends of the Jewish worker in Eretz Israel to strengthen the central financial institution of the Histadrut for aid and constructive work — the Palestine Workers' Fund (KPAI).

The magistrate takes over the hospital. Jakub Erlich vice-chairman of the city council

After a break of 6 weeks the city council held a session on Tuesday. The session, which took place for the first time in the magistrate's own building (the former „Piast“), was at moments interesting and rich in incidents. The walls of „Piast“ heard for the first time a declaration read out in Yiddish. The „pernutsine“[?] Endeks and the „BBs“ could not bear this and left the hall.
Before proceeding to the agenda the chairman, Mr. Fürstenberg, announced that there were no fewer than 12 urgent motions and interpellations to be considered, submitted by the magistrate, Dr. Rechtman and the PPS.
The magistrate's motion is that the city council should agree with the city administration that the county (powiat) hospital pass into the magistrate's charge. After a short debate the motion is adopted.
The urgent motions submitted by Dr. Rechtman and others concern: 1) the city administration should set up a municipal library; 2) the admission fee to the park on the „Góra Zamkowa“ should be reduced to a minimum; 3) because of the hard winter the communal taxes for the years 1924, 25 and 26 should be cancelled entirely, and for 1927 to the present the taxpayers should have the right to pay over 6 weeks without any penalty; 4) the statute of the municipal power station should be read out; and 5) the teachers of the evening courses should receive their pay („pensions“) regularly.
The 1st, 2nd and 5th motions are adopted; the 3rd motion is sent to the budget committee and the 4th motion is rejected.
Then declarations of all tendencies are read, except the merchants... On behalf of the Left Poale Zion faction councillor Rotenberg reads a sharp declaration in Polish and in Yiddish; the Endek and „BB“ councillors jump out of their skins („kelim“) and leave the session.
On behalf of the PPS club a declaration is read by secretary Laskowski, on behalf of the artisans — Lakhgik[?] Goldsztajn, on behalf of „Hitachdut“ — Dr. Rechtman, and on behalf of „Poalei Emunei Yisrael“ — councillor Herszel Erlich.
After that the first item on the agenda is considered: electing a vice-chairman. The PPS puts forward the candidacy of councillor Jakub Erlich.
The vote takes place, and with 13 votes Erlich is elected vice-chairman. 23 councillors were present at the vote.
At the session councillor Rotenberg turned to the city administration with the question regarding the fate of the market tax, which is being „plucked“.
The president (mayor) declared that at the moment he is not „prepared“ with any answer...

To the Jewish public in Sosnowiec
To the sad, notorious deeds of the "Jewish"[?] rag "Unzer Tog" ["Our Day"]
has been added another fact, which only proves what the "editors"
of "Unzer Tog" are capable of.
We, the undersigned, worked hard and bitterly under the worst conditions
in the printing shop, and never did we have the opportunity
to receive our wages. So that by the eve of Passover the editors
remained owing us a debt of 358 złoty. Seeing that we would not
get the money amicably, we went on strike.
Last Tuesday we came to the editorial office to demand our debt.
Because of this it came to an exchange of words between us and the "editor"
Zachariasz, who threw off his jacket and began
to beat us murderously. In revenge we ran and scattered the type. And
right away the incident[?] was reported[?] at the police station, where a few minutes
later the editors Kohn and Zachariasz arrived, and on the strength of
their accusations against us we were taken under arrest, from
where the next morning we were taken in chains to the examining
magistrate, who released us only at midday.
Let this fact that cries out to heaven speak for itself, and let the Jewish
public in Zagłębie learn who the publishers of the printed word are.
Let the Jewish public pass its just judgement!
Salomon Lancman, Moshe David Adlerflügel, Salomon Fridman.

Friday, 7 Iyar 5689 — „What's New in Zagłębie?“ — Piątek 17 maja 1929 [Friday, 17 May 1929].
Small traders protest against the high turnover tax.

In connection with this year's high assessment of the turnover tax, by which most small traders were badly wronged, the Sosnowiec Small Traders' Association held a protest meeting on Sunday at the „Hotel Polski“ on this painful question.
After speeches by chairman Moszkowski, Aliner and secretary Mr. Gancwajch[?], the following resolutions were adopted: 1) the meeting protests against the incorrect assessment of the turnover tax; 2) the appeals should, before being sent off to Kielce, be examined by the local „urząd“ [tax office]; and 3) 3rd- and 4th-category trade licences should be entirely exempted from the turnover tax.
—o—
Construction of the „Orphans' Home“ resumed.
On Wednesday evening, in the premises of the gmina [municipality] in Będzin, a meeting of the building committee and finance commission of the „Orphans' Home“ took place under the chairmanship of Mr. Fürstenberg.
After the reports given by engineer N. Weinzieher and Mrs. Z. Szein, it was decided that the building work should resume next Tuesday.
The meeting also adopted a protest against the Będzin kehilla leaders, who did not subsidise the „Orphans' Home“ in this year's budget.
Ben-Zvi in Będzin.

Yesterday morning the well-known Jewish labour leader Mr. Ben-Zvi arrived in Będzin from the Land of Israel.
In honour of the distinguished guest a festive academy [gala evening] was held yesterday evening at the „Nowości“.
On Saturday night after the Sabbath a banquet will be held in honour of the guest in the premises of „Haba“[?].
Ben-Zvi's visit has aroused great interest in Jewish workers' circles.

The Significance of the General National Exhibition in Poznań

By Dr. St. Wachowiak (President of the Exhibition Committee).
A whole literature has already been written about the economic and cultural significance of the great exhibitions that have been held abroad. The influence of these exhibitions on the development of the individual [?] states is enormous. It is enough to point to France as a typical example, which — one can say it without exaggeration — thanks to its marvellous exhibitions transformed Paris into the metropolis of the whole world.
In reawakened Poland the General National Exhibition is the first record undertaking in two respects: first, because the exhibition was built in a surprisingly short time, not even two full years; second, because the exhibition came into being with meagre means compared with its scale. That the exhibition truly answers our living economic and cultural needs, all of Poland has given the answer, by taking an active part in the exhibition and not sparing considerable sacrifices for it.
The General National Exhibition thus arose on the basis of a general national understanding for the cause. In the last ten years there have been very rare cases in which such an impressive consensus of all strata in all regions of Poland prevailed.
Our national character is inclined [printed "genoygt"] to outbursts, flare-ups, which vanish very quickly. We are less used to coordinated work. The General National Exhibition is like a herald that something is beginning to improve in this respect. The united front of the whole population morally helped the initiators of the exhibition a great deal to complete this greatest constructive work created in the last ten years of liberated Poland. The work is all the greater in that it was created at a time of economic depression, which reached its lowest point precisely when we finished our hard work.
The secret of this success is that we managed to maintain the good mood that arose right at the beginning, when we set about creating our great work.
This is not the place or the time to discuss the impressive organisation of the exhibition. But allow me to point out the consequences that the exhibition will leave for good [in] our national economy.
The economic aim of the exhibition was to raise domestic consumption and exports, to improve working methods and propaganda abroad.
The rich French and German literatures supply a series of instructive proofs that exhibitions had a decisive effect on domestic consumption. What this means we shall easily understand when we bear in mind that consumption in the various parts of the Republic is far from equal. It will suffice to compare the consumption of Upper Silesia with that of the Eastern Borderlands [Kresy]. Thanks to the exhibition, hundreds of thousands of Polish citizens will come from those parts of the country where consumption is meagre. There is no doubt whatsoever that the exhibition will serve as a desired [?] factor in this respect — all the more so when government circles and the self-governments, appreciating the importance of the exhibition, make every effort to organise excursions of all decisive circles, above all in the self-government economy. As for exports, until now foreign countries have had no opportunity to become acquainted with our export capabilities as at the present exhibition. In Poznań all of Polish industry, crafts and agriculture are now represented.
The exhibition will also do no little to help improve working methods. I shall point only to agriculture. A peasant from the Borderlands will be able to convince himself of the good effect of artificial fertiliser; he will look at agricultural machines he has never seen in his life. As for industry, already while the exhibition was being organised a certain movement of concentration was noticed: new associations were formed, people became acquainted with one another's achievements. This will naturally have the effect that the old boundaries that hampered the development of industry and trade will be removed.
What more need one say about propaganda? No field in Poland has been as neglected as propaganda. Foreign countries did not know us, and therefore they had no confidence in us. That is precisely why it was so hard to obtain foreign loans, which after all rest exclusively on confidence. Even before the exhibition was opened, it was talked about all over Europe; there is not a single language used in Europe in which the exhibition has not been written about. From all over Europe and from America a great number of visitors are preparing to come to us. Excursions to Poland are being organised on a very large scale. Such a thing is happening for the first time since Poland has existed.
I am convinced that the economic circles which made so many sacrifices for the General National Exhibition will feel the good effect of our great national exhibition in all their fields of endeavour.

Let the Union Be Formed

[Zagłębie — city councils; editorial.] (The budget question in municipal self-government.)
Several times already we have had occasion to speak about the economic affairs in Zagłębie, about the advantages and shortcomings brought about by our city councils.
There were times when, watching how our self-governments operate, one came to the conviction that 50% of the representatives are only now "practising", and that after they have gone through the practice they will understand how to set right what is bad; afterwards, the critic was sure, we would have well-trained representatives who would know how to create great, important and modern things that would bring benefit both to the city and to its inhabitants.
So people were sure, so every perceptive eye could grasp it, and so, roughly, one could figure out with one's reason what would be in the future.
But what do we see now? What do our representatives look like after going through the school? Have they become better or worse? Do they understand more or less? Are they more skilled, and do they know better how to manage the administration of the city's interests, or have they learned nothing at all?
It is hard, very hard, to give a correct answer to the questions posed, although many councillors have learned a great deal and find their way considerably better than before — and yet less good is achieved now than in the previous city council.
That is how it is in general among the councillors, and even more so among our brethren, the Children of Israel. With us it is unheard of. We are constantly busy tearing at each other, and each one only lies in wait to play tricks on the other and to trip him up.
Never mind when it concerns matters that concern us little — that can still somehow be tolerated; but as soon as it comes to questions that must interest us vitally, and then no understanding is reached, the moment is exploited neither in our favour nor for the sake of our honour.
We now face the municipal budgets in the city councils of Zagłębie, and at such a moment, at such an important occasion of taking up the discussion of budgets of millions, it is surely, surely not favourable for us; at such a time not to be united is surely, surely dangerous.
We must not forget that the budgets now run into the millions, and we know that the greater part of them is covered by Jewish money. So does any of the councillors give himself an account [printed "ביט", misprint for "גיט"] of how the budgets may turn out amid such chaos? Does any of our representatives reckon what consequences all this may bring for the Jewish population?
In the past we had a Jewish "koło" [caucus], where people would meet and decide how to act when this or that economic question concerned the Jewish population; and they went in unison, together, so that the unity itself commanded respect among non-Jews, and thus they had to reckon with it and indeed often also showed solidarity with the Jewish members.
Now there is no longer such a Jewish club; people do not meet, and on an important question one pulls this way and one that way; no one knows anything of decisiveness or unity — and in just such a state, in such chaos, they take up the budget question.
It goes without saying that the Christians — however divided they may be, however much they may want to spite one another — as soon as a question has any bearing on Jews, all factions will then unite and form a common front against the Jewish population.
Does anyone understand the damage that, for example, Jewish Będzin may suffer if the budget question is taken up under the prevailing conditions? Does anyone ever give it a thought?
Apparently now there is no longer any need for a Jewish union; it is no longer necessary to be united, to consider every question logically and to adopt decisions and a proper position. Our representatives no longer need to wear any bridle, because they themselves know how to act; apparently they know their way around on the spot and can determine their own position by themselves [doubtful reading].
So one might have thought, so one might have understood; but as soon as one watches how the sessions proceed, how each one only waits to catch the other out and trip him up, one must conclude that the situation in the city council is anything but brilliant, and those who do want to accomplish something can achieve very, very little amid such fragmentation, amid such chaos.
One must not forget, however, that the matter now is drawing up a budget that is covered by the urban population — and, of course, mostly or chiefly by the Jewish middle class, artisans and small traders. One must by no means approach it fragmented, with each acting according to his own opinion and his own understanding.
A unified union must now be formed among the Jewish councillors, who should approach the matter consciously, and each should know in advance what it is about and how he must vote.
With a budget one must not rely on God's counsel. Every councillor must approach it consciously, with a crystallised position, so that he knows how to defend and protect himself, if it is not to the benefit of his voters.
Enough fragmentation, enough of the sulking dance! One must turn to productive work that will bring benefit to the general population as a whole and to the Jewish one in particular.
Let people seriously begin to consider in what an unfavourable position the councillors find themselves, and how hard it is in such a situation to work for the benefit of the local economic interests, which may even bring harm to the Jewish population.
Selekt.

Salvation

[Feuilleton — a parable on the Jewish party struggles.] By Dr. M. Bodenheimer [Dr. Max Bodenheimer].
(Dedicated to the Jewish party struggles.)

At the door of a poor dwelling stood Salvation.
She had been sent by God to help and rescue three poor brothers, who lived in that dwelling in want and in misery.
The brothers came of an old, distinguished family. Their forefathers had had an estate of their own, fields and gardens, from which they drew an honourable livelihood. They loved the land, the mountains and the valleys and the rivers of their homeland. The air was full of the fragrant scents of wildflowers, violets and roses, citrons and oranges, almonds and balsam, and the eye delighted in the play of colours of the flower-covered hills, of the clear blue sky and of the great purple-hued sea. But all that had long since vanished; now their family lives, for as long as anyone remembers it, in a rented flat, now with this landlord, now with that one, and it must depend on the mercy of hard landlords. Whenever they did not pay the rent punctually, they were thrown out into the street, and with humiliations and pleadings they had to look for a new flat, for nobody would willingly let them in. And since the family was burdened with many children and they lived in cramped quarters, sickness and misery reigned among them, and they became an object of shame and mockery because of their miserable, broken appearance — a target for insults, slights and humiliations. Scarcely had they begun to acquire a bit of property through their diligence, through their industriousness, than the envy of their neighbours flared up, and even the landlords of the street begrudged it to them. They were afraid lest the paupers might in the end rise up, work their way to a house of their own and become established householders in the street. So they would curse and revile the foreign family and beat it. The old father finally died, and the three brothers remained living in a neglected flat. The eldest lived strictly according to the commandments of their forefathers; the second had already seen the world and had been through a great deal; the third was a poor one, living on fantasies, on ideals.
Not a day went by that they did not talk about happiness, about Salvation, which God must after all send them some day to raise them up and restore the splendour of their house. Each one of them claimed — God alone knows how often — that only on his account would Salvation come, that to him alone would their family owe the beautiful, shining future.
And just at the moment when they were again quarrelling among themselves about that very thing, they heard a very quiet and modest knock at the door. All three cried out at once: "Who is there?" And they heard a voice which, as with little silver bells and the tones of flutes, answered: "I am Salvation, open up for me!"
The eldest pushed his way to the door and spoke thus: "If this is indeed the true Salvation, then surely she comes on my account; therefore I must first of all look in my holy books to see whether all the signs are indeed fulfilled that this is Salvation, and whether this is indeed the day appointed by God for Salvation to come. You wait, for I am the eldest, I have kept, and I know, the laws and customs of our house. I am the most important of you — only I alone may open the door."
The second dashed from his place and said: "I am the one who must open the door. I have seen the world, served in rich houses, I know how to behave among educated people, I know the social manners, I know how to receive a high guest properly; from my employers I received a fine Sabbath garment, and I shall put it on now. You wait. And as for you," — he turned to the eldest — "it is no concern of yours at all, for you speak a corrupted, uneducated language."
The third, the youngest, placed himself before the two of them and spoke thus: "I am the one among you who called Salvation. I am the one who always carried in his heart the hope of Salvation. In that way I strengthened your courage, so that you would not run away from your worries — and indeed we stayed together and waited for Salvation. Day and night I dreamed of her; I paid no heed to what was going on around me, the good things of the world did not interest me, and always I thought about Salvation, who is to bring our family back to the home of our forefathers. If this is the true Salvation, she will speak the same language in which she spoke to our forefathers, when our family still lived in its home. So she will understand only me."
"And meanwhile, as the brothers were quarrelling so among themselves, Salvation quietly went away..
After the long quarrel, when they bethought themselves to ask whether Salvation was still there — there was no answer any more. Salvation had vanished.

Bankruptcies and Lawlessness (On the Founding of the Committee to Fight Malicious Bankruptcies)

[Będzin — economy and trade; opinion.] However good things may be in Poland, however fine the situation may look, however excellent the economic conditions may be — for whomever they are so, it is only for a certain contingent and by no means for the community as a whole, for the broad masses of the population. And if there are people of the middle class, of those whom we consider well-off, the conditions in which they live are very, very hard, so that more than one firm, when we [sic], of the better-situated, go under as soon as they are taxed more heavily for one year or have greater obligations than they could afford.
This in itself shows how "strong" our better-situated element is, the one that more than one person envies seven times a day — to say nothing of the not-well-situated, of the second category.
After all, we live today in enormously hard conditions; after all, the incomes [sic; perhaps "expenses" was meant] are so great and the obligations so heavy that one false step and one position that did not work out [?] can throw one off balance, and one can only rarely climb back up to the former level.
So easy is it in our times to slip and no longer be able to catch one's breath again.
After all, we no longer live in the old days, when every penny's expense was precisely weighed and measured; today one must know how to arrange one's life, how to make one's combinations, so that one can live and exist, remain standing on one's feet. To live in today's conditions means to study life, to acquire experience, to be shrewd and to know the tasks and the meaning of existence.
Be that as it may, we have great worries about tomorrow and grave cares about how to get through today. The steep decline, the heavy burdens that lie on almost every citizen, often make it impossible to secure one's existence for the future.
And when we hear today how big firms suspend payments, it is a self-evident thing; nobody is surprised, people know that everyone has great obligations, taxes, debts and unforeseen expenses, so that he could not, as the saying goes, get over — so he had to go under.
To go bankrupt is today one of the easiest things; it is also understandable, because if firm X or Y received protested bills of exchange instead of cover, it was swept along against its will by the current [printed: "geviser"], and the catastrophe happened.
Such bankruptcies are excusable, because one understands that they could happen and are quite often unavoidable.
But there is also a second kind of bankruptcy, a bankruptcy for which one prepares slowly, step by step, consciously; one takes up such a matter with deliberation and studies it closely, so that the business should run as well as possible and the combinations should succeed on as broad a scale as possible.
These reckless, speculative deeds too are called by no other name than bankruptcies.
We know that people go bankrupt, or better said take money, not because they were not paid, but because they want to get rich all at once; the business pays off for them, whatever may come of it and whatever may happen.
More than once one hears that Shmerl or Berl took goods on credit for so-and-so much, took them for himself and vanished to where the pepper grows; a second sent false bills of exchange out into the street to be discounted; a third went into a business with his bare thumb [i.e. empty-handed], risked nothing in cash — and what the end of such combinations is, is self-evident. One sees afterwards that no foundation for existing was ever laid in the first place; nobody reckoned on going a straight, normal way; nobody was after anything but taking and taking for as long as it would go.
One understands that a person can go bankrupt; one understands that a misfortune happens and the merchant gets caught with people [i.e. loses his money with debtors] or fails with a business and falls — these are understandable things, and to such people one must extend a hand and help them up.
But by no means may one compare those who come consciously and maliciously to take money and people's toil with those who go bankrupt out of need, because they, let us say, failed in one season.
And therefore the founding of the committee that has been formed at the Będzin "Merchants' Association" (Sokhrim-Fareyn) is to be welcomed; its task is not to allow the dangerous microbe to spread. The committee has taken upon itself the task of fighting malicious bankruptcies.
Certainly such recklessness must not be allowed in the Jewish street; certainly unheard-of swindles must not be allowed, swindles to which the reckless people have already grown accustomed as to perfectly kosher means; certainly one must fight against the unheard-of deeds that constantly poison the air in the Jewish street.
There must be a fight on the right and on the left to uproot the dangerous microbe that has only just burst into the world of commerce.
The investigation must be properly carried out in every case, so that not only the one who grabbed should be punished but even the one who gave, if it turns out that the latter gave only because someone came to take...
One struggles for existence, one struggles to be able to trade honestly, to earn and to remain standing on one's feet — and at such a moment simple speculators sneak in and want to get lucky all at once from other people's labour; to this one must respond with due severity.
One must help the honest merchant to remain standing on his feet in case of a catastrophe, and take revenge on those who come consciously to snatch other people's hard toil.
R. Les.
Deeds Worthy of Gratitude

(A visit to the girls' "ochronka" [children's home].)
By Ben Amotz.
...We children of the Jewish people are poor [? two unclear Hebrew words, "betsikhes uvikhsos"]. Only in one field are we "rich" — in the field of societies. There is no other people on the whole globe that possesses such a "wealth" of philanthropic institutions as we Jews.
We do not puzzle over which institution is more useful, deserves more sympathy and support. No, that is nobody's concern. The motto "Whoever stretches out a hand is given" we uphold firmly. Thanks to this, public-workers grow like mushrooms after rain; no sooner do a few "personages" get together for the public good, people who possess a certain measure of audacity, than they immediately found a society. Where the income will come from does not worry them; all one needs — they say — is donors, and donors, thank God, will not be lacking...
And societies are created, collectors come and the public pays... Not only the monthly dues, but every few weeks a fresh outcry [? "vayitsaki"]: Jews, to the rescue, the society is in danger...
From such squealing something does come into the till. In truth the society does need money, and a great deal of money, so that it suffices for collectors, for publishing newspapers — and what about [?] other expenses? Such as photographs, banquets, mi-sheberakh money and the like...
An exception in this field are the "orphan homes", the so-called "ochronkas". These modest institutions were created and exist to this day thanks to the Jewish intelligentsia, which took upon itself the task, like the assimilationists of former days, of creating productive [people] for the Jewish masses.
The "ochronkas" are run to this day by people who strive to create "something out of nothing", to bring the poorest, most neglected children up to the level of useful, accomplished people in society; and in the managements of the "orphan homes" we do not find the types of today's public-workers, so to speak [?], who push their way onto the "benches" for the sake of publicity, and a large part [of them] for their own benefit... but people who do not trumpet every Monday and Thursday, who work quietly and achieve a very great deal...
———
On the ground floor of the house at Kołłątaja 55 is the "ochronka" for girls. We paid our visit on the Sabbath, while the children were eating the Sabbath meal.
Scarcely have you crossed the threshold of the bright rooms of the ochronka, being greeted with a broad "Gut Shabbes", than you are already bound by a special affection to the institution.
In the first room, which serves as kitchen and dining room, about ten girls sit around a long table, many of them already on the way to a "goal": they have already gone through all the grades of the elementary school, learned a trade and become self-supporting...
In the second room — younger children, dressed in their Sabbath clothes, are eating lunch. Their outward appearance and physical development bear witness that the children, thank God, have an appetite, and nevertheless there are leftovers [?] too. On the table lie, "abashed", whole "untouched" challahs; apparently this "luxury" is no "novelty" for them...
After lunch. The children are sated; it becomes very joyful; one sings, the second recites, and the "programme" is concluded with "Zug o Prat" [Even or Odd], recited by a pupil of the "Yavne" school; she is not the one and only one at "Yavne". The very gifted girls of the "ochronka" study at "Yavne", where they make good progress in their studies.
Twelve-year-old Gutshe [?], a pupil in the first class at "Yavne", curtsies politely and tells you about the moment when Joseph's brothers came to Egypt and did not recognize their brother Joseph, who was by then already second to the king...
While the dark, charming [?] little girl from the "ochronka" tells the story, I think to myself that the same story is topical today too: if the rich ladies [?] of Będzin had known the abject state of these same 48 children back then, when they were taken into the institution, and came in today and saw how the once stunted children, candidates for parasites and tramps, have grown up on a par with decent people, brought up (let it stay between us — perhaps even better) like children of educated homes, they, like Joseph's brothers, would not recognize them...
Like a splendid thread runs the short report given by the faithful, devoted educator Miss [Frl.] Szarf, and once again the same truth is confirmed: talented children are to be sought only in the low alleys, among the poorest strata of the people.
Yes, one has to see it: it is very interesting to leaf through the school exercise books and see the children's abilities, to look at their own embroidery. "What more do you want?" — the educator says to me — "if some lady, of the intelligentsia of course, wants to decorate her salon with a magnificent piece of handwork, she orders it from the 'ochronka' girls..."
— Does anyone visit the institution?
— No, I get the answer; apart from the "opiekunki" [patronesses] of the "Dobroczynność" [charity society], nobody of the town's "notables" comes to us. Whom do such "trifles" interest — how orphan girls are brought up?...
— Truly so: who indeed bears such "trifles" in mind? Above all, they, our ladies, have no time to occupy themselves with such matters, for in winter it is cold, after all, and in summer one must enjoy the fresh air; and then, where are the toilettes, and other similarly important matters?...
— My thoughts are suddenly interrupted by a little girl with big, diamond-bright eyes, who asks me:
— "When will the building for the 'orphan house' be finished already? Oh, I so don't want to go home to sleep"...
— Don't worry, little lamb — I began to comfort the child — it won't take long now. The Jews of Będzin are blessed with a good trait: interest they have in nothing at all, but when someone cries out:
— Reb Yid, give money! — they don't think long and count it out...
— Good Shabbes, dear children! See you soon in the new building...
— Would that it were so! Would that it were so! — rang out the little children's voices...

The Misled Girl (4)

[Serialized novel — Jewish life, conversion; "The Misled Girl", installment 4.]
Dr. A. Weissman.

(A novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts.)

"Mania is not guilty, Klara. Everyone accuses her, everyone curses her, because nobody knew her. She is not the only one who falls into such a misfortune. Hundreds of Jewish daughters fall into their hands, each for a different reason; very few are themselves to blame for their misfortune. But I will not rest until I have rescued her from their hands — if only I regain my strength. I will demand nothing of her; I only want to rescue her from their hands, into which she has fallen."

"Her parents have already gone to look for her; perhaps they will find her."

"Unhappy parents! What will they be able to do, even once they know where she is? It is hard to tear out of their hands the unhappy victims whom they rob from us with fine and pious little speeches!"

Wearily he let his head sink onto the back of his chair [?] and stopped talking.

Quietly, without words, the two of them sat on the veranda. Night began to fall. The last rays of the setting sun played on the leaves of the trees. The shadows grew and took up more and more space.

Little by little the women began to leave the synagogues; the men were already at the end of the evening prayer. Another minute or two, and the number of people coming out of the synagogues grew and grew. The men stopped by the synagogue and sanctified the new moon, which strolled proudly across the clear sky. It looked as if it had been waiting here by the synagogue a long time for the Jews to finish praying Maariv and come out to sanctify it.

Tired from fasting, the crowd walked slowly home from the synagogue through the shtetl and dispersed into various lanes. From some distant monastery, in the quiet, bright night, various tones of the monastery bells rang out over the shtetl; the crowd shuddered, remembering what they had lived through that day, having seen how Reb Zelig Sore's and his wife had driven off after their daughter to look for her.

Involuntarily the crowd looked toward the side from which the monastery ringing could be heard. Far away, somewhere out of a [?] village, they saw the spires, gleaming proudly golden in the bright night.

"Who knows, maybe Reb Zelig's daughter is in that monastery!" someone called out. "Maybe they are converting her right now.."

At that the crowd trembled with fear.

"Maybe the apostate herself is ringing the bells," an old Jewish woman called out, "because, as they say, it has been the custom for many years that when a Jewish child is converted, the apostate, man or woman, must first ring the bells of impurity for a whole month."

"Grandma, I'm afraid!" called out a small child who was walking with the old Jewish woman.

"Don't be afraid, my child! God will protect us."

"Grandma," the child asked, trembling, "is hell burning now?"

"For her, for the apostate, all the hells are burning now. Us, together with all Israel, God, blessed be He, will guard and save."

The child held on tighter to the grandmother, who was walking home together with the whole crowd.

The monastery bells did not stop ringing out in the air. From their echoes, on that night, a dread fell upon the whole shtetl. — — — —

Chapter Five.

In the night, when in the shtetl K. the Jews, after the great fast, sat in their houses at laid tables, eating and drinking and each telling in a different version about the terrible misfortune that had befallen Reb Zelig Sore's, who had driven off that day with his wife to rescue their child from conversion — on that same night, in the little village named after the local stream "Zastavke" [Zastawka?], where Reb Zelig Sore's family lives, the old Jewish woman Dvoyre, Reb Zelig's old mother, sat all alone at a laid table, looking at the "kapores" that had been prepared and cooked since yesterday:

The village of Zastavke lies only one mile from the shtetl K. — the same stream that runs through the village also runs by the shtetl.

"Zastavke" is a narrow stream that winds from somewhere far away. Here, by the village, it spreads out wider and digs deeper. At this spot stands an old water mill, which from many years back belonged to Reb Zelig Sore's father, Dvoyre's husband, Reb Yitskhok Hersh Sore's.

The mill is a small, old, [neglected?] building with a large wheel which the water drives slowly; before Passover, when the water rises, the wheel turns faster, more lively, and the whole old mill takes on a somewhat youthful look and fresh strength. Next to the mill, on a small hill, stands an old house with several small windows, where Reb Zelig has lived with his family for many years.

When everyone left yesterday for the shtetl to pray, they left behind Mania and the old gentile from the mill, whom they had told to keep an eye on the house.

Having learned of her misfortune later than everyone, Dvoyre drove home right after the fast, thinking that perhaps they, her son and daughter-in-law, had already arrived.

But she found no one except the old gentile from the mill, who, as on every night after Yom Kippur when his masters came home from synagogue, had taken out the cold kapores, set them down on the table and put up the samovar.

Old Dvoyre sat and looked sadly at the kapores.

Three white hens and one white rooster she had hatched herself and fed the whole summer. By day she fed them from her own hands, and every evening she let them into the chamber to sleep. The whitest and prettiest hen, without a single black feather, she picked out and said:

"This will be a kapore for Manyechke on the eve of Yom Kippur!"

And now the cooked kapores lie before her eyes on the table, and there is no one to eat them all day.

Dvoyre listened to every rustle, to every creak of the door — maybe someone is coming — but [printed "amer"] nobody came.

"If only Khayim would come! Why doesn't he come? Everyone, everyone has abandoned us!"

She could not sit still in the house. She went out in front of the house, sat down on a log and gazed into the distance; from all the roads and paths leading to the house it seemed to her that Manyechke was coming, Manyechke was speaking. There, she hears her sweet voice. But no. It is only the running stream speaking, quietly and sadly...

Suddenly her eyes stopped on a large house that stood on a hill on the far bank of the stream. The house now looked out from among the trees with lit-up windows.

"Surely guests have gathered there. Once again a birthday, a party, a celebration at their place," Dvoyre muttered. "Gentiles remain gentiles; what else should they do but rejoice and carouse? What do they lack in the world?"

Dvoyre sighed.

"They begrudged us such a precious diamond, and snatched her from us, tore her away. Woe, [?] woe!"

She could no longer look at the house from afar.

"Oh, if I were younger, if I could run, I would run, I would drive. I would turn the whole world upside down and rescue my child!"

Dvoyre went back into the house, but she could not sit still. Every moment it seemed to her that someone was driving up by the window. Several times she went out, but she saw no one.

Suddenly she heard the familiar heavy steps of the old gentile who works in the mill.

"What is it?" she asked. "Has someone arrived?"

"No, only a letter that someone gave me for you."

With trembling hands she tore open the letter and read the terrible words, in Yiddish, in [her?] own hand.

"My dear ones! Save me! I am in a locked room, but where — I don't know. I am a little to blame myself for my great misfortune, but save me. I ran away from you through the 'wild forest', through the shtetl Ts., and further on I don't know. Your Manyechke."
