Everything in the World Speaks

[Feuilleton — parable and essay.]
In my cheder years I greatly envied King Solomon on account of one thing. I begrudged him neither his kingdom, nor his wondrously beautiful palace, nor all the costly foods and drinks he ate and drank, nor — to make the distinction — the thousand wives he possessed.
My envy concerned only his knowledge of many languages. I longed to know thoroughly, as he did, the language of birds, the language of leaves, the wooden and stone languages, the tongues of fire and water, of mites, of ants and of all other kinds of little creeping things.
I began my first studies with stones. In our shtetl there were very many of them, and they were very conspicuous — and they landed on the heads of the shtetl Jews... Gentiles they did not love: when a Jew would sometimes throw a stone at an enemy of Israel, the stone would bounce away a verst from its target... But every time a gentile threw a stone at a Jew, even offhandedly, that hard "inanimate object" would hit precisely and split his skull. Such lovers of Israel were the stones of our shtetl...
So I took a stone that was stained with Jewish blood and argued it out with it: "Just tell me, you hard murderer," I asked it in a stern tone, "why does your kind bear such hatred for us Jews? By rights, it seems, you ought to have stood by the 'children of Israel' as firm as steel and iron, since the Torah did take pity on you and forbade lifting a hammer or a sword upon you when building an altar"?
The stone did not reflect for a minute and at once gave me the following answer:
— Your question, son of man, is a foolish one. You suspect the innocent when you think that we stones have something against Jews in our hearts. Stones have no heart at all, the way you humans do, and therefore they are not capable of "pleasure" [?] or hatred... We are nothing more than blind messengers of nature, and nature evidently willed it so: that wherever a stone is thrown, it should fall on Jews...
My naive childish reason told me then that I was already done with the stones, that I already understood their language and knew their nature, and I set about the plant world. I took my life in my hands and stole into the garden of a poor peasant. There grew various kinds of flowers whose names I had not the faintest idea of. But they were all so charming, so enchantingly beautiful — yet they paid me no attention at all. They were amusing themselves [?] with the golden sunbeams that caressed them, and probably paying them sweet compliments...
I went up to a young blossom that was still lying in its bud-cradles and greeted it tenderly. But — not a sound, not a response; it does not answer. I go on, and see: on an old, aged flower, already wilted in places, there stands a big bee, buzzing murderously and sucking its flower-blood. I grab and chase away the bloodsucker and rescue the innocent one from its poison. Then I heard a voice, a voice of fragrance, a rarely delicious voice of aromas that resounded into my nostrils... and the voice was accompanied by the following words: "First of all I thank you, unknown but noble son of man, for saving me from certain death. Although, to tell the truth, we flowers don't much care about living anyway [?]: death always hovers over our heads, every minute we expect to be plucked, and that is a terrible feeling. The constant fear of death is worse than death itself. Our misfortune lies in being too delicate and too beautiful. Your humans are in love with us, and so they tear us out before our time. A strange love your two-legged ones have: it uproots its beloved... Yes, a great part of your kind are vile hypocrites: they do us all sorts of wickedness and still consider themselves friends of humanity."
I lowered my head in shame and quietly slipped out of the garden. I did not want to hear any more of the disgrace of my kind, and I already regretted the whole business. I will gain no honour [?], I thought, from holding conversations with the creatures of the non-human worlds. And from then on I stopped envying King Solomon.
Years went by. All that time I was a prosaic, practical man, who hated every form of mysticism — only the "revealed"; only things that were open and manifest to all interested me. But lately the old inclination toward the "hidden" has awakened in me, because the present-day "revealed" is not at all pleasant [?]; one can do nothing with it. Here we had thought, for example, that we Jews could, in today's modern times, make do with natural means to bring about our redemption — yet it begins to look as though without miracles altogether it really will not work... For we cannot build on the justice of man and on the liberalism of nations. I began to believe that there is more justice and also more intelligence in stones, in plants and in every living creature than in the one who proclaimed himself the topmost rung [?] of creation.
So once I was sitting by the seashore, sunk in a dreadful melancholy, gazing with mute looks at the mighty king of waters. Right up to my feet swam a little wave, and it spoke to me thus:
"You wonder why we, the waters, do not speak to you humans. If so, you are mistaken. We speak to you constantly. But you are never quiet enough to be able to hear our words. Not only we, but everything there is in the world has a language and speaks. There are only individuals, a chosen few of your kind, who understand the rustling of the wind, the notes of birdsong, the voice of water, the script of the clouds and the colour-ideas of flowers.
"Perhaps you wonder why you cannot grasp and attain the conversation of birds as the heroes of the legend did, and perhaps you doubt altogether whether in the crow of a rooster, in the miaowing of a cat and in the bellowing of an ox there is any sense and content. All this comes from your not grasping how far up or how far down ideas can reach. There are, for example, some sounds that are too high and some that are too low for the human ear to be able to catch them.
"There are also many colours besides white and black and green and yellow, etc., that are too delicate for the human eye, and it cannot distinguish them. It is the same with thoughts, or with the perceptions of the soul. There are great worlds of ideas that are too simple for you to catch, and there are other, infinitely great worlds of ideas that are too lofty for you to comprehend.
"And not only are the lofty ideas of the upper worlds higher than your highest ideas, but many ideas of the lowest worlds, too, are weightier and contain more meaning than the highest thoughts you boast of so much.
"Bow your head, O man, before all the beings and creatures found on our planet! You understand no more than we do, and you are no greater favourite of Divine Providence, for we do not go against her will. We do not stray from the direction she marked out for us from the six days of Creation on, whereas you rebel against her — she gave you [?] the way of humans, and you walk in the way of beasts."
Such a lofty sermon the little wave delivered to me in a single breath — and then it melted away into the water...
Ploni ve-Kohen.
In what light Zagłębie is seen through the eyes of foreign visitors

I.
The editor of the "Lodzer Togblat", Mr. Israel Kahan, who a few weeks ago paid a visit to Zagłębie and Upper Silesia, conveys the following impressions, which we consider it important to acquaint our readers with, although in certain details they are painted with a great deal of light and and also shadow... Ed.
Smelters and pits.. chimneys and smoke..
Kilometres long they stretch here, the mighty workshops below and above the earth. The scrawny, sooty factory chimneys rise up uncannily and spread [?] over God's little world, spitting black smoke upon people and land, which veils the bright radiance and gives the whole region such a strange colouring...
That is the first impression of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia — the most important industrial district of Poland, one of the most splendid and richest industrial districts in the world.
The coal and iron basin is a kingdom unto itself, a kingdom of feverish labour, an underground one, hidden from the stranger's eye. Hundreds of thousands of human lives are risked here every moment in extracting nature's inexhaustible treasures from the bowels of Mother Earth.
At every step one runs into problems here — underground and above ground; questions of a social character and of the forces of nature become entangled with the burning issues of economic life and the struggle of nationalities, and everything flows together and carries the observer off into a new, unknown sphere, shaken by foreseen and unforeseen explosions, underground floods, catastrophes.
It is a world unto itself. A restless, feverishly working, fascinating world.
But for the time being this underground world does not interest me. I want to become acquainted with what goes on above these hidden hells — with the creating and doing, with the trade and traffic, with the hubbub and commotion around the coal pits, the iron and zinc smelters with their choking smoke and poisonous gas, which has become the most delicious perfume, luring, tempting and drawing hither the unfortunate, livelihood-less Polish Jew...
———
My first visit was to Będzin. An old town of lineage, with a past that reaches back a full thousand years.
One cannot say that the people of Będzin pride themselves on this lineage. It is true that a great many Będzin inhabitants [printed "Bendiger"] do not even know of their honourable past. This is, as they say, "a little America", and apparently one values personal merit more than ancestry.
I took a walk to the greatest sight of old Będzin, to the ruins of the historic royal castle on the hill beside the river "Czarna Przemsza". A castle and remnants of a very old fortress, said to date back to the years 1001—1020. My companion was a local journalist. But however hard I tried to find things out, he was extremely sparing in his explanations.
I also spoke with several Będzin "obywatele" [citizens], one-hundred-percent Poles. They too were scarcely informed about Będzin's pedigree. Only at the Jewish vice-president of the town were some riddles solved for me.
It is astonishing how little understanding there is in Poland for antiquities. In another country such a historic corner as the castle ruin with its fortress ramparts, which are still living witnesses of the Swedish invasion in the 12th century [sic] and of the uprising battles of 1863, would have been guarded like a relic. With us, however, it was forgotten and neglected, and only the "Jewish magistrate" took care to lay out a decent "square" there. It preserved the ruins and saved the stone remnants of the castle from complete disintegration.
———
Będzin, with its old lineage, which bears the name of the armour-bearer of the Polish king Bolesław Chrobry (Będa), has a glorious, stormy past behind it. Many historic battles were fought out here; here the Polish king Jan Sobieski III had his headquarters, and here the attacks of the "Ślązaks" [Silesians] with their predatory ambitions were repulsed.
But later Będzin became a forsaken backwater [?]. Only the influx [?] (the enemies of Israel call it an "invasion") of the Jews pulled the town, richly blessed by nature, out of the "higer-plet" [?], raised it to a new life and made it the liveliest commercial centre of the whole region. Today Będzin is the most Jewish town of Zagłębie. One can say — a Jewish town, Jewish through and through. Up to 75 percent of the population (about 70 thousand) are Jews. Commerce and manufacturing are mainly Jewish, the chairman of the town council is a Jew (the great industrialist Mr. S. Fürstenberg), and a president the Jews of Będzin also have who is Jewish — that is the vice-president of the town, Mr. L. Rubinlicht; even the only newspaper (a weekly) appearing in Będzin is a Jewish one.
I spent more than an hour in the office of the Jewish vice-president of Będzin. Various senior officials of the magistrate came in during our conversation to settle current matters, and all of them addressed Mr. Rubinlicht as "Panie Prezydencie" [Mr. President]. Respect and esteem could be felt in that attitude. He has considerable merits for the town and truly deserves this regard. For 12 years Vice-President Rubinlicht, a merchant by profession and a Zionist by conviction, has been active in the field of municipal self-government. Formerly he was chairman of the town council; now he is vice-president, already in his second term.
The municipal economy has risen greatly during the period of his rule, and the public-utility institutions have grown to such a degree that they also bring the town a great deal of income.
Because of his high office President Rubinlicht has greatly neglected his private business. But he has the satisfaction that the Jewish population is now treated by the magistrate as an element with equal rights. The Będzin Jewish gymnasium "Yavne" enjoys an annual municipal subsidy amounting to 5000 zł.; the Jewish orphanages are fully maintained by the town (last year the subsidy reached 30 thousand zł.); the same goes for the old-age home, the Jewish maternity clinic, the free-loan (gmilus-khesed) fund, etc. Even the "Yiddish Scientific Institute" [YIVO] in Vilna receives support from the Będzin magistrate. True, not a large one — altogether a few hundred zł. — but it was a matter of principle. And when the local magistrate arranged two [summer] colonies for needy schoolchildren, 50 thousand zł. were earmarked specifically for a colony for Jewish children with a kosher kitchen.
With us in Poland all these are exceptions, gratifying exceptions. Especially the subsidy for the Jewish gymnasium — let it be recorded.
* * *
Nevertheless it had to take more than ten years, even in this "Jewish town", before the municipal parliament dared to bring itself to a resolution that all official announcements which the magistrate issues to the population should appear, besides in Polish, also in Yiddish...
When I was in Będzin a real war was going on over this. The Endeks and the "Sanacja" made every effort so that it should not come to such a "desecration of Polishness" — the Sanacja had its own motives in this, since the Jews had not formed a bloc with it during the town-council elections — but this opposition was powerless. The resolution later went through by a majority of votes... After all — a Jewish town!

What's Happening in Zagłębie? — Będzin: Stormy debate at the 2nd reading of the budget. "Jews are spies!" shouts a councillor of the "BB"

[—] Thursday[?], and this Tuesday and Wednesday, the town council of Będzin, chaired by Mr. Fürstenberg, considered in the second reading the important budget expenditures for the year 1929/30.
Interesting and amusing was Thursday's session; the councillors did not stint on humorous material for the gallery. Hardly had one councillor come out with some proposal than others did the same, which led[?] to many moments of self-[—].
Under the item scholarships for students, a proposal by Dr. Rechtman is adopted that the sum be raised to 2 thousand zł., to be divided as follows: a thousand zł. for Jewish students and a thousand for the non-Jewish[?] "Koło" [student association] in Zagłębie.
Under the item culture and art, councillor Kleinman puts[?] a proposal to allot a sum of 1500 zł. to the People's University at the Artisans' Association.
Immediately afterwards alderman (ławnik) Żebrowski proposes that such a subsidy also be allotted to the Christian artisans.
Almost all the clubs [council factions] do the same, demanding subsidies for their libraries (even ones that do not exist)...
———
At Monday's session the first item was: care for school children[?]. Dr. Rechtman protests against the budget committee, which struck out the sum of 2,70[—] zł. for a dental clinic, and he demands that the sum be increased to 6 thousand zł., so that school youth may have the possibility of receiving dental care.
After a short discussion the proposal is adopted.
Councillor Mrs. Ratner proposes that the item for supporting poor women in childbirth be raised by 3 thousand zł., so that the new mothers can stay in the hospitals at least 10 days.
The proposal is adopted.
The item for feeding school children is raised, on Dr. Rechtman's proposal, to 11 thousand zł.
Before considering the item social welfare, President [mayor] Michał[?] gives a short exposé, in which he points out that a sum of 411 thousand zł. has been provisionally set in the budget for social welfare.
At the item sending children to summer camps, councillor Feiner draws attention that this year the system of favouritism must not be repeated, and that the children who need it should be sent to the summer camps.
A surprise for the "Agudah" councillors was the proposal of Mrs. Ratner that for the Jewish children sent by the municipality (Magistrat) to Busko for a cure, care be taken that they have kosher food, because every year the children eat treyf food..
To this the municipal administration declared that on this question they must come to an understanding with the municipalities of other towns in order to obtain together a ritual (kosher) kitchen...
With this the session ended at half past twelve at night.
———
Wednesday's session was a stormy one. Here once again the axiom was confirmed that when it concerns a matter connected with Jews, they come out against them from the extreme left to the extreme right. The antisemitic agitation was caused by the innocent and just proposal of Mrs. Ratner, who demanded that the Jewish orphans supported by the municipality be subsidised with equal rights[?], i.e. that for the Jewish orphans too the municipality pay 70 zł. a month instead of 30..
The first to come out in the "agitation" with antisemitic "flowerlets" was alderman Hetmańczyk, the "comrade" of the right P.Z.[?]. But the antisemitic "record" was beaten by councillor Gac[?], of "Eig-sl"[?]; he used such arguments as that the Jews have no merits toward Poland, but are only spies..
At these words a great uproar arose among the Jewish councillors, and after the sharp protests of Dr. Rechtman, who demanded that Gac be excluded for 3 sessions, of Mrs. Ratner and of M. Lewin, the Jewish councillors (except the Left P.Z.) left the session in protest.
Unheard-of scandal at the "Hanukkat ha-Bayit" celebration of "Ahavat Chesed". Cantor Żupowicz insulted in a base manner

[—] On Sunday evening there took place a 16th-anniversary jubilee celebration and at the same time a "Hanukkat ha-Bayit" (house-warming) of the premises of the "Neu"[?], "Ahavat Chesed".
At this celebration the town cantor, Mr. Żupowicz[?], who had been invited by the institution's board to lead the evening (Maariv) prayer, was insulted in a disgraceful manner.
The scandal was caused by the following reasons:
At the head of the institution stands the well-known "town president", who wants on every occasion to display his rule... When the board of "Ahavat Chesed" decided to invite cantor Żupowicz, the president, who is [—] a member of the kehilla board[?], took upon himself the mission [of seeing that] the gmina [community] should commission[?] the cantor to pray on Sabbath at "Ahavat Chesed".
The cantor fulfilled his mission and [—][?] was there on Sabbath and prayed Musaf at "Ahavat Chesed". The official celebration took place on Sunday, and in order that the celebration be an elevated one, the board of "Ahavat Chesed" decided that the cantor should pray Maariv with the synagogue choir.
The above-mentioned president, knowing that he himself had also agreed to dismiss Mr. Kalmus as choir conductor, worked hard throughout Sunday so that the choir would sing along as well. To this end he intervened several times with the kehilla president, and also sent messengers to the cantor [saying] that "he takes the responsibility upon himself", as long as the cantor would pray together with the choir.
But the cantor declared categorically that as long as he did not have the consent of the kehilla president, Mr. Prawer, he would not pray.
The "pisiner"[?] president, however, wishing to show his authority, casually engaged the conductor with the choir, and informed the cantor that "the choir will not be there".
When the cantor came up on Sunday evening for Maariv and found the conductor with the choir, he again declared that he would not pray with the choir, because so the president of the kehilla instructs him.
Then the president turned to the conductor and choir that they should leave the premises, and the cantor began to prepare for the prayer.
But just as he wanted to begin, the president's "Walanens"[?], the she-eino-yodea ("one who does not know") type, Jaskierowicz, sprang at him and showered the cantor with the most disgraceful insults.
As a result of the disgraceful abuse Mr. Żupowicz turned to the president asking what he should do, and received the answer: go home...
The cantor took off his tallit and left in great humiliation..
Maariv was then prayed immediately afterwards by the conductor with the choir...
———
From a "neutral" source we are informed as follows:
The hatred toward the cantor began as soon as a delegation of "Ahavat Chesed" approached him and invited him to pray on Sabbath and on Sunday — Maariv.
The delegation left dissatisfied, because the cantor's wife set such conditions as could not be accepted, and in general the delegation was not received properly. The cantor also performed the Sabbath prayers hastily... and because of this the board of "Ahavat Chesed" decided that, so that the celebration should be complete, the cantor should pray with the choir.
— We refrain for the time being from expressing our position on the substance of the matter, but the attack on a prayer leader (shaliach tzibbur) in public we brand as a base deed.
Killed by lightning

On Saturday afternoon, for a short hour, a torrential downpour fell, accompanied by strong lightning and thunder. One bolt of lightning struck a 54-year-old Christian woman who was grazing goats in Gzichów, and killed her.
“Don’t Climb Where You Needn’t”..

On Sunday two young Christians made a bet that whoever climbed up onto the “szczyt” [top] of the castle on the “Góra Zamkowa” [Castle Hill] would get a present and a bottle of brandy.
One of them decided to take the step and began to climb, but when already near the “szczyt” he fell down and broke both his legs.
In a very grave condition he was taken to the municipal hospital.
The Water-Mains Work Begins on Monday.

On Tuesday the water-mains committee held a meeting at which the tenders for awarding the water-mains work were considered.
The committee decided to accept the tender submitted by Eng. G. Weinzieher.
The work begins next Monday. The work will start on Modrzejowska Street.
An Important Circular Concerning Closed Bakeries.

The local bakers’ guild (cech) has received a circular (okólnik) from the starosta, informing the bakers whose bakeries were closed on sanitary grounds that the bakeries may be reopened once the bakery meets the sanitary regulations.
Whoever wants such a commission [inspection] must pay 50 zł. at the starostwo.
Mr. Shefner’s Lecture

which took place last Sabbath gave the listeners an intellectual treat. The lecturer brilliantly portrayed the roles and types of the former and present Sejm deputies.
In a fine Yiddish and in a successful satirical tone Mr. Shefner gave us a gallery of types that splendidly illustrated the “activity” of the deputies in the Sejm, so that the audience gained an idea of the former and the present parliament.
A Concert of the Living Word.
The artists of the Vilna Troupe, Messrs. Weislitz, Kamen and Orleska, will present this Sabbath, 1 June, at 2 p.m., at the “Corso” theatre, sketches and recitations from the best Yiddish classics.
Sosnowiec — The First Plenary Meeting of the Local Chamber of Commerce.

A request to the government to abolish the turnover tax.
On Monday the Chamber of Commerce, by order of the Minister of Commerce, held a meeting. The meeting took place at the “Club” of the industrialists in Dąbrowa.
Instead of at 11 a.m., the meeting began at 2 p.m. In the meantime consultations took place about the election of the president and vice-presidents, and above all the commerce councillors were very “active” at the free buffet...
Jewish councillors were present not only from Zagłębie but also from Zawiercie, Częstochowa, Kielce and Radom.
The meeting is opened by the election commissioner Salaszyński [?], who greets the councillors in the name of the government and invites the oldest councillor, Senator Hempel, to take the chair.
Then a president, six vice-presidents and a board are elected. As one of the vice-presidents councillor Mr. M. Geifeld [?] (Częstochowa) was elected, and as a member of the board Vice-President Mr. Rubinlicht was elected.
After adopting several formal points, among them the budget, it is decided to send telegrams of greeting to the President of the State, Marshal Piłsudski and Minister of Commerce Kwiatkowski.
Then a motion is adopted to intervene with the government so that the turnover tax, which undermines the existence of the Polish merchant class, be abolished.
—o—
“All May Slaughter” — but only whoever has a slip from the gmina.
Lately a measure of lawlessness has arisen in the local slaughtering question: the shochtim slaughtered for Modrzejów butchers against slips from those who represent the community there, and thereby the local gmina treasury suffered loss.
Because of this a meeting was held at the gmina with the participation of members of the rabbinate, who decided to instruct the shochtim not to slaughter except for those who bring slaughter slips from the gmina.
—o—
The Synagogue Is Being Repaired
At last the community board has realised that the synagogue cannot remain in such a low state, and is proceeding to repair it. Meanwhile the roof is being repaired — it is summertime, after all — so that the worshippers in the synagogue should not suffer from the rains...
—o—
From the Labour Court.
On Wednesday the labour court was to hear the case against the publishers of “Unzer Tog”, whom the typesetters Adlerfligel, Friedman and Lantsman have sued because they are owed a debt of about a thousand zł.
Because an important witness was missing, the case was adjourned.
—o—
Political Arrests.
The local police have arrested for anti-state activity Messrs. B. Reizman, M. Singer, Ch. Poltorak, Y. Spitzberg, Dora Kaiser, Sala Warszawska, L. Rabak and Goldshlak. The last-named came here from Chmielnik only last Friday, and the next day, Saturday, he was arrested as a participant in a demonstration.
—o—
A Bicycle Injures a Jewish Girl.
Miss Gimliakewicz, while walking in the street in Modrzejów, was run into by a bicycle, which injured her hands and feet.
—o—
From the “Merchants’ Association”.
On Sunday the new board of the “Merchants’ Association” (Piłsudskiego 12) held its constituent meeting, at which a presidium of the following persons was elected:
President — Mr. Y. M. Weinreb; vice — Sh. Warman; treasurer — R. Czapnik; and house manager — B. Zelinger.

the local district court sentenced Mrs. Sarah Mentlik to pay 385 zł. or 19 days’ arrest.
The cigarettes and tobacco found during the search were confiscated.

What, Don’t They Have Time?

[Zagłębie — opinion; traffic and road safety.] You have surely heard the story told of the old Kotzker [Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Kotzk]: how Hasidim once came to him and told him that a railway was being built on which one would travel in 6 hours instead of the 3 days one spends dragging along in the covered wagon. The Rebbe heard out the news, thought it over and finally asked:
“But what — don’t they have time?”
This question of the old Kotzker always comes to my mind whenever I hear of catastrophes that happen with automobiles, trams, motorcycles and other instruments of destruction of our time. What, don’t they have time? — I ask. People already drive twenty kilometres an hour, twenty-five, thirty, forty, up to eighty kilometres, and it is still too little; they insist on having “kefitsat ha-derekh” [miraculous shortening of the road], they insist on being at the destination before they have even moved from the spot.
I am not so naive as not to understand that time is money. I understand that rapid transport, the possibility of going to Warsaw and back in one day, is today a necessity and one simply cannot do without it. But everything must have a limit! One must, after all, also take the other person into account and not put his life in danger merely because I think that I have no time!
Here before me lies a letter from a father who begs for mercy, that something be done to save the children who play in the street in summer and are run over like chicks by the racing automobiles. The father believes that this is more than carelessness on the part of the chauffeurs, that there is recklessness here and perhaps something more. The cars, driven by irresponsible people, run children down, and nobody cares in the least about it.
The complaint seems a little old-fashioned. The automobile must hurry, must race, because the faster it goes the better for it; the more it earns. But the question arises: is the public there for it, or is it there for the public?
And as for the complaint being old-fashioned — even that is not so bad. In Switzerland, which lives off foreign tourist traffic, there is a canton — Graubünden is its name — in which it was simply forbidden to drive an automobile. The peasants did not want these destroyers among them, of which the horses are frightened, and a ban was imposed on this devil. And the rich tourists who roam across Switzerland in their elegant cars had to turn back at the border of the canton, or leave the car standing and go on by horse. Whether the ban is still in force today I do not know, but in my time it was in force. And if Switzerland could allow itself such a thing, we may surely at least allow ourselves to prevent the wild chase of cars through the town.
The question does not concern Zagłębie alone. Elsewhere, too, people cry out against the bloody orgies that the destroyers perpetrate. Elsewhere, too, measures are taken against the racing. But if elsewhere it is only a question of public safety, with us it is a question of life and death for hundreds of innocent children, whom one cannot — and is not obliged to — keep locked up at home. The children must be let out into the so-called[?] fresh air. Our magistrate [town council] has not yet managed to provide the population with a little garden where the children could catch a bit of air. Our children have to knock about in the streets, and there they are trampled by the automobiles that run like demons and kill old people and children...
Death will come to them anyway — so what, don’t they have time?
Ch. Landau.
Sports

[Sports — football; Zagłębie.]
“Sosnowiec”—“Maccabi” 1:1 (0:1).
The above match was supposed to be a championship match, but because the referee did not turn up at the ground, a friendly match was played.
“Sosnowiec” took the field with the best forces at its disposal. “Maccabi”, on the other hand, was weakened by several reserve players.
“Maccabi” showed a very fine technical game and carried out very fine attacks; nevertheless “Sosnowiec” managed to score a goal in the first half. The first part of the second half belonged entirely to “Sosnowiec”, but the defence and the goalkeeper of “Maccabi” cancel out everything. “Maccabi” begins to bombard the opponents’ goal, and from a header by Fiszel “Maccabi” equalises. Best on the field: for “Sosnowiec” Stechan[?], Bergel; for “Maccabi” Schlesinger, Schmidt.
“Zagłębie”—“Świt” 1:1 (0:0).
In the championship match which took place on Sunday at the “Victoria” ground, “Zagłębie” took the field with 9 players. The first half ends without a result.
In the second half “Świt” begins to play with more ambition and scores a goal. “Zagłębie” wants to equalise at any price, and only manages it before the end, and the match ends in a draw. Referee Mr. Mazur — weak.

In the important championship games “Hakoach” again won a great victory, and that in a strange town, on a strange ground. From the start “Skra” has a slight superiority. Letters to the Editor

I.
In issue No. 22 of your esteemed paper a would-be protest was printed against us because we used "uncultured expressions" with regard to the meeting. In that protest the "majority" spoke groundlessly and did not have the courage to publish their names — proof that they were afraid the disgrace before the outside world would be too great. Heaven forbid the Jewish street should find out who the poor protesters are, and who takes the floor on the laws of parliamentarism and intellectuality... As to the matter itself, the situation would have brought much benefit: first, one would have seen "who are they that go" [Exodus 10:8], and second, we would have been spared polemicising with such people. But because the "pipige" [?] protesters did it anonymously and were ashamed of their "firms", we are compelled to explain the following:
At the last general meeting of the "Bank Ludowy" [People's Bank] a handful of people from the so-called opposition gathered, forming a "majority" of 10 (read: ten), and incessantly used a "something" language, i.e. the whole time they made a racket that "something is being said", "something is being told", "something is going on" and "something has flown". Naturally, as long-serving, untiring bank manager, who has stood like a faithful soldier at his post for several years, and as devoted members of the board, we demanded open criticism, the truth in its full breadth. If — we declared — we are no good, then take over the bank yourselves; you are, after all, "cultured", "intelligent", so with you the bank will only now be truly raised up...
Naturally, had the "majority" not had provocative intentions, they would have accepted our proposals with open arms. But the gentlemen "intellectuals" do not want to take over the bank at all; they just went on talking about "something". Then we forgot the principle "Answer not a fool according to his folly" [Prov. 26:4; misquoted in print] and in great agitation we threw out the words: "You will not have the privilege of discovering any malversation [embezzlement] with us, and such destroyers and wreckers should go to the eighty winds"...
Yes, gentlemen of the "majority"! It may be that in the "cultural sense" you stand much higher than we do, but the institution we have built, and for which we went through the seven chambers of hell, we will not hand over to such hands as yours; and in general we promise you that we will no longer polemicise with you, for you yourselves will admit that it is beneath our dignity.
Respectfully,
B. Rechnic, Y. Mintz.
II.
Most honoured, esteemed Editor!
Having read last Friday in your esteemed paper about the great humiliations and bloodshed inflicted on me last Sunday at "Ahavat Hesed" at the dedication of the house, I ask you, esteemed Editor, to publish the following:
As for the insolent and vile act that the "well-known" Jaskierowicz committed against me in public, I do not see fit to speak of it now, for it is beneath my dignity — let the public see and judge. But regarding what you wrote from the "neutral" source, I declare categorically that when the delegation of "Ahavat Hesed" came to negotiate with me, neither I nor my wife set any difficult conditions whatsoever, and we received the delegation with the greatest respect; Mr. Meir Leml Sendyszew, who was in the delegation together with Jaskierowicz, can bear witness to this. In general, whoever comes to me I receive with the utmost honour.
With feelings of respect,
Ozer Menachem Żupowicz
Cantor (shaliach tzibbur) of the town of Będzin.
Great Success of the Polish Rubber Industry Abroad

In 1924 a rubber enterprise came into being in Łódź, founded by an English-Swiss-Polish rubber-industry joint-stock company "Gentleman", which at the exhibition in Nice gave proof that Polish products in this field can compete with foreign articles.
The exhibits of the "Gentleman" firm, which were examined at the exhibition in Nice by qualified experts, were awarded the highest distinction, a large gold medal.
The high recognition by the administration of the exhibition in Nice confirms that a brilliant future awaits the rubber industry, young in this respect, and only when one can compete with abroad with our products — and not only satisfy our domestic consumption, but also export and acquaint foreign countries with a new branch of our industry.
The success in Nice of the "Gentleman" firm should be a source of pride for every Polish citizen, because it confirms that our industry stands at its proper height.

Olkusz — The murderers of the murdered Natan Dawid Zygman caught
Soon after the attack on the train in which the Radom chairman of the merchants' association, Natan Dawid Zygman, fell victim, the police began an energetic investigation and discovered the murderers. Their names are: Julian Żuryła [?], 23 years old, and Jan Cembruszyński [?], 21 years old, both from Olkusz. They have confessed to the attack. The report in the Warsaw press that tens of thousands of złoty were robbed from those attacked does not correspond to reality. In total the following was robbed: from Avromele Żargowicki 10 zł., from Alter Szapir 18 zł., from a Jew from Łagów [?] 8 zł., and from Dawid Zeliger 50 gr. Nor is it true that the slain man tried to tear the revolver from the bandit and resisted; he merely rose from his seat out of surprise, for which the bandit shot him. The same bandits also carried out, on the second day, the attack on the train to Ząbkowice.
A. B.

Wolbrom — On the Interest-Free Loan Fund

[Wolbrom — welfare; free-loan fund.] Here in Wolbrom a gmilus-khesed (interest-free loan) fund has already existed for 6 months, and it has already issued 170 loans to small traders and craftsmen. The local Jewish community has given us an annual subsidy of 750 zł., and the "Urząd Gminy" [printed "Ushand gmine" — the municipal office] has also approved 200 zł. for us. Last Sabbath the chairman invited the visiting chief cantor (Ober-Kantor) Mr. Baruch Grajs of Drohobycz to give a concert for the benefit of the free-loan fund, which truly turned out very well.
Aszlg.
Our Popular Interests (The Downfall of the Sosnowiec „Small Traders’ Association“ and Its New Birth)

To what extent everything [?] among us is ownerless, to what extent we treat everything with criminal indifference and banality, can be illustrated by the sad affair of the Sosnowiec „Small Traders’ Association“ (Kleinhendler-Fareyn).
The abuses that took place there, the unheard-of, impermissible deeds that were smuggled in there — so that it came to the point that the association was broken through and through, that the institution was rotted and destroyed through and through.
This is simply unheard of, that an institution counting nearly a thousand members could collapse in the blink of an eye; and after all, we measure the usefulness of an institution by the size of its membership: the more members an association has, the more justified it is, the more chances it has to take a place at the top and to play a social role in our life.
That is how it always [?] is with us: as soon as an institution attains a right to exist, as soon as it turns out that it must occupy a place in our social life [?], a sudden storm wind comes and wipes everything out. And it is no small thing, how necessary an institution is once it reaches a membership of a thousand.
Since our economic interests are at such a low level, the Jew who is a member of a „Small Traders’ Association“ needs so much social support, so much enlightenment in the social sense, that hardly has he become a member there and received some support from the institution — and hardly has it collapsed — it is truly a catastrophe for him. After all, we know well that an association must be for its member a guide, a „moreh derekh“, that must show him along which line to continue his life’s path and how to fight on his hard road of life.
After all, we constantly agitate among the popular masses that they must be united in a social institution, that they must have the body that will care for their tormented today, and that they should have the possibility of reaching a better tomorrow.
After all, we feel at every step how hard life is becoming for these people; on the shoulders of the broad popular masses lies the difficulty of continuing their poor existence, since one wants to fence off the road on which they walk and block the small path they have found for themselves and from which they draw their poor livelihood.
And people like these start being persecuted, they start being chased away: here they may not stand, and there they must not sit; and on top of that they are wronged by the tax authority, and it reaches the point that even if they were already to sell their bit of poor merchandise, they still would not have enough to pay what is demanded of him.
After all, we know how helpless a Jew remains when he reaches this stage. And here the question arises: who is to speak for him at such a terrible moment? Who can fight for him and get it done that he is not broken? After all, we know that such a Jew is in no way able to act for himself. Neither can he, nor does he know, in such brokenness, what to do and how to speak, nor will anyone listen to him. Besides, we know from practice that as long as everyone goes on his own, nobody achieves anything. But one cannot compare the great benefit that social concentration has at such a serious moment. After all, we understand the importance of an institution when it goes to intervene for its members. And an institution — the greater the number of members it counts, the stronger the power it has to demand justice, the more courage it has to claim what is due to it.
Can we then estimate the great value an institution has when it counts nearly a thousand members? We cannot even imagine the strength and the power such an institution possesses for the community. Such an institution must be reckoned with everywhere: the authorities, the headquarters in Warsaw and the whole community alike look upon such a united body as upon a giant that must be reckoned with, willy-nilly.
And when such an institution collapses, when abuses are committed in such an institution, one must react properly to such unheard-of deeds, which degrade the Jewish community; and meanwhile the small trader is orphaned: he has no one to speak in his name, no one to defend him.
And therefore the fact is to be welcomed that the institution has now been reorganized and a fresh stream of life has been poured into it. It is to be welcomed that the accused have been removed and in their place people have come in who have taken upon themselves the power of work, the power of initiative, the power of the will to achieve for the broad strata of the Jewish popular masses.
Let these people see to it that the institution is properly reorganized, for there is a broad field here, and it stands and begs to be reaped; there are members who stand ready to support such an institution, provided only that it defends their honour at the time when it [sic; probably: they] needs it.
Let our „Small Traders’ Association“ show from now on signs of life, signs of activity, signs of awakening — and that will then give it the proper satisfaction.
Let the new board prove to us that it understands how to run such an apparatus, which is so necessary to us in our life, both in the economic and in the general social sphere.
The institution has the possibility of bringing its members to a higher level, both in the economic field and in the social sense.
We therefore wish to place great hopes in the new board, which must understand its important tasks on the new road of life.
Selekt.
The Law on Holidays for Workers and Employees

[Poland — labour law; holidays.] On the occasion of the start of the holiday season we wish to inform our readers about the exact[?] regulations concerning holidays.
First of all it must be noted that the right to a holiday belongs to workers employed in industry, mining, trade, office work, transport, hospital service, institutions of public welfare and other workplaces, even if they make no profit, and regardless of whether these workplaces are private property, state-owned or a body of local self-government. An exception are workers in seasonal enterprises in which work lasts less than 10 months a year. All workers employed in the enterprises mentioned have the right to enjoy an 8-day holiday — [for] workers who have been employed for a year in an enterprise — and 15 days when he has been employed for 3 years in an enterprise. Workers younger than 18 have the right to a 14-day holiday after a year of work. And although the industrial and craft establishments [in question] are not subject to the holiday law, the pupils and apprentices ("terminators") in those establishments nevertheless also have the right to enjoy a holiday, just like the juvenile workers.
Mental (white-collar) workers employed in office work in commercial and industrial enterprises have the right, after half a year of work, to enjoy a 14-day holiday, and after a year, a paid holiday of one month.
It must be noted that the holiday period, i.e. 14 and 15 days, is counted by the calendar, so that Sundays and holidays are also included in the holiday. If the worker in the establishment concerned interrupted his work through illness, an accident, or because he was called up for military service, this is not regarded as an interruption of work.
If a worker breaks his work contract without prior notice, to which the employer was entitled, that worker loses the right to a holiday. The holiday period must also be paid. But if a worker works during the holiday in another enterprise, he loses the right to claim wages during his holiday. If the work is contracted on piece-rate ("akord") or by the piece, the holiday pay is then calculated on the basis of the average earnings in the previous 3 months before the holiday. Apprentices ("terminators") and learner-boys may not receive for the holiday period a lower wage than the sum[?] on which they must be insured in the sickness fund.
If the worker has fallen ill and cannot enjoy his holiday, the holiday must, at his request, be postponed to one of the following 3 months. If the worker broke off relations with the enterprise and resumed them no later than within 3 months, his previous working time must be credited to him for the purpose of the holiday. If there are several workers in an enterprise, they can agree among themselves on the order of the holidays and arrange it with the management, but in such a way that in the period from 1 May to 30 September at least [—] of the workers employed in the enterprise concerned enjoy their holiday.
If in a craft enterprise more than 4 workers have worked for a period of more than 6 months, the workers there have a right to a holiday. If a partial or complete change of the owners of the enterprise occurs, the workers do not lose the right to a holiday. If the worker does not take his holiday at the time set for him, he loses the right to his holiday and has no right to claim compensation. In his work contract he cannot renounce his holiday, nor restrict it. The employer may count the holiday period as a notice period. The beginning of the working period is reckoned as the day on which one reports for work, even if through the employer's fault he has not started his work.
As "workers", regardless of their age, the holiday law regards the following employees: [those] performing administrative and supervisory activity and not performers of physical labour, such as managers, stewards (intendants), operational staff such as engineers, technicians, foremen, warehouse managers, forwarding clerks, office and chancellery work, accountants, draughtsmen, cost calculators; those performing commercial activities, such as shop and bookshop assistants ("subiekci") who have completed a vocational or secondary school and have done a practical training; [those] in drugstores, pharmacy, cashiers, dispatchers, agents or canvassers, artists, musicians, artist painters and draughtsmen, and those employed as staff at a doctor's.
The wages for the holiday period are paid later. If there was no other agreement, the normal wage during the holiday is calculated according to [how] the worker is paid — by the day or by the hour. If a worker works in an enterprise fewer than 6 days a week, the holiday pay is calculated proportionally, as if the worker had worked the whole month.
Time Is Air

L. Kosman
One needs to take a holiday now and then, not so much to rest one's own spirit as to discover things you do not notice at all in the daily hubbub of big-city life.
Thus on my present holiday I discovered that time is a curious thing; it has properties you can see better from afar than from near, and it is altogether more play, more imagination than reality.
In the city, when you are busy, you have no time to think about time; you do not notice it at all — it simply slips away from under your hands. Part of your time goes in trains and trams, where it seems to you that every sense of time and space vanishes. The regular hours you work are not time to contemplate either. And the time left over besides work, sleep and eating can hardly be considered time that can be noticed and reckoned.
Only when you are on holiday, far from the city and the bustle, between sky, mountain and valley, where time lies shaped[?] together with nature and plays along with nature's play — when sunshine is time and rain is time, and you notice the difference — only then do you see what perspective time has and what a curious play it is in our life.
And so freely does time lie among mountains and valleys that you begin to measure it in decades, whereas in the city you lack even the measure of a day, because it is not yours.
The measure of week and month is handed to you in the calendars that are sent to you.
And having time to think about time, you discover that time is a precious article whose value you know only when it is entirely yours. The trouble with time in the city is that it is bought from you, and then it loses its true value.
And one more thing I discovered in the lap of nature: that one could do far more with time than city civilisation allows it. The only trouble is that few people know the secret; when more come to know of it, a nature-revolution against civilisation will yet break out.
And perhaps such a revolution will never come, because people by nature like to be forged into steel and stone.
People think of a social revolution, of making man equal to man. That can never be, as long as some people will forever sit between sky, mountain and valley, and some within great walls, in steel fortresses.
Inequality does not begin with the "tempele"[?] money, but with the little bit of air we breathe into our lungs.
As long as all people do not breathe one and the same air, no social revolution will be possible.
Let the barrels of money be divided into big bowls — it will not help. One must begin with the division of air, and the money will melt away of itself.
It is the breath that distinguishes one man from another, not money. The latter is an addition, not the beginning of inequality.
And so, walking between mountain and valley under a clear sky (even the overcast one is [dear?] to the heart), I cried out: give everyone equally to breathe this air, and you will have social equality.
The communist friends at my side at first wanted to raise a protest. They do indeed think highly of fresh air — the proof being that they came out to draw it in — but somehow they are used to hearing of other differences in social inequality, and my remark sounded too "pure-airy".
Long debates were not needed. Here, in the lap of nature, on whom the sky smiled equally, the mountains beckoned equally and the air streamed equally into our nostrils, we quickly came to agree on the airy part of social equality.
And then I saw the significance of air. Let it only stream equally into everyone's nostrils, and the social question is solved. Here, at the health resort of the air-drinking guests, the question was already a solved one.
The only trouble is that too many remain in the city, in the steel fortress, and are unable to grasp our great truth.
And as regards time, I became convinced that for it too there is a remedy on the other side, far from the steel fortress.
But the fortress calls me back, and I fear that here I shall forget both the remedy for time and the blessing of the air.
Only the awareness that somewhere there are sky, mountain and valley, where time has value and air is apportioned[?] to all equally, will stand by me.
Antisemitic little flowers... — (When you demand justice, you get spat upon with insults)

(When you demand justice, you get spat upon with insults.)
And once again the old, familiar antisemitic ditties have been heard — the ditties we thought already belonged to the past, that would at long last find their place in the historical archive.
So it quite often seemed to us, and so we had a right to think and to be sure, to feel and to understand. Quite often we believed that our former accusers felt that they had sinned against the Jews in Poland; we were sure that they instinctively feel this and see it at every step along their path of life. And we also had grounds to think so, because, working together in the public field, sitting under one roof and running the local self-government, the municipal economy, people had the opportunity to confirm that Jews are not only honest and loyal citizens, that they do not merely carry the citizen's burden on their shoulders, but that we are burdened beyond our strength, that we strive beyond what is possible to bring everything together in brotherhood and unity, if only the country may flourish, if only the state may find itself in a better condition and on a higher level.
Many times we thought that people see it, that they feel it, how[?] they had sinned against us when they accused us of dishonest intentions and exaggerated deeds. And not once were these people honest and sincere and admitted to us that they had been mistaken and had greatly exaggerated at our expense; they were not ashamed to tell us so openly at a moment when they had succeeded in carrying out, in the city council or elsewhere, a common, brotherly public activity with which they remained satisfied.
And that too is quite understandable, for who knows better than we do that one can get along with us, that we always stretch out our hand in peace, not even reckoning with the dreadful thought that the outstretched hand might be left hanging in the air, that it might be insulted. And how many times has that actually happened? How many times have our Christian councillors in the city council repaid us with evil instead of the good, the glory and the honour we gave them?
And nevertheless we pretended to have forgotten everything, we did not want to make a fuss about it — and who knows, perhaps precisely for that reason they found the courage to insult us at every step and on every occasion to throw shame and disgust in our faces.
And here these fine, "pearly" insults have once again been hurled from the public tribune of the Będzin city council. Our antisemites, who, it seemed, had already got used to living with us, have once again displayed their "cultured" nakedness and shouted that we Jews are the traitors of Poland, that we have shed no blood for the country, that we pay no taxes, that we are this and that, such-and-such..
And what was it all about, what were these shameful insults over? It is a disgrace to say, a shame to utter it. It was, all in all, about nothing more and nothing less than subsidies for innocent orphans.
After all, the civilised world does not know how to distinguish between a Jewish and a Christian orphan; an unfortunate, forlorn child is equally unfortunate, whatever nationality or country it may belong to.
And when Councillor Mrs. Ratner came and spoke to hearts, to human hearts, and showed that the Jewish orphan must not be wronged as against his Christian companion; when she said that the unfortunate children are all equally unfortunate and demanded equal rights for them — there arose the terrible scandal that we are rich and need to be given nothing at all.
And it is characteristic how far the egoism of our antisemites reaches. They cannot bear to "give" us such a subsidy for our orphans as the Christian orphans receive. And it is interesting that when it comes to granting subsidies, people forget — or perhaps they pretend to forget — that it is we who are the givers and, heaven forbid, not the takers, for it is very well known who is burdened with taxes in a Będzin like this.
And what did Councillor Ratner say? That the Jewish orphan should be subsidised with the same 70 zł. a month as the Christian one, whereas for the Jewish orphan only 30 zł. comes out. So this is a wrong — to allow oneself to demand such a thing[?], i.e. to compare Jewish children with Christian ones. That the money comes from Jewish pockets, and that despite all this the Jewish child is nevertheless wronged — that does not matter, that is nonsense..
It truly cries out to heaven; it is unheard of to allow oneself so much oppressing and insulting and reviling and disgracing, and all this only because a councillor has the courage to demand what is due to him, what common sense dictates — that his rights must be recognised.
The only thing to regret is that the chairman of the city council did not react as he should have to these unheard-of deeds, which he ought not to have permitted, for it is high time not to let ourselves be whipped over the head for nothing and once again for nothing.
Perhaps the lesson would have taught our councillors something for the future? Perhaps we too would have learned to answer the way one is greeted? For we must prove once and for all that one has to reckon with those who carry all the civic duties on their exhausted shoulders, and that they do not deserve, in return, to be insulted in hooligan ways and to have people incited against them for all the world is worth.
R. Let.
A Little Feuilleton. The Hatless Intellectual...

[Feuilleton — humour.] Pan [Mr.] Feliks Kracbarszt, a modern young man and, frankly, a "pierwszorzędny" [first-rate; reading uncertain, see note], has been pestering me for weeks now, ever since summer began: why don't I follow the fashion, and why do I wear a hat in the street?
— What do you need a hat on your head for? [?] — he wonders at me. — Why, that's szaleństwo, zacofaństwo [madness, backwardness]! And who? You! A man with wykształcenie [education], with intelligence, a man w ogóle [altogether] modern! Jak panu nie wstyd? [Aren't you ashamed, sir?]
— Przecież [surely] a person, i w szczególności [and in particular] an intelligent person — my young man goes on — must distinguish himself (wyróżnić się) somehow from the rabble (hołota); a na przykład [for example], just as he once distinguished himself by his hat when the rabble wore little hats of every shape; a jeżeli [and if] fashion orders the hat thrown away and put in mothballs for good, then it is bardzo naturalne [very natural] that we, the intelligentsia, must follow the fashion. Czy nie mam racji? [Am I not right?]
— Doskonale rozumiem [I understand perfectly] — my young man develops his theory of hatlessness further — that a nowoczesny [modern] intellectual must distinguish himself from his otoczenie [surroundings] not only by his bare head. An intellectual, a prawdziwy [true] intellectual must be nicely combed, must always have a fresh crease in his trousers, must wear elegant "lamshn" [? shoes] and jedwabne skarpety [silk socks], must wear an intelligent tie, i tak dalej [and so on], ale to co jest najważniejsze [but what is most important] is to go about the street without a hat, nawet [even; printed "gavet"] in the greatest heat, in the thickest dust (kurz) and in the worst weathers (pogody).
— Co prawda [true enough] — my young man continues in one breath — going about bare-headed has become so rozpowszechnione [widespread; misprinted] nowadays that byle kto, a lada stary kamasz, przepraszam za wyrażenie [any nobody, any old boot, pardon the expression], who has never held a comb in his hand, stawia się [shows off] today with his bare head, whereas dotychczas [until now] it was only for the wybrańcy [chosen few], for the śmietanka społeczeństwa [cream of society], and only a director, a doctor, a hairdresser, a dancing master used to go hatless, ale to się nie liczy [but that doesn't count], because, as the przysłowie [proverb] says, "Poznać pana po cholewach" [you know a gentleman by his boot-tops], and an intellectual wants, jednak [after all], to distinguish himself from others. Czy nie tak? [Isn't that so?]
— I wie pan [And do you know, sir] — my young man urges me with ever-growing pathos — that going bare-headed is, oprócz wszystkiego [besides everything else], simply a brilliant [?] and practical wynalazek [invention]. Po pierwsze [firstly], you save a hat for the time being, which nowadays też coś warto [is also worth something]. Po wtóre [secondly], you save the bowing with your hat, and with one "Moje uszanowanie" [my respects] you're done; you also save a... jednym słowem [in a word], it's good, it's nice and praktyczne [practical]. Po co tu dużo gadać? [Why say much more?] — Dlatego właśnie [that's exactly why] — my young man won't let go of me — as a prawdziwy przyjaciel [true friend] of the whole intelligentsia, radzę [I advise] you zarzucić [to throw off] the hat and go only bare-headed, just like me and the whole nowoczesna [modern] intelligentsia, and jak Boga kocham [as God is my witness], you will always be wdzięczny [grateful] to me. Zobaczy pan! [You'll see, sir!]
I had to promise my przyjaciel [friend], Pan Feliks Kracbarszt, to follow his advice, and only that way did I barely, with great trouble, get rid of him.
M. Mandlzon.
Greetings from Home, from Eretz Israel.

[Eretz Israel — letter; Zagłębie people in Palestine.] (From our special correspondent).
In Tel Aviv the series of festivities, manifestations and demonstrations is already over, and Tel Aviv, drunk with joy and enthusiasm, is again getting down to "Bereshit" — to the daily cares of creation and work. The dozens of holidays, jubilees, receptions, balls, concerts and plain "neshafim" [soirées] are over; the press, which announced new "festivals" to the reader every day, has suddenly fallen silent, and the city kiosks, which hour by hour were plastered with huge, shrieking posters heralding new surprises, now stand poor [?] and bare.
Who is able to convey all the festivities we had here from Purim until after Passover? Do not all the reports and letters about the Purim carnival, the "Exhibition", the 20th jubilee of Tel Aviv, the 25th jubilee of the Second "Aliyah" and of the "Teachers' Federation", about the Maccabi "Kenes" (conference) and the house-warming of "Ohel Shem" of [?] the "Oneg Shabbat" come out pale and feeble next to the real thing?
But Tel Aviv can do more than dance and sing: it can also create productively and do physical work.
Go out in the morning into the streets of Będzin, Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec and see how many Jewish workers hurry to the coal pits, factories and workshops — couldn't you count them on your fingers? And in Tel Aviv at 6 in the morning the street swarms like a beehive with the workers running to work. Often I stand for hours watching the Jewish "Manchester" in miniature, and my heart swells with pride seeing workers in short knee-breeches, with rolled-up sleeves and bagel-rings in hand, running and riding to work — some on a bicycle, some on a bus and some by train. For a long time in the morning hours I wander through the workers' neighbourhoods, the workers' quarters, from which stream hundreds and thousands of women and men loaded with shovels, hoes and other work tools, and I cannot tear my gaze from those whose forefathers built Pithom and Raamses for foreign nations and whose grandchildren today build with blood and sweat a land of their own for their own people.
Blessed are you, Jewish people, when you hear again the beat of the hammer in the Jewish smithy, the noise of the machines in the factories and the work song "Labour is our whole life" of the halutz who cuts the ripe ears in the Jewish fields!
———
I met the sons of the Będzin rabbinical decisor (moreh hora'ah) R' Hanokh David Fridberg — Shlomo Yoel, Chaim and Menachem — who work in the colony of Petah Tikva. Shlomo Yoel has a post in the "Labour Exchange" of "Hapoel Hamizrachi", Menachem is a locksmith, and Chaim has no fixed, definite job.
With Shlomo Yoel, who was an active worker in the Będzin "Tzeirei Mizrachi", I had a long talk about his situation, of which he does not complain. True, he had bad times, he was ill, but he accepted everything with love, because the work of building Eretz Israel, a difficult task, demands much perseverance, strength, love and attachment to the land.
Mr. Meir Gożelany [?] of Będzin has a good post with a nice salary as a bookkeeper in an English-Jewish firm in Jaffa.
Miss Chana Szental of Będzin has a post in the "Culture Committee" in the cultural department of the General Federation of Jewish Labour. Miss Sh., whom the Będzin theatre public still remembers as a talented actress of the local "Mu'a" [?], plays in the local dramatic section "Ha'Ohel", directed by the talented "Habima" actor Mr. Moshe Halevi. In all the "productions" (performances) the "Ohel" has given so far — "The Fishermen", "Jacob and Rachel" and Peretz's staged [...] [?] — Miss Sh. too appeared in responsible roles and was received, like the whole splendid ensemble, with great success. The "Ohel" is now preparing to bring to the stage the drama "Jeremiah" by the German-Jewish writer Stefan Zweig, who is coming to Eretz Israel especially to attend the premiere.
In Nes Ziona, which lies between Rishon LeZion and Rehovot, I visited Mr. Alter Erlich of Sosnowiec. Mr. E. is a teacher in Nes Ziona and at the same time a bearer of culture, a lecturer for the "Culture Committee". Mr. E. gives lectures on subjects from world literature, such as Romain Rolland and Rabindranath Tagore. Mr. E. is an active labour activist in his colony, a member of the "Nes Ziona Workers' Council" and head of the local branch of "Hapoel Hatzair".
Mr. Yosef Abba Szlezynger, who came to the country with the Fourth Aliyah without any definite plan made in advance and without vocational training, has structurally "revolutionised" himself together with his children and turned from a scrap-iron dealer into a "nagar" (carpenter). In the first period after his arrival in Eretz Israel, when there was as yet no room for small iron dealers, Mr. Sh. abandoned his trade and worked on road building. During the crisis, from which Mr. Sh. also suffered, he learned carpentry; today he works in this trade and makes a not-bad living.
His eldest daughter is a dental technician and works in the dental factory of Mr. Blum, who in recent weeks became well known in Eretz Israel by putting up a fine, specially built house (it cost him 25 thousand dollars). The middle daughter works in Jaffa in a large underwear [soft linen] factory. Mr. Sh. owns a little house of his own and is spared rent, which is many times dearer than in Poland.
Further greetings and answers to letters — to follow.
M. Hampel.

The Misled Girl (7)

[Literature — serialized novel; installment 7, including the start of "Chapter Eight".]
Dr. A. Weisman.
(A novel of Jewish life in the old world, based on historical facts.)

"God, what has happened here, something so terrible? How dare you speak like that about Mania? She is a brilliant child! You yourself and all of us always adored her — something terrible must have happened."
"Something terrible really has happened," Ludwig answered with a deep sigh, and a terrible sorrow covered his face.
Everyone was frightened by his appearance.
"Who knows what has gone on here?" they all exclaimed in fright, exchanging glances with one another.
"Go on[?], Ludwig, you must tell us; after all, you are not the only one mixed up in this. You must — we are telling you."
Open-mouthed, they all waited for Ludwig to calm down a little and begin his story.
"I can't tell you anything today. Leave me in peace today. You will know everything, but not today. If I weren't in such company right now, I would have walked out. Leave me in peace, we'll put it off until tomorrow. Let us talk today about whatever you like — only not about Mania."
"But where is Mania now? That much you must tell us."
"Where else would she be now? With Sister Irina."
Everyone sighed with relief[?].
"If so, she is in good hands," Aunt Fanny spoke up. "Mania will be ours yet; no one has ever got out of her hands."
"You are mistaken. Sister Irina is indeed clever, pious, good and learned, but none of you knows Mania. Mania regrets the whole affair. Do you hear? Mania regrets it."
The word "regret" struck them all like thunder. They all clapped their hands together and almost screamed:
"If she manages to escape from there, then we are all ruined!"
"Ruined!" — the second aunt did not stop wringing her hands.
"Calm yourselves," said Aunt Fanny. "No one has ever run away from Sister Irina yet. I have always believed in her 'bryhshaft'[?] [prob.: skill / resourcefulness]; this very week I will go down to the convent especially. I must know everything."
"Will you see Mania?" they all asked.
"I don't know; I'll see there how things stand. I would never have believed it," she said, fanning herself with her 'gauze'[?] [perhaps a gauze scarf / a fan]. "Mania was so well prepared already, she was burning to escape as fast as possible from the accursed Jews. I don't believe it, I don't believe it, it is impossible!"
"So — you don't believe it? You can ask Jan: he disguised himself as a coachman and drove the horses when we ran away."
Jan was the younger brother of the ekonom [the estate steward], a shaygets, a 'piper' [whistler, ne'er-do-well], a 'marim'[?] at murder, a fanatical Catholic and a hater of Israel. He too served at the same estate-owner's manor, and he too was present that evening.
The nieces, the old maids who used to hang about him and had more than once tried to match themselves to him, sought him out and brought him to the company of conspirators, so that he would testify that Mania had come to regret it.
"Is it possible?" they asked him.
"Let Ludwig tell you himself."
"He has already told us."
"So what do you want from me?"
"We want you to confirm it too, because we don't believe such a thing."
"Why won't you believe it? Besides the fact that she regretted it, Ludwig also got a big, fiery slap in the mug from Mania's pretty little hand."
Ludwig jumped up and threw himself at Jan, but the women intervened. The rest of the company present that evening came running; everyone wanted to know what was going on, but the women hushed the story up.
"I will go to the convent 'mun haytige'[?] [prob.: this very] week," said Aunt Fanny. "From them, from the two young men, we will learn nothing."
The company had already sat down to supper. There was a clatter of knives and forks, and they ate of everything the world rests on with great appetite and gusto. They clinked glasses and goblets one with another, and showed 'bryhshaft'[?] and prowess in drinking and in emptying the bottles of brandy.
That evening Ludwig drank more than ever and got as drunk as Lot. All the guests praised him for entertaining the company.
Those who knew Ludwig more closely wondered why he had suddenly begun to drink so much. He was drinking truly like a goy.
Jan looked at Ludwig with disgust for his heavy drinking. Ludwig kept shouting aloud that he would kill Jan.
Everyone laughed at how Ludwig was talking out of drunkenness.
It goes without saying that the whole crowd drank, guzzled and boozed, and soon began to blame the Jews for Mania's change of heart; to vilify the Jews and throw mud at them for — — for being Jews.
"Certainly the Jews won't keep quiet. Zelig and his wife set off this very day to look for Mania. We thought Yom Kippur was the safest day — nobody would chase after them; but in the end, nothing at all is holy to the Jews, and they went after her on Yom Kippur."
"They say their rabbi ordered them to travel on Yom Kippur!"
"There you have an accursed people, to whom nothing is holy!"
"Mania is too close," one woman called out, "and that is very dangerous."
"The convent is too close; Mania will have to be taken a little farther away!"
"That's right," all the drunken men and women agreed. "It must be done as quickly as possible, or else a disaster may still come of it for us!"
"We must go tomorrow already."
"That is still too early. They may still notice and follow us. Old Dvoyre already suspects us now of being to blame for her granddaughter's flight."
"But it can't be put off. It may still become too late. We must go to the convent tomorrow already. We must consult with Sister Irina, so that she sends Mania farther away."

Chapter Eight.
When you ride a few miles out of the shtetl Z., you see from a distance the golden[?] spire of a cloister. It seems as if the spire reaches right up into the clouds. But the farther you ride, you notice how the gilded spire separates from the clouds, and before your eyes you see a great hill. On the hill stands a large old building, surrounded all around by a walled park.
It is quiet all around. Only the ringing of the bells disturbs the silence from time to time. The sound of the bells carries far, far away and so reminds the shtetls that in the walled parks there are living people who lead a separate life — a closed-off, secluded world.
This is the Catholic convent, and it reminds us of the closed monasteries of Spain, where the terrible victims of the Spanish Inquisition were locked away. There, between the stone walls of the Catholic 'murte'[?] monastery, languished the unfortunate Jewish souls who had the misfortune to fall into the claws of the Jesuit band of soul-snatchers. There they were tortured for long years until they gave themselves over to apostasy; or — when they stood firm and withstood the trial to the end, refusing to exchange the Jewish 'rendl' [gold coin, i.e. their Jewishness], and laughing at all manner of harsh tortures and bodily torments, just so as not to deny, God forbid, the living God and to remain faithful to the belief in the oneness of the Creator — they were burned alive on the pyre[?], at an auto-da-fé, with the Jewish "Shema Yisrael" on their lips.
