Letters from Home.

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton, letter to a friend.]
B.H., week of the portion “Number the sons of Levi” [Bamidbar]...
My friend Reb Shlomo, may his light shine.
After my greetings: I ask you not to bear me any grudge for not writing you an answer immediately[?]; the reason is precisely today's Torah portion. — You will surely wonder: “what has the Sabbatical year to do with Mount Sinai” — what connection does my answer have with today's portion? So I ask you, Reb Shlomo, to look into the Midrash on today's portion, and only then will you understand that the two things, my answer and the portion, are connected with one another.
The Midrash on today's portion brings a question about an infant born at six[?] months on the Sabbath: may one desecrate the Sabbath for its sake? The question was put to Rabbi Abbahu, and he answered: ZYT“A[?] IPT“A UT“H ARNU“N.
The very same question is today very topical among merchants. All of a sudden that kind of money has vanished from our globe, and there exists a new “currency”: an oblong piece of paper ruled with black lines, with only a little space on the back for signatures...
Well, when one goes today to any merchant to buy goods, he faces a hard question: “whence do we know that one born at seven months is viable” — will he still pay the bill of exchange? And the answer is:
— “ZYT“A APT“A UT“A ARNU“N”...
That is: he has been, and will be, bankrupt...
Yes, today is “the season of our bankruptcy” [a pun on the festival formula “the season of our freedom”; pleyte = bankruptcy]. Once, when mankind was not as “cultured” as today, when impudence did not have such great power, a bankrupt of this sort had to flee the country, go off to distant lands, leaving a stain of shame, a yellow patch, on his whole family; it was hard to make a match when the family contained an “ansetser” [a defaulter]...
But today, when the fashion of nakedness is at its height, when in the name of honesty and justice all sorts of deceptive deeds are performed, “there is not a house where there is not one dead” — there is no merchant who is not already up to the second verse of the “Song of Songs” [“bay'm bay'm” thus doubled in print]; it has come to such a pass that when two merchants meet in the street, the first greeting is:
— Where are you at?
— Me? Already past the “regulation” [composition with creditors].
And do not think, Reb Shlomo, that after the regulation anything is left in the pocket — God forbid! The merchant does not go bankrupt for profit. His whole “work” is only so that the bailiff should not take away his last belongings...
That is how our economic situation stands. On the political field, on the other hand, we have stayed behind... we are going backwards.. All fashions lose their value, their gloss, and our eyes and senses yearn once more to live in the old world..
Some two or three years ago we lived in a “political” world: everything, deed or thought, and in general anything that happened at all, had a political basis; even such an innocent matter as breaking up the yeshiva in the Będzin beth midrash, or celebrating a siyum of a Talmud tractate, had political significance. Yes, that was once, but today “it has grown darker on the political horizon”, and instead of going forward we go back, back to the old system[?], to the old way, as our “fanatical” forefathers used to do...
The “greatest grief” has been caused us by the Radomsko and Aleksandrów Hasidim, who took upon themselves the mission of spreading Torah, and for that purpose opened yeshivas[?] where they study exactly as in “the old days”.. not even one day a week do they study “Daf Yomi”..
I even turned to one of the “Agudah” leaders, before whom I poured out my “bitter heart” over the “audacity” of the non-partisan Hasidim; the “Agudah” leader calmed me and gave me to understand that I need not worry — the yeshivas, he assured me, will not exist anyway; they, the non-partisans, “have no money”...
In the field of kashrut, too, a broad “change” has come about: all of Zagłębie is steeped in a sea of prohibitions. From the border shtetl of Modrzejów to Dąbrowa there stretches a chain of prohibitions and bans; wherever you go and stand you hear of new prohibitions issued by this or that rabbi. It has gone so far that even in our town council the kashrut question became topical; the only difference is that from the prohibitions issued by the clergy, złotys “wink” out..
In the town council, on the other hand, they are concerned with “abolishing” prohibitions, that is: that Jewish children whom the Magistrate sends to Busko for a cure[?] should not, as until now, eat treyf...
The one who laid the treyf dishes “on the plate” was, God forbid, not some “Agudah” councillor, who went into the town council to “defend the Jewish religion”, but in fact a Zionist — better said, a Zionist activist, Mrs. Ratner, who came out against the great injustice done to Jewish children who must eat “kosher-kvitsh”[?] during their cure..
Naturally, none of the Jewish councillors supported the motion — whose business is it? And the whole question depends on the grace of the President, who promised that “it will be done”... But be that as it may, the Zionists are very pleased that their councillor defends kashrut matters, and, as people say, the board of the Zionist Organisation has decided that when the appointment of a fourth moreh hora'ah [rabbinical decisor] becomes topical, the Zionists will put forward the candidacy of Mrs. Ratner..
And believe me, Reb Shlomo (let it stay between us), if this resolution were carried out, kashrut matters in our town would stand on a higher level than today.. and in the synagogue the shammes would not be announcing that the sausage at So-and-so son of So-and-so is nevelah and treyfah...
As for your questions, such as: has the spiritual chaos in the synagogue stopped yet? how much longer will the present dozors [members of the kehilla board] stay in power? and about the scandal that happened at “Ahavat Chesed” — I shall not write this time, because I am hurrying to the lecture of a certain Dr. Szalman, who “knows” the secret of “how to become rich”. I have a great desire for that — not for the lecture, but to become rich. A fine[?] thing is the little coin: for a little coin you have the world, and never mind after a hundred and twenty years — surely, surely: eulogies pour from every corner, the “Talmud Torah” children cry “Righteousness shall go before him”, and thousands of people whisper with their lips: “May good angels come to meet him”...
So have a good Sabbath, wishes you — your
Ben Amotz.
The main thing I forgot! I have just read in the newspapers that the mysterious poison casket of the terrible and beautiful Lucrezia Borgia is being put up at a public auction in Berlin; do take the trouble and buy it for me. Oh, how useful such a little box would be for cleaning out our “domestic mouse-plague”... The above.

In What Light Zagłębie Is Seen in the Eyes of Foreign Visitors

[Zagłębie — impressions/essay; series, part II.]
II.
And yet Będzin has no great joy from its Jewishness. One could say — quite the contrary. Because of it, it has plenty to sing and tell about [i.e. it suffers for it]. Here in Poland we have not yet reached the point of judging social phenomena objectively. People do not want to know that one yardstick can apply in municipal and economic life — achievement.
The favour of the deciding circles has turned away from Jewish Będzin. Goodwill is being transferred more and more to its neighbour S o s n o w i e c. Some 50 years ago this place was a village, known for its large, beautiful pine forest, and nothing more. From that very word — "sosna" [pine] — the name of the town is also said to derive. The "witz" [pun: Yiddish "vitz" = joke, and the town's ending -wiec] comes only now...
Sosnowiec — where Jews make up altogether about 15 percent — is now consistently favoured at the expense of Będzin. A chamber of commerce for Zagłębie is created — its seat is not Będzin but Sosnowiec; the district court and the labour court have been placed in Sosnowiec. The big Polish joint-stock companies establish their branches there. In short — Sosnowiec becomes the "metropolis", the one that sets the tone. Będzin stays behind. It is being reduced to a second-rate town.
It is a system. It is a tendency, although it has no great practical significance.
Zagłębie has grown greatly in the last ten years and climbs ever higher on the ladder of industrial and commercial development. The borders between one town and the next are steadily being levelled. D ą b r o w a–B ę d z i n–S o s n o w i e c is today in fact one large centre: one power station supplies current and light to all three towns, one telephone exchange serves all three places, and one electric tramway — which, incidentally, has been running for only 1 year — connects them.
When one travels from one town to the other, whether by tram or by train, one must be an excellent connoisseur of local conditions to be able to establish where Dąbrowa ends and Będzin begins, and where the Będzin–Sosnowiec border lies. Along the whole line — one long row of industrial establishments, one dense net of chimneys.
Still, there is a difference. Dąbrowa and Sosnowiec are mainly industrial centres; Będzin, on the other hand, concentrates the nerve of trade for all of Zagłębie. A trade that blooms and grows, where Jewish agility, Jewish initiative and enterprising spirit work wonders.
Zagłębie is today the liveliest, most bustling trading place in Poland. It is the bridge that links the crisis-stricken, bankruptcy-ridden [?] Łódź textile region with rich industrial Upper Silesia. A mighty crank [?] turns from the impoverished towns of "Congress Poland" to Katowice, Königshütte, far out to the German border, and keeps alive [?] in the present bitter-hard time tens of thousands of livelihoods that the economic crisis has crushed.
A tumult, a fair, as far as the eye can reach; a swarm of people; the pavements, the roadway — one tangle, colourful, noisy, mobile; merchants and shop assistants pull [passers-by] by the coat-tails, the passers-by are dragged into the shops, one is offered even bird's milk. Commerce is in full blaze...
I am on the "famous" Modrzejowska Street in Sosnowiec — the "Nalewki", the "Nowomiejska" of Zagłębie.
It is a remarkable picture that catches the eye. The crowd that fills the street so densely is a strange, unusual one. Young and old, men and women, more women than men, all in shabby clothes, neither townish nor rustic — it is something peculiar, special.
These are the "Ślązaks" [Silesians].
One recognises them at once. This is not the human material of core [?] Poland, of "our" Poland. Here there is none of the costumed wealth of colour of the Łowicz peasant dress, there is none of the pleasant primitiveness of the "Krakowiaks", nor is the slovenly finery of the "Congress-Pole" to be seen. The people and the clothing — grey, monotonous, exactly like the industrial region they come from, like the coal pits and smelters that have just spat out most of them, or their men, and that will soon swallow them again for long, long hours...
And this crowd, so foreign and strange to our eye [?], speaking the typical "Wasserpolnisch" and itself flowing like water, fills the town, draws in long, almost closed rows from the railway station to "Modrzejowska" Street and back to the station...
The essence of the story:
Once, in very ancient times, the local chronicles relate, Zagłębie was the point at which the attacks of the "Ślązaks" were aimed. They came running here armed, eager for war, to rule this neglected but blessed province, which had the misfortune to lie right by the Prussian border..
Today they come here again in their thousands, whole camps — it is a new kind of "invasion", a good one, a dear one, a welcome one: day in, day out they stream to the shops, empty the shelves of goods, but on leaving they leave the shopkeepers full drawers of takings. It is a rush that brings an abundance of livelihood, a golden (now only a "silver") rain of luck and blessing.
Appeal!

[Zionism — Congress elections.] We have been asked by the Central Bureau of "Et Livnot" in Poland to print the following appeal:
Fellow Zionists!
We are entering the election campaign for the 16th Congress. The time has come for soul-searching for every Zionist, who must think over the achievements of the movement and the great tasks it has to fulfil in the near future.
This year's Congress is, more than all previous ones, a Congress of decisions for Zionism. Not for mandates, not for personal honours, but for correct ideas, for the right path in today's work of building up — that is what this struggle must be about. And not phrases and polemical passion, but life and the experience of recent years shall decide which ideas are the correct ones and who has shown the right path.
1) We, the "Et Livnot" group, were the pioneers of the idea of the enlarged "Jewish Agency" back when a large part of the Zionist movement set itself against this plan, when others wavered, and still others supported the plan half-heartedly; when [printed "ווי"], out of necessity, we of "Et Livnot" saw in the realisation of the "enlarged Jewish Agency" the beginning of a new era for the building-up work in Eretz Israel.
6 years have passed since the struggle over the Agency began, and today the overwhelming majority of the Zionist movement awaits with faith and joy the historic turning point, when all the creative forces of our people will take upon themselves, together with us, the sacred right and the heavy burden bound up with the establishment of our national home.
2) Years ago we put forward the slogans of intensive upbuilding of Eretz Israel with all forces and through all forces of the Jewish people. At a time when the upbuilding of Eretz Israel had become one-sided, when colonisation rested on individual strata of the people and towards the others an attitude of disbelief and distrust had developed, we promoted faith in the creative Jewish hands and minds, without distinction of strata and classes. We argued that all strata must be treated equally by the Zionist movement, because they all hold within them great creative forces which sooner or later will develop for the good of the Jewish land and for the strengthening of the Jewish nation.
We were alone in defending this slogan. 6 years have passed, and the ranks of those who have understood the correctness of this slogan have grown enormously. The majority of the General Zionists in various countries, the Revisionists, a large part of "Mizrachi" and, to a wider extent, also the workers' parties today recognise the creative significance of the Fourth Aliyah, which developed and raised the percentage of the Jewish population in the country (from 11 per cent in 1922 to 19 per cent in 1928) [and not] only [printed "נור אויך"] also the number of industrial enterprises, artisans' workshops, plantations, business connections with abroad and with the neighbouring countries, investments of large private capital, which is now flowing to Eretz Israel in a rising trend, creating more and more possibilities for a larger immigration.
Today it is clear to every seriously thinking Zionist that the success of our colonisation depends on correct economic methods, that the creation of new employment opportunities and the enlargement of the aliyah are closely bound up with the development of private initiative and — apart from the national funds — with the influx of private capital into Eretz Israel.
3) With complete devotion and enthusiasm for the pure Herzlian idea we go to the elections for the 16th Zionist Congress.
For years, "statist" propaganda and genuine statist concepts have contended within the Zionist movement. While part of the movement played at statist fictions (government and opposition, etc.), we, the "Et Livnot" group, demanded rational administrative methods in the conduct of our work in Eretz Israel. For years we fought for a strong and purposeful leadership in Eretz Israel, which should not be a plaything in the hands of political passions, but should carry out unswervingly the programme of the building-up work as it is adopted by the Congress.
After long years of debates and differences of opinion, the Fifteenth Congress carried out our idea and elected an Executive for Eretz Israel. The objective observer will admit that this very Executive, despite all the difficult conditions, for the first time mastered the situation in Eretz Israel and became the leading factor in our building-up work.
4) For six years a debate has been going on in the Zionist ranks about the Zionist Organisation. The opposition groups swear their loyalty to the idea of the Organisation and at the same time they fragment the forces of the Organisation through internal struggles and exaggerated factionalism. We, the "Et Livnot" group, declared from the beginning that the Zionist Organisation must remain the decisive factor of ideas and that within the framework of the Jewish Agency it must play the leading role and provide the spiritual leadership. That is why we were against fragmentation, against the development of the process of splitting into factions and against any struggle for power within the Zionist Organisation. Precisely in order to strengthen the Zionist Organisation and to secure for it its natural leading role we strove for consolidation in the world movement and for peace and unification in the Zionist ranks in Poland.
These moods of consolidation and peace have now become universally popular; let it therefore be recalled here too that the first word against internal fragmentation and Zionist fratricidal struggles was spoken by our group.
This is the historical sum total of our course of ideas. The 16th Congress has to carry through the work that was begun and to carry out to the end the tasks that were outlined. The Jewish Agency must be realised. The further building-up work in Eretz Israel must rest on all strata of the people and take into account sound economic methods. The leadership must be strong and purposeful, the Organisation must be united and closed in its ranks.
For this we have fought for years in the ranks of the Zionist Organisation. For this the struggle must still be waged during the elections to the forthcoming Zionist Congress.
The formulation of these guidelines, as well as the exact setting of the tasks our delegates will have at the Congress, will be determined by the conference of "Et Livnot", which will convene on 9 June in Warsaw.
On the eve of the final victory of the ideas for which we have fought, confident of the trust of the broad Zionist circles in Poland, we call upon our members and sympathisers and urge them to strengthen our ranks and to continue with all their energy the work of enlightenment in all Zionist circles and groups.
Our way leads through today's Eretz Israel to the redeemed Jewish people, and through today's Jewish masses to a built-up, free Eretz Israel!

Będzin — Municipal budget before the plenum of the city council.

Tuesday's session of the city council was chaired by the vice-chairman Mr. Yaakov Erlich. Before the agenda, 3 urgent motions and one interpellation were considered. An urgent motion by Dr. Rechtman that the city administration should deepen the river in Małobądz in order to protect the neighbouring streets from flooding during a downpour. The interpellation, also by Dr. Rechtman, was addressed to the presidium of the city council concerning the repressions against the traders of the Old Market. The urgent motion is adopted, and regarding the interpellation the chairman declares that an answer will be given at the next session.
On the agenda: second reading of the budget. At the item "healing the sick", councillor Feiner proposes that a sum of 10 thousand zł. be set aside for sending sick people to various health resorts. Councillors Kleinman and Mrs. Ratner speak on the question, and Dr. Rechtman's amendment was adopted, that the item should also apply to support for those who are[?] undergoing a cure outside the city.
At the item "pension for the veterinary doctor", Mrs. Ratner and Dr. Rechtman speak, pointing out that the veterinarian, who is employed barely 3 hours a day, earns no less than about 18 thousand zł. a year...
None of the councillors from the other clubs reacted to this argument, and the question of reducing the pension is taken off the agenda.
The continuation of the second reading will take place next Tuesday.
School commission cleansed of Jews...

A few days ago a plenary session of the school commission (Dozór Szkolny) took place in the local magistrate under the chairmanship of President Michał, at which 2 representatives of the school system were to be elected. For years, 1 Christian and 1 Jew had always been elected without discussion, but at the last session the mood changed. No Jewish representative of the public (powszechne) schools was elected any more.
The Jewish candidate Mr. Rapaport received 1 vote...
“Der Iker” (“The Main Thing”) is playing today with the Vilna troupe.

The Vilna Troupe, which consists of first-class stage talents, made itself an excellent[?] name among the local theatre public with its staging of “Kiddush Hashem” and “Unterwelt” (“Underworld”). Today they are giving the not-yet-performed, rich-in-content play “Der Iker” (“The Main Thing”), a drama in 4 acts.
It is to be expected that this time too the Jewish theatre public will receive the artists as they deserve.

On Wednesday the presidium of the city administration signed the purchase agreement for the plot where the cattle market is located. The plot was bought from the French-Italian company for 236 thousand zł.

Mr. Lidobarski, who had entered the city council as representative of the small traders, has resigned as councillor. In his place Mr. Dawid Gitler enters.
Esperantists' convention in Będzin.

In the hall on “Góra Zamkowa” a convention of the Esperantist associations in Zagłębie took place on Sunday.
The participants in the convention were almost exclusively from among our Jewish brethren, mostly minors, who are, as always, the first bearers of culture...
The convention is opened (in Polish) by Dr. Jungster of Sosnowiec, who invites the leaders of the Esperanto language in Zagłębie to the presidium, reads the greetings of the organisations that did not come to the convention, greets the representatives of the city council, the city administration and the school authorities, and proceeds to the agenda with a lecture on the significance of Esperanto as an international language.
After the lecture the Esperanto hymn is sung and greetings follow.
On behalf of the Będzin city council the chairman Mr. Fürstenberg greets, on behalf of the city administration — ławnik Żebrowski, on behalf of “Frayhayt” (“Freedom”) — Mr. Weissalz (in Esperanto), and others.
Then the Esperanto hymn is sung and Mr. Wojciechowski gives a lecture on the development of the language. The speaker stresses that through the language the Esperantist becomes a citizen of the world, who unites all mankind into one culture.
As a demonstration, the Misses Gleitzer and Rozen recite very beautifully (in Esperanto). With this the morning session ends.
At the afternoon session the question of propaganda was discussed. A resolution was adopted to intervene with the school authorities so that Esperanto be taught in the public (powszechne) schools.
In the evening an entertainment took place, where the youth amused themselves “in the Esperanto manner”...
Subsidy for the “Orphans' Home” raised.
At the last city council session councillor Mrs. Ratner moved that the subsidy for the “Orphans' Home” be raised from 30 to 35 thousand zł. After the factual justification the motion was adopted.
Schoolgirls' excursion to Poznań.
Yesterday evening 48 schoolgirls of public school No. 4 left for Poznań and Danzig.
A Jewish Little Girl Falls into a Latrine Pit and Is Rescued

[Będzin — accidents.] In the house of Mr. Gisler on Modrzejowska Street a Jewish little girl fell into a latrine pit. At the girl's cries people came running, and with the help of a rope they pulled the child out of the pit alive.
Because of a "Mistake" They Committed a Burglary...!

[Będzin — crime.] On the night from Monday to Tuesday thieves broke into the electrical-supplies shop of Mr. Goldfeld, from which they stole goods worth a few thousand zł.
The thieves worked hard until they broke open the safe, where they found no more than 2 zł.
The next morning one of the thieves was arrested. Under interrogation the thief declared that they had carried out the burglary "by mistake" (al pi ta'ut), because they had had quite different plans..
The Summer Colonies Will Be Better Arranged This Year

[Będzin — welfare.] This week the Commission for Social Welfare held a meeting, at which it was decided that comfortable places for the children to sleep are to be arranged at the summer colonies in Sławków.
Academy in Honour of the Co-operative Holiday

[Będzin — economy.] In the "Korso" hall the management of the Co-operative Bank in Będzin held on Sunday morning an academy (festive assembly) dedicated to Co-operative Day, which was celebrated throughout the world.
The academy was opened and chaired by the vice-chairman of the bank's board, Mr. L. Bauszykowski [?], who invited to the presidium representatives of neighbouring co-operative banks and other communal workers, and gave the first word to the bank manager, Mr. Goldsztajn, who spoke on the significance of co-operation and its great benefit.
Messrs. Pesachson and the representative of the Credit Bank, Mr. Tenenbaum, also spoke on the subject.
In conclusion the bank's chairman, Mr. Fürstenberg, took the floor and said a few true words: that at the present time, when the Jewish masses are living through such a crisis, he very much doubts whether any family can save anything...
Sosnowiec — Plenary Session of the City Council

[Sosnowiec — city council.] (Sh.) After a rather long break, the 10th plenary session of the city council was convened on Tuesday; this time it was distinguished by its quick pace and by the adoption of all the magistrate's proposals almost unanimously.
———
With an hour's delay Chairman Dr. Pawełek opens the session. After the report of Dr. Rządkiewicz [?] the following resolutions are adopted unanimously: 1) to confirm the conditions of the Bank Gosp. Kraj. [Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego] regarding the loan of 150 thousand dollars (the loan project had already been adopted at the last session on the 27th of last month), 2) to take a loan of 100 thousand zł. to complete the building of the school on Okrzei Street. The 3rd item on the agenda — the election of a member of the Voivodeship Council — is also dealt with quickly, and with 18 votes Dep. Bień is elected. Further, Dr. Burzyński [?] is elected as a member of the commission of the "Hungarian" [?] hospital in Będzin, and at about 9 in the evening the chairman closes the session.
On the Day of Their Father's Yahrzeit They Lost Their Mother — Tragic Death of a Jewish Woman

[Sosnowiec — accidents.] A tragic accident happened last Friday afternoon on 3 Maja Street.
Walking along the street was the 52-year-old Rykla Sztajnic, owner of a fruit shop on Warszawska Street. When she was not far from the "Cukiernia Warszawska" (confectionery), the passenger bus of the Tabiasz firm arrived. In the same direction, from the other side, a droshky was also driving, and the driver, wishing to avoid a collision with the droshky, hastily turned the bus back. At that moment Mrs. Sztajnic was close to the bus, and from the strong blow she was thrown against a tree, and from the impact against the tree she suffered a concussion. On the way to the hospital the unfortunate woman died.
The funeral of the tragically killed woman took place on Sunday. The wailing reached the heart of heaven. The coffin was carried along Modrzejowska Street and stopped at the house of Mr. Tabiasz as a sign of protest.
On the same day as the funeral a circumcision (brit milah) was to take place at Mr. Tabiasz's, which had already been postponed twice, and this time too the brit was postponed because of the tragic incident.
The killed woman left several unmarried children. On the very same day on which they lost their mother, their father had died a year ago.
The Trial of the Jewish Merchants — Adjourned

[Sosnowiec — courts.] Great interest was aroused by the trial which was to take place in the local district court against the merchants Dawid Fiura, Bernard Grajcer, Eli' Fiura, Wacław Mediński, Tomasz Banach, Józef Klimas, Josef Urbach, Szymon Ehrenstein and L. Gotrajch, who were accused of bringing goods from abroad in an illegal manner.
Also sitting in the dock were several officials of the customs office who had a connection to the affair.
138 witnesses were summoned to the sensational trial. The defence consisted of six of the best lawyers from Warsaw and three from Sosnowiec.
Because a few principal witnesses were missing, the court agreed to the defenders' proposal to adjourn the trial to an unspecified date.
The defenders also wished to release from prison the merchants Dawid Fiura and Jekl Grajcer against 10 thousand zł. and Eliasz Fiura against 20 thousand zł. bail.
—o—
Died at Her Son's Bedside.
[Sosnowiec — deaths.] At the age of 80 the esteemed lady Taubele Neufeld died in recent days. She died suddenly while visiting her sick son Heniek.
—o—
The Present Board Throws Off the Old Sins..
[Sosnowiec — organisations.] On Sunday the new board of the Merchants' Association (Piłsudskiego 12) held a meeting, at which the question was discussed of why the association has no representative in the Chamber of Commerce.
It was decided to issue a communiqué that the blame for this lies with the previous board.
—o—
A Bloody Fight over the Evening Prayer...
[Sosnowiec — community.] With a bandaged head Mr. Efraim Galenzer came to us at the editorial office and told the following:
Last Sunday G. was standing at the prayer stand (amud) in the beit midrash to lead the evening prayer (maariv). At that moment Mr. Jechiel Fajger came up and demanded that Galenzer let him take the amud, and when Mr. G. refused the demand, Fajger threw off his coat and threw himself on Galenzer, inflicting on him with an iron door handle several deep wounds in the head.
First aid in the beit midrash was given by Dr. Zalk, who with great effort stopped the bleeding and bandaged the wounds.
—o—
Guest Performances of "Ararat" in Zagłębie.
[Zagłębie — theatre.] The first Jewish chamber theatre "Ararat" of Łódź, under the direction of the poet Moshe Broderzon, has come to Zagłębie for a number of guest performances. On Wednesday and Thursday "Ararat" played in Będzin and had an enormous success.
Tonight a performance in the local "City Theatre". The programme: "Shoshanat Yaakov" and "Everything Dances".
On Saturday afternoon in "Nadaszczy" [?], Będzin, 2 programmes will be given together.
—o—
Town Administration in Czeladź — Resigned.
[Czeladź — municipality.] This week the town council in Czeladź held a meeting. At the meeting the mayor and deputy mayor made declarations that, because the government categorically refused to grant a loan, the town administration cannot run the town's economy, and they are laying down their mandates.

The Small Trader

[Article — small trade and taxes.] What does the small trader want? What does he demand? It is hard to formulate, to express in a few words what this kind of person demands, what hurts him and what he asks for. Whichever way you turn, it is all troubles; when there is no sound limb, how can one point to one particular point, to one fact? It seems to me, therefore, that the situation can be characterised by the fact that the small trader is fighting to be recognised as what he is: that it should be established once and for all and recognised by law that there exists in the world such a kind of person, such a kind of merchant, belonging to the category [printed "k tegoria"] which in economic language is called "small trader" — and that he should be treated accordingly.
On the ladder of economic life there are, after all, various strata. The government has, for example, recognised that there is the peasant, an ordinary farmer, and there is the squire, the owner of a large estate. Among landowners there are certain categories as regards paying tax. Thus we know, for example, that a peasant who owns 15 morgs of land counts as a poor man and is entirely exempt from tax. Yet this poor man is, even by our standards, a rich man, since he owns property worth 50 thousand złoty; but in agriculture it is held that his income is minimal and that he cannot pay any taxes.
In the urban economy there is hardly any minimum income at all for which one is exempted from tax. At most there is such a minimum for the worker, but that too is so small that only someone who is actually dying of hunger [printed "higiner"] is exempt from tax. Worst of all is the lot of the so-called "merchant". For him there is no consideration at all. He is measured straight away at full size. Here lies the misfortune of the small trader: it is a misfortune when someone is made into a rich man so that afterwards he can be turned into a pauper.
Does one need to give examples of this? Go into the small traders' association of whatever town you like, and listen to what people tell about the assessments of turnover tax for the last year, and you will be convinced that there is a forcible drive to make people into rich men, into big merchants with enormous turnovers. From almost everyone you will hear that his turnover has been reckoned at two or three times as much as a year earlier. Here, a grocery shop was assessed a year ago at 18 thousand zł., and this year already at 36 thousand zł. A second grocery shop was assessed a year ago at 25 thousand, and this year at a full 60 thousand. For one butcher the turnover was raised from 50 thousand to 135 thousand zł.
Such examples can be given without end. One sees that a tendency prevails to do away with the small trader as a type, to make everyone into big merchants. That would be very good and one could welcome it if one really saw [printed "geven"] the turnover, and hence the profit, grow. By putting a large turnover on paper one at most makes that man into a big pauper, but not into a big merchant!
And the whole [unclear word, printed "firenyit" — apparently "wrath/burden"] is poured out only on the small dealer, shopkeeper and merchant, because the big one keeps books — him one cannot assess just out of thin air, him one cannot estimate, and so all the anger is vented on the small trader who keeps no books and cannot defend himself at all. But the question arises: where is justice? Has anyone ever [?] seen many merchants who keep books whose turnover grew two-fold or even six-fold in the course of a year? If it does not happen there, one must understand that with the shopkeeper and dealer — a branch that suffers terribly from competition — it is surely impossible for the turnover to grow so much!
The small trader therefore fights for his recognition. He demands that a minimum for trade be fixed once and for all, just as it exists in agriculture, and that the minimum be stable, that it not depend on the good or bad will of an "inspector" or official; that it be known that the fourth category pays at most so much, the third so much, and so on. Let the assessments and the surprises come to an end.
That is how we understand the demands of the small trader, and we hold that the decisive factors must listen to the demands, for surely nobody wants to ruin a large stratum of the population!
S. J. Stupnicki.
Sport

[Sport — football.]
1. F.C. "Kattowitz" — "Hakoach" 3:4.
Had "Hakoach" come out for this match in a better line-up and not underrated the opponent, it would certainly have won the match. The best proof is the score up to half-time, 3:2 in "Hakoach"'s favour. In the second half the young players of "Hakoach" run out of strength, cannot keep up the strong pace, and lose the match. The goals were scored by Richter, Goldsztajn [printed "Noldshteyn"] and Lask. Weigberg distinguished himself in the "Hakoach" goal.
D.F.C. "Sturm" (Bielitz) — "Hakoach" 2:2.
The guests from Bielitz [Bielsko] showed fine football, playing technically and at a fast pace; above all the good positional play caught the eye — wherever the ball fell, a "Sturm" player was already waiting there. In the first half "Hakoach" plays very weakly, chaotically, without ambition; in the second half "Hakoach" shows play that is truly a pleasure to watch. The 2 players Rotenberg and Jankielewicz 2 stood out in particular.
In the first half "Sturm" scores 2 goals. 5 minutes before half-time Richter manages to score the first goal for "Hakoach" with a sharp shot from about 30 metres. In the second half "Hakoach" equalises from an eleven-metre kick [penalty] through Rotenberg. Although "Hakoach" now has great superiority, it does not manage to achieve the deserved [printed "ferdigisn"] victory, thanks to the ambitious defence of the guests. It is also worth singling out the young players Jankielewicz 3 and Nugberg, who stood in very well for their older comrades. Referee Mr. Jarza — good.
"Kraft" — "Shtern" 0:4.
The match between the above-mentioned workers' clubs ended in a deserved victory for "Kraft", which had a slight superiority over "Shtern" the whole time and scored 2 goals in the first half and another 2 goals in the second half.
Korn and the "Kraft" goalkeeper distinguished themselves. On the other hand the reserve goalkeeper of "Shtern" was weak. Referee Mr. Szywek. M. Z.

To You, Comrades — Matriculants!

[Keren Kayemet — appeal of the gymnasium graduates; a "Ring".] The day on which we receive the matriculation certificate brings a colossal change into our way of life. We leave the school benches and hurry to the higher schools, universities, polytechnics etc., in order to prepare ourselves to take a suitable place in social life. In this joyful moment, however, we must not forget the duty which rests upon us as members of Jewish society. We must not forget that we must come to the aid of our scattered and dispersed brethren. We, as young people, understand best and feel most strongly the injustice which is done to us at every step, and therefore it is our duty to join the ranks of the builders of our old-new land, in the land of our fathers; with our sweat and toil we shall carry the bricks for the great building of our beautiful future, which awaits us only in Eretz Israel. We therefore consider it our duty at the present moment to help the upbuilding of Eretz Israel. To this end we are organising in the columns of the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" a "Ring" for the Keren Kayemet LeIsrael, whose task is to buy back the land of Eretz Israel from foreign hands. The land is [printed "in"] the foundation of every people, and therefore the KKL devotes its entire activity solely to the redemption of the land of Eretz Israel.
We hope that the action [—] which we are organising in the col[umns of the] "Zaglembier Tsaytung" will [—] with the greatest success. [—] [—]

From the Chess Tournament in Zagłębie

[Zagłębie — chess.]
The chess tournament, which began two weeks ago for promotion to the extra class, is already at the end of the first round. The 8 players taking part show equal strength, and no decisive superiority of any single player can be noticed, so that there is not a single player who is undefeated. Joint-Stock Companies in Poland

[Economy — joint-stock companies in Poland; a reference book; probably an advertorial.]
In the countries of high economic culture a dominant role is played by joint-stock companies and enterprises in which capitals are united. In this field banks and big industry figure, but trade too makes use to a great extent of this form of organising capital.
In comparison with other countries, the development of joint-stock companies in Poland is weak; nevertheless, after the crisis of 1925/26 the Polish joint-stock companies succeeded in consolidating their finances.
There was an urgent need to publish a book of addresses and information for the wide circles about the joint-stock companies in Poland.
The publisher "PAR" — "Joint-Stock Companies in Poland" — has satisfied this need, providing all kinds of information about all joint-stock companies in the whole of Poland. Indicated are: seat, branches, year of foundation, purpose, amount of capital, names of the management and supervisory board, etc.
The book has appeared in French, English and German, so as to give the possibility to those who do not know Polish.
The publication "Joint-Stock Companies in Poland" is therefore an information book for the wide scholarly circles, and also for those interested in money investments in the country.
The book can be obtained at the publishing and advertising bureau "PAR" in Poznań [?] and in all its branches.

Public honour and benefit — (What is going on with the Sosnowiec "Linas Hacholim"? How can we improve our institutions?)

(What is going on with the Sosnowiec "Linas Hacholim"? How can we improve our institutions?)
Not long ago we read a notice in the newspaper about how a Sosnowiec porter complained that the local "Linas Hacholim" did not want to lend him a bathtub for his sick wife, even though the porter wanted to give a pledge on the bathtub. The chairman — it was said there — gave as his reason that he could not grant the request because the person concerned is not a member of the institution.
And the question arises: does the institution care only for its members? Does it serve with its appliances only the people who maintain the institution? If so, then such an institution is perhaps entirely superfluous, because those who pay and are able to pay never need to use the equipment of the "Linas Hacholim": a Jew like that, if he needs a bathtub, has one at home, since such a person has a bathtub with all the conveniences and thus has his own bathroom.
We believe, however, that it is — and must also be — otherwise: that the well-to-do families maintain such an institution only so that it may be able to serve and benefit the poor strata of the population, those who cannot afford sick-care institutions of their own and those who do not have dwellings with all the conveniences.
We know that a "Linas Hacholim" exists among us, we know that it is a philanthropic institution, but unfortunately we never hear whether the institution is alive, whether it is breathing, and what its activity consists of. Nor do we hear that the institution ever gives an account to the population, that it convenes a general meeting where we could learn about its good and bad sides, its merits and its shortcomings.
Surely such a philanthropic society should not be a stranger in the eyes of the local citizens; surely such an institution ought to be popular in town, so that everyone knows about it and everyone is aware of what it does and what it provides. And if such an injustice occurs that a poor family cannot get any item on loan there merely because it is not a member of the institution, then the members ought to react to such a thing, and the leaders of such an institution ought to be reproached for it, because such a society must serve exclusively the poor strata of the population; for we are certain that the rich and well-to-do families want to maintain a "Linas Hacholim" so that it serves those who need its support, those who need to come there to borrow whatever it may be.
It often happens that the members of a society do not know whether the institution provides anything, and to what extent it provides for the community. People know only that they pay their monthly commitment when the collector comes in for the amount due. And that is precisely where the fault lies.
It is high time that we knew what we are doing. For just as it is a failing when one does not properly support what ought to be supported, so it is a failing when one supports an institution merely out of indifference, only because for many people the small amount plays no role. This system must disappear. We must not support any institution when we do not know whether it is entitled to exist, when we do not know whether it brings the community the proper benefit.
The system of supporting institutions merely because the amount plays no role must be done away with once and for all. We must not support public institutions just to discharge an obligation, just as we must not remain indifferent to them. We must never forget, once and for all, that public enterprises belong to the whole community, and as such they must be dear and beloved to us, congenial, and we devoted to them.
It goes without saying that we do not mean by this that our "Linas Hacholim" is undesirable or that it should be abolished; nor do we mean to say that it brings no benefit. But we do say that it is an enormous injustice when such an institution does not serve the poor strata of the population. In general, we are far from expressing any opinion whatsoever about an institution which stands far from public activity. Unfortunately we do not hear to what extent it is active, to what extent it brings benefit or harm to the population.
And this, we say, must not be: indifference, apathy and helplessness must be eliminated in our little world. We must know once and for all why we patronise this or that institution and why we do not sympathise with another institution. The system of supporting public enterprises simply to discharge an obligation must finally be eliminated. It must not exist on the public level. Either — or: either we recognise that the institution has a right to exist, and then we must maintain it — not because it would be unseemly otherwise, but because a sacred duty lies upon us; or we see, on the other hand, that the society is no good, that it is not congenial to us and brings no benefit to the public — then we must have the courage and boldness to declare openly that the institution is not worthy of being supported by the public, and therefore it should take up no place among us.
We must once and for all get used to looking with open eyes and always boldly proclaiming the truth. Only in this way can public interests among us take a different turn; only then can we hope to have truly useful public institutions, which will bring us honour and the wider public — benefit.
Dr. Papuri.
Little Feuilleton: A Hard Question

[Feuilleton.]
A Hard Question.

So whom, after all, should I write about, eh?
I always thought that one has to write about the living. As it says there in the verse: "And the living will lay it to heart" — the living will take it to heart. Something may stick, and it will have an effect.
But my honoured reader tells me right away [?]:

— Oh, go on! Why [?] should you pester him? A bill of exchange of his is circulating on the stock exchange, his daughter is in the middle of matchmaking, and just like that — a living person. Don't you know? "Mountain does not meet mountain, but man meets man" — eh, leave him in peace!

So I thought it over: perhaps he really is right, my honoured reader! One must not start up with a living person. As long as a person is alive, one can never be sure of him; tomorrow he may himself become an editor and even teach me manners — "such things" happen here too.

So I had better write about a dead man. A dead man has many virtues — he cannot become an editor, he cannot give you a slap, and in general he has already closed his account, so one may surely draw up a little bottom line...

Then my honoured reader is here again:
— God be with you, what are you doing! You are going to disturb one who dwells in the dust? Don't you know that of the departed one speaks either good or nothing? And what do you think, his relatives and friends will keep silent with you? And what is the point of writing it at all? He can't put anything right anyway now!... No, the deceased you shall not pester, do you hear!

That means: not a living one, and not a dead one either — so whom, then, am I to touch?

Perhaps I should write about those who have not yet been born? With them too I am not quite sure — they may still settle accounts with me later on.

One single remedy remains: to write about the not-yet-born who will never be born.

About abortions...

That is also [printed "אוב"] very piquant, and my honoured reader will lick his fingers. I have known for a long time that my honoured reader would sooner read a thousand tales from the bedroom than one story from everyday life...

But again there is a trouble: these innocent and harmless miscarried little ones have, after all, living people around them, who brought them into the world and who brought them out of the world.

So once again one has to pester a living person...

In short, brothers, it's bitter...

For the time being it is still not too bad. It is cucumber season [the silly season], so I will write about cucumbers. But what will happen later? About what, about whom will I then write after all? — —

Argus.
Letter from Krynica

Krynica lies 740 metres above sea level. — Krynica of the past and of today. — Antisemitism then and now. — The consequences and significance of the spa. — Efforts are being made to improve everything. — How can one settle in practically? — The weak season and the crisis in the country.
Krynica is the most popular spa in Poland, among Christians as well as among Jews; it will therefore be worth dwelling a little more broadly on this spa.
Krynica lies 740 metres above sea level; moreover, it is surrounded by mountains upon mountains, which purify and distil the air. But that is the least of it. More important are the waters, which often cure people in an extraordinary way. There are various springs here with which the best take their cure; the Krynica mineral waters (spring water) and the borowina (peat-mud) baths are also reckoned the best in Poland. The truth of this is confirmed by the fact that many guests from abroad stay here year after year.
Not only as a spa is Krynica counted among the first-class ones; in the material sense, too, it is the most expensive. Here both the baths and lodging in the boarding houses are dear, and whatever you touch, you are first of all made to pay well, so that taking a cure in Krynica is bound to cost a tidy sum.
In the high season unheard-of things happen here. A year ago, for example, there was a panic [?] over tickets for the baths, so that — God preserve us — people got up in the middle of the night and stood at the ticket offices so that their turn would come sooner; and, as in every such case, speculators immediately appeared who exploited every moment. The porters of the villas, too, are well aware of this and take advantage of the moment on the spot. They make various combinations with the tickets and have them at any time.
Krynica thus stands in Poland as the most first-class and most elegant spa: here we see the Polish nobility, the intelligentsia, ministers, the "gilded youth", and whoever just wants to have a good time [?] comes [?] to Krynica.
This is also where the antisemitism here comes from, for to the Polish nobles, when they came to Krynica and saw sick Jews, it was like a spider [sic] in their eyes. Antisemitism used to play first fiddle, but with time the situation has changed, and relations between Jews and Christians are now considerably milder, so that one can somehow bear it. Apparently the government has understood after all that stirring up antisemitism in the spas is far from cultured.
Whoever comes — or rather, whoever came to Krynica for the first time a few years ago — was disappointed. One had heard so much about Krynica, about its dearness, splendour and luxury, that one imagined everything here to be first-class, and found the opposite: everything was so primitive, so simple, that you got the impression of having landed in a village. Until not long ago there were no paved roads, pavements or the various modern facilities that every spa usually has; even the bath-houses were not properly arranged, so that even now, after the new bath-house for spring water has been put up, a great deal is still lacking.
Still, a will to remedy various defects is now noticeable, so that there is a revival both in introducing order for the benefit of the patients and in building in general.
Thus, for example, modern villas are constantly being built in all parts of Krynica, already equipped with the most modern technical facilities, thanks to which prices are not rising as they used to from one year to the next.
The spa administration, too, is now considerably better than it once was, and efforts are being made to improve everything step by step.
On the 4th of this month, for example, spa tickets were issued up to the 14th; it turns out that already on the 4th of the current month one could no longer get tickets for borowina baths, so that one would have had to wait until the 15th, when the issue of fresh tickets would resume — and waiting two weeks for a bath is, after all, a most pleasant thing. At the same time one must not forget that a year ago there was no shortage of borowina baths at a time when Krynica had more than twice as many guests, for last year at this time there were 6,000 guests, whereas up to the 4th there were not yet even 3,000. And so the question arose: what combination has suddenly happened here? Why should tickets run out so early? In the past this would have interested nobody, and the disorder would have gone on progressing. Now, however, the spa administration reacted properly to this incomprehensible phenomenon, and by the next day tickets could already be had for every day.
The fact that the spa administration has given the opportunity and is accommodating in the building of new villas [has caused] the "price screw" [?] of the boarding-house keepers to burst. There are now, for example, boarding houses where a day with board costs 10–12 zł.; competition in this field is thus already noticeable, which a year ago was out of the question. Besides, one can now get cheap rooms at 3–5 zł. a day and eat lunches in a restaurant, where it comes to about 3–4 zł. a lunch.
In Krynica, then, the situation is getting better, conditions more normal and relations friendlier.
The director of the spa establishment, Eng. Gawatorski [?], is striving to introduce proper order that will provide comforts for the guests taking the cure.
Director Gawatorski [?] also assures us that the spring-water baths are exceptionally good this year, just as they were in 1927.
As of today there are not yet even 3,000 guests, whereas last year at this time the number reached more than twice as many. From Zagłębie there is a very small number of guests, and from Łódź, too, there are very few people. This is explained by the great crisis in the country, although Director Gawatorski assures us that the reason is that the public believed that foreign passports would become cheaper and would then travel abroad.
In any case, one can now settle in quite well in Krynica, because there are still few guests and the boarding houses are eagerly awaiting them; and for the same reason one also gets tickets for whenever one wishes.
Y. Sh. [?]
Greetings from Home Folk in Eretz Israel

[Eretz Israel — letter; Zagłębie natives in the Land.]
(From our special correspondent).
With every week that I stay in Eretz Israel I keep getting acquainted with new Jews from Zagłębie whom I never knew, or even saw, back home. Every post brings me not only letters from interested [?] landslayt from Zagłębie asking me to visit their relatives and to answer them directly in writing or through this newspaper — the post also brings me letters from "home folk" now living in Eretz Israel, asking me to set aside time for them for conversations and interviews.
From the dozens upon dozens of talks and meetings I have already held in the course of this time, I see that the Jews of Zagłębie form a fairly large community here and, despite the recent re-emigration, occupy an honourable place in the building of the Jewish land.
Even among the many human sacrifices offered on the altar of pioneering in Eretz Israel there are several Zagłębie people, older and younger, who fell in the work and in the conquest of Eretz Israel for the Jewish people. Honour to their memory! May their names always be sacred to us!
Zagłębie in general and Będzin in particular have a name not merely as a large Jewish settlement as such — our region is well known and popular in Eretz Israel as a strong Zionist fortress and centre. Half a year ago, in connection with the Keren Hayesod campaign, when Będzin was the topic of the day in the Warsaw press, not only did Jewish Poland triumph with Będzin, but Eretz Israel too spoke of us with pride. Special telegrams were sent from Poland to the Palestinian papers announcing that of all the towns in Poland, even Warsaw and Łódź, Będzin had distinguished itself especially in its contribution to the Redemption Fund.
Barely half a year has passed and once again our town has been publicised in the columns of the local Hebrew press. Among all the political telegrams there appeared in "Davar" a large dispatch reporting that Będzin had again shown its understanding for Eretz Israel by contributing a thousand dollars to the Eretz Israel Workers' Fund (Kapai) during Ben-Zvi's stay there. The news aroused great satisfaction in the pioneer circles here, and members of "Hitahdut ha-Ovdim" and "Hapoel Hatzair", knowing that I am from the "popular" town of Będzin, treated me like a man of distinguished lineage... Mr. Leib Jaffe, whom I met in Tel Aviv at the conference devoted to the persecuted Zionists in Russia, also took pride in the "Davar" report, crediting the victory also — and rightly so — to his own account. "I succeeded," says Mr. Jaffe with satisfaction, "in conquering the hearts of the Jews of Zagłębie for Eretz Israel, and of that I am proud."
———
Mr. Józef Cwi Rajs of Będzin, who before leaving for Eretz Israel was a broker and money-changer on the exchange there, has thrown off here his easy "air-livelihoods", which have no place in Eretz Israel, and returned to his old trade as a "pehah" (tinsmith). Mr. R. is permanently employed at the "International" motor garage, which manufactures sheet-metal bodies ["carousels" in the original] for buses. I visited him in the craftsmen's quarter "Mahlul", where he has his own "tzrif" (hut), standing on Keren Kayemet land. Mr. R., who at first went through critical times, today does not complain about his situation and speaks with praise of those who made it possible for him to come to Eretz Israel.
Mr. Icchak Ingber of Sosnowiec came with the "Fourth Aliyah" and in the first period took up "zifzif" (beach gravel), which is used in building houses. But since with the outbreak of the crisis came also the stagnation in building, Mr. I. threw off his "gmalim" (camels) and set off for the village of Kfar Saba, which lies next to Magdiel. Mr. I. bought 50 dunams of land and planted an orange grove, from which he will be able to draw his livelihood at a profit. In any case, in 3–4 years he believes he will have his first oranges and later make a fine life.
It is worth noting once again on this occasion the orange plantations, about which I have already written in the "Zaglembier Tsaytung". Eretz Israel possesses only an area of 250 thousand dunams of land suitable for orange groves, of which about 50–60 thousand are already planted, and the rest of the area awaits redemption. The fruit of Eretz Israel, which is famous throughout the world and competes with the chief suppliers of oranges on the world market, gives those who will provide themselves with a piece of orange grove the surest guarantee of a quiet and contented life.
Mr. Jakób Welner of Będzin, a hard-working young man and a strong nationalist, has found work in Kfar Saba at various kinds of unskilled labour. Mr. W. is content with his pioneering life and never goes about sullen. At Purim he "made a pilgrimage" to Tel Aviv and took part in the carnival procession with a group of masqueraders who portrayed the rebbe with his Hasidim.
On the way into the Emek I passed through an Arab village, Jenin (Ein Ganim), where there is one single Jew — and a Będziner at that — Mr. Hersz Józef Liter, who serves in the local police. At the Jenin "police station" (commissariat) I asked after him, and before me appeared a tall, sturdy, broad-shouldered man in police uniform, and I at once recognised Mr. Liwer from my school days. Mr. L. describes his life to me, which is rich in interesting details of police criminology. One detail is worth dwelling on: Mr. L., who was riding to a nearby village on duty, was attacked by two Arab bandits who, shooting, killed his horse and wounded him, and only by a miracle was he saved from certain death. The bandits, whom it proved possible to catch, were sentenced to heavy hard labour and severe imprisonment in the Acre prison.
"The life," says Mr. Liwer to me, "of a Jewish policeman in a strange, remote environment among half-wild Arabs and Bedouins is not especially pleasant, but still I accept everything with love, for I love the country and I believe in a better future."
Mr. Jakób Goldszer (Będzin, Sanczewska [?] 15) — your letter received, and I have visited your 2 brothers-in-law, Messrs. Jechiel Majer and Abraham Menkarski, who have taken the name Kimchi here. For 8 years they lived in Jerusalem, where they ran a hotel, "San Remo", and only last year did they move to Tel Aviv, where they have already settled in. The Kimchi brothers have built themselves a house of their own for 800 pounds, have 2 confectioneries on Allenby Street and on the seashore, as well as a bakery of their own. They are very, very satisfied with their situation and life. They send you their greetings, and also to their brother Mr. Menkarski of Sosnowiec.

M. Hampel.
In What Light Zagłębie Is Seen — Through the Eyes of a Foreign Visitor

[Sosnowiec and Będzin — economy and Jewish–Polish relations; a visitor's impressions, part IV.]
IV.
Sosnowiec, people say here, is the "crown of Zagłębie", and the precious stones that give this crown its charm and value were set in it to no small degree by — Jews.
The Jews, the Jewish merchants, may not know very much of all the seven things called economic science, but they understand a great deal about trade. They know the craft of exploiting a market situation and of creating favourable ground for business opportunities.
The Jews in Poland have, on top of that, a dear (oh, a very "dear"!) teacher — cruel want, the shaky economic ground and the frail[?] hopes of recovery and equal rights...
The bitter times of the constantly renewed economic crises pushed the Jews to seek rescue from their need. Their sound mercantile instinct directed them on the road to Upper Silesia and — Zagłębie.
Over the last years Sosnowiec has grown, grown greatly, commercially and industrially. In industry too, Jewish initiative, Jewish diligence and the Jewish mercantile spirit contributed much to its prosperity. Small, inferior workshops developed under Jewish management into significant factories, which employ legions of workers and blaze the trail for Polish production abroad as well. So in Sosnowiec, and so also in Będzin.
But the Jews' chief merit for Zagłębie lies in the field of trade. Not only in "Jewish" Będzin, but also in Sosnowiec, where the Jews make up barely 15 percent of a population of over 100 thousand souls.
Certainly the antisemites do not like this. With every stratagem they try to undermine the economic positions of the Jews, but they succeed little. On the contrary, they themselves often break their necks in the attempt.
In the heart of Modrzejowska Street, the liveliest place of trade in Sosnowiec, I was shown a splendid "Rozwój" bazaar. Not long ago there stood on this spot a simple market hall. Poor Jews stood here with "little tables" and with hard toil and effort scraped out a living. This was a thorn in the eyes of the "swój do swego" ["each to his own" — the anti-Jewish boycott slogan] people. Partly by Jesuitical, partly by hooligan tricks, the little Jewish shopkeepers were driven from this spot, the stalls torn down, the hall removed. A fine, splendid bazaar was put up here — with a row of "genuinely Polish" shops under the aegis of the Jew-devouring "Rozwój".
Now the boycott heroes, poor things, are in very narrow straits, and the whole enterprise has been exposed to shame and ridicule.
* * *
In the end, trade in Zagłębie too lies in the earth, but deep in the earth. Not "noyn[?] ilan artsa" [a Hebrew phrase, "a tree … to the ground"?] as we say, but much deeper — — in the coal mines...
There, in the bowels of the darkened, meagre earth, from which human labour and human devotion draw out, in pain and sweat, the black diamonds.
The coal mine is here the impulse of all doing and working, the energy of the whole economic life.
Dr. A. Weissman — The Seduced Girl (a novel of Jewish life in the Old World, based on historical facts), instalment 9

[Serial novel — "Di farfirte" (The Seduced Girl), by Dr. A. Weissman; instalment 9.]
The "Sister" spoke such kind words to Mania and looked at her with such gentle eyes that Mania soon became attached to her as if glued.
This Sister was called "Maria" in the convent, a woman of some forty-odd years, younger than her years, with a dark, very sympathetic face and kind eyes. She spoke very quietly and her voice always sounded like a soft, weeping voice that roused in new people a kind of sympathy; people were drawn to her very easily and became open-hearted with her. The younger "Sisters" of the convent, on the other hand, used to treat her coldly and keep their distance.
After lunch "Sister" Maria went out with Mania into the garden for a walk.
— Don't be afraid, my child — said Maria as she went out of the room with Mania — don't think that a convent is a prison, as most people think; on the contrary, it is an institution, a kind of refuge, where the human soul must rise above the worldly chaos; and all the more so for those who are already sick of life — for them our convent is happiness.
— Sister Maria, I love life more than anything in the world, I love life with my whole "vengeance" [sic; read: soul]. For old, worn-out people such a refuge, as you call it, may be necessary, but I am still young, I want to live and only to live.
— Unhappy girl! It is precisely for such as you, who strain so hard toward life, that is, toward the sinful world, that our convent would be a happiness. A sinful soul would be saved, one that wanders about like a poor lamb and can find no place for itself. Tell me, my child, have you already found what you want, what you are looking for?
— I will still find it, I am still young, Sister, I will still find it. It is true that I am wandering, but I will search so long until I find what is mine.
— Do not sin, my child; precisely because you are so young you do not yet know what you yourself are saying. I think that your wanting to leave us is only because you imagine that life with us is too monotonous, tedious, boring. But you are mistaken, my child. I must tell you that besides the soul being calmed here and one finding consolation here for all the misfortunes a person meets in life, one lives here richly, with all the pleasures of a rich life. And were it not as I tell you, the richest girls would not come to us in the convent — girls who lack no dowry and have no worry about getting rich bridegrooms.
— Sister, for the rich the convent may be a calming, a consolation. They have lived and I have not yet lived; they know of wealth — I know of poverty, want and troubles, as much as a Jewish daughter of poor parents can know.
— How then did you come to us here? What brought you to us?
— The terrible want, troubles all around. Seeing no end, no way out, no bright ray in the future. And together with the strong will to live and enjoy life, it all turned my head so much that I became entangled.
Mania burst into tears like a small child. The Sister wiped away her tears with a handkerchief.
— My child — said the Sister warmly, as tears rolled from her kind eyes — it is precisely for such as you, who come out of so unhappy a people, that our house is a rescue. God help me! May you be able to understand me: first calm your unhappy soul, and afterwards you will choose for yourself and do what your heart desires. You can find everything with us, so that you may find yourself happy.
When they came out into the courtyard many "Sisters" came running, and those who were not in the courtyard looked out of the windows. All were curious to see the newcomer.
Some said that Mania was very beautiful, and some — that Mania was not beautiful but very attractive.
Some voiced the opinion aloud, so that Mania could hear, that Mania's face showed that she would not submit so easily, that there would be a lot of work with her...
Mania turned pale and asked "Sister" Maria to explain to her the meaning of the words she had heard.
