What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Investment Tax Confirmed. Session of the City Council.

[Head of the local page; Będzin — City council.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 13 / 13 Sivan 5689 — Piątek 21 czerwca 1929 [Friday, 21 June 1929].)
Będzin
The investment tax confirmed.
Session of the City Council.
Monday's session, which had been called to consider the incident between Pres. Michał and Dr. Rechtman, did not take place, because the matter was settled in a peaceful manner between both sides.
On Tuesday, under the chairmanship of Vice-President Mr. Ehrlich, the continuation of the budget in the second reading took place.
Before proceeding to the agenda, Dr. Jaroszembowski reads, in the name of his club (B.B. [BBWR]), a protest against the excesses that took place in the city council on the 11th of this month, which degrade the prestige of the city council.
The vice-president declares that the presidium of the city council likewise condemns such deeds and stresses that in the future such deeds will not be permitted.
The budgets of the municipal electricity works, the bath establishment, etc. are adopted without any discussion.
A longer discussion developed while considering the extraordinary budget. Councillor Fajger submitted a desideratum that Jewish workers also be taken on for public works. This did not please the Endeks, who threw out the accusation that Jews would not work at all at public works...
A longer discussion developed while considering the statute and confirming the investment tax, which has risen again from the dead and amounts to a sum of 120 thousand zł.
On this question the fragmentation among the Jewish councillors showed itself clearly: confusion of minds reigns among them, and one group votes against the other, and only thanks to the chaotic situation among the Jewish councillors was the tax confirmed.
Councillor Rechnic made a proposal that the entire tax statute be rejected, because in the present situation one cannot impose new taxes. Councillor Garczarczyk spoke in favour of this opinion, whereas the other councillors, such as Gitler, Klajnman, Jakubowicz, Goldfeld, Fajger and Lewin, tried to ease the situation of the taxpayers and introduced a series of amendments; among them was the far-reaching proposal of Mr. Lewin that tenants living in up to 2 rooms be exempt from the tax.
The tax was defended by the presidium of the city administration, which declared that the tax is for carrying out the water mains [?] in the city.
The upshot was: Mr. Rechnic's proposal received no more than 2 votes. The same fate befell Mr. Lewin's proposal, which failed thanks to the votes of the artisans (except Jakubowicz).
On the other hand, the proposal of ławnik [alderman] [?] Hetmańczyk was adopted, that tenants of 2 rooms who live outside the city and, if need be, also in the city, may, at the discretion of the magistrate, receive reductions on the investment tax.
A Distrainer and His “Assistant” Arrested for Taking Bribes

[Będzin — Crime.]
At the local tax office (“Urząd Skarbowy”) one Czesław Hain[?] was employed as a distrainer (sequestrator); he appropriated a sum of 1,500 zł. which he had collected from taxpayers.
Besides this, the distrainer, with the help of his companion, one Morgensztern, took bribes from various taxpayers.
The distrainer and the assistant have been put in prison.
A Hebrew “Gan Yeladim” (Kindergarten) in Będzin

[Będzin — Education.]
On the initiative of the Zionist women's association “WIZO”, the first Hebrew Froebel school, named “Gan Yeladim”, will be opened for the new school year. It will be run by first-class seminary-trained staff of “Tarbut” in Warsaw and will be organised according to the latest system of education and pedagogy.
The Froebel school will be located in the new school building of the Fürstenberg family.
The news has without any doubt caused joy among parents who strive to give their children a national education.
The Matura Examinations Concluded

[Będzin — Education.]
On the eve of Shavuot the matura examinations were concluded at the Jewish school named “Szymańska-Fürstenberg” in Będzin (“Yavneh”). Matura certificates were obtained by all the pupils who sat the examination. They are: Goldberg, Landner, Wajgreb[?], Brojner, Czarny, Gertner, Grundman, Kokotek, Lachman, Lewensztajn, Śmietana and Sztibberg[?].
Hooligans Stab a Jew in the Street

[Będzin — Violence.]
On Saturday evening Mr. Abner Brodes[?] was strolling along Małachowski Street when he saw young hooligans beating a Jewish boy.
When the Jew turned to the hooligans asking why they were beating the boy, they fell upon him with knives, with which they inflicted several serious wounds on the Jew.
Sudden Death of a Jewish Woman

[Będzin — Misfortune.]
On Saturday, the second day of Shavuot, in the morning, 57-year-old Mrs. Chana Opoczyńska went into a courtyard lavatory, where she was taken ill and died.
Visit of the Kielce Voivode

[Zagłębie — Authorities.]
Yesterday the Kielce voivode, Mr. Korsak, visited Zagłębie. The purpose of his visit was to confer the decorations in honour of ten years of Polish independence.
3 Workers Seriously Injured

[Zagłębie — Work Accidents.]
On Tuesday 3 workers were seriously injured while working in the “Koszelew” coal mine; they were taken to hospital.
Annual General Meeting of the Small Traders' Association

[Będzin — Economy and Associations.]
On Sunday, after a break of nearly 2 years, the annual general meeting of the local small traders took place.
The board, wishing to arouse the interest of its members, issued appeals in which the sore points[?] of every member were touched upon. The appeals mentioned that the meeting would deal with the most painful questions.
The “experiment” succeeded relatively well and a larger number of members came — and a rare sight: the hall was packed full of half-dead people, without any life, with despairing senses, human shadows who no longer have the strength to take the floor on whatever question it may be, indifferent to everything, who nod their heads as a sign of agreement...
———
The president, A. Lidzbarski, opens the session with an introductory speech full of grief over the present situation of the Jewish small traders. “We are not living through a crisis,” says Mr. L., “but a time of despair, and the only rescue will come only when the Jewish small trader is united in a strong, powerful organisation.”
The chair is handed over to Mr. M. Cymberknopf; Messrs. Anszel Oppenheim, Hirsz Jama, Hirsz Altman and Szlomo Rajchman are invited as assessors, and Mr. Trefer as secretary.
A lengthy report on the activity to date is given by Mr. Josef Rus, who enumerates what benefit the board has brought the members during this time. Thus, for example, the association has gained positions in all government and municipal bodies and obtained various discounts for the members.
The treasury report is given by Mr. Herszel Stopnicki. The report, which is enriched with various sayings, at the same time ends with the fact that the treasury has a deficit of barely 14 guilders...
The report of the audit committee is given by Mr. Herszlewicz.
Nobody takes the floor on the reports, and the motion of Mr. Granek to express a vote of confidence in the outgoing board is immediately adopted.
On the item of reorganising the association, Messrs. Herszlewicz, Lidzbarski, Stopnicki and Rus speak.
Then the following motions are adopted: 1) from Mr. Lidzbarski, that a registration of all members be carried out and that sections be created for every branch of trade; 2) from Mr. Jama, that nothing at all be done against members who fail to pay the monthly dues for a period of 3 months. On this the amendment of Mr. Iser Kryciler is adopted, that the board conduct a survey among the members and find out for what reasons they do not pay the monthly dues; and 3) from Mr. Herszlewicz, that a court of honour be created at the association, to be registered at the Sosnowiec district court.
The budget, in the sum of 7,500 zł., is adopted.
After the resolution to found a mutual aid fund, the elections take place, with the following result:
To the board: A. Lidzbarski, J. Rus, D. Gutensztajn, H. Stopnicki, J. Szwajcer, A. Flak, Z. Feldberg, K. Hajdes[?], L. Rozenblum, Z. Zygelbojm, D. Gisler, H. Herszlewicz, N. Tenenberg, S. Rechnic and M. Cymberknopf. Deputies: H. Gutman, A. Fajgenbojm, J. Granek and H. Kornbrot. Audit committee: D. Landner, H. Strachlic and S. Gutensztajn.
Birth pangs of the kehilla budget
[Sosnowiec — Kehilla.] The kehilla budget for 1929 has been sent back by the voivode, because the expenses are not justified — for what purposes they are needed.
General meeting of the Small Traders' Bank

[Sosnowiec — Economic institutions.] Next Sunday afternoon a general meeting of the members of the Small Traders' and Artisans' Bank will take place at the "Hotel Polski". Important points will be discussed, and it is desirable that the members take an interest in this meeting.
Lecture by Dr. Yitzhak Schiper

[Sosnowiec — Culture.] Next Sunday the former Sejm deputy Dr. Yitzhak (Ignacy) Schiper will give a lecture on the topic "When did Jews come to Poland". The same lecture will also take place on Saturday in Będzin.
The Dembitzer Rebbe has died
[Sosnowiec — Obituary.] At the age of 74 the well-known Dembitzer Rebbe (of Dębica), Reb Avraham David Okstein [?], died in the local Jewish hospital.
Piłsudski's speech on the radio

[Upper Silesia — Politics.] On the 28th, 29th [and] 30th of this month a congress of reserve officers will take place in Katowice. In connection with it there will also be demonstrations in honour of the union of Upper Silesia with the Polish Republic.
Marshal Piłsudski will greet the congress by radio.
—o—
Recruits smash windows
[Sławków — Antisemitism.] On Saturday the Jewish residents of Sławków lived through a fright. A group of recruits began to run wild around the houses of Jewish residents, where they smashed windows and went so far as to commit excesses.
Thanks to the energetic intervention of the police commandant the rampage was stopped and the culprits arrested.
—o—
French guests in Zagłębie
[Zagłębie — Economy.] Last Saturday an official French delegation headed by Ambassador Noulens stayed in Zagłębie. The delegation acquainted itself with the industry of Zagłębie.
Olkusz — From the town council

[Olkusz — Municipality.] At the town-council sessions on Saturday night and Monday the provisional budget for the year 1929/30 was set at a sum of more than 1½ million zł. Among others it contains the following items: 200 thousand zł to build a public (powszechna) school for girls, 10 thousand zł for sewerage, 5000 zł for a children's colony, 2,500 zł for a children's colony in Busko, 2,700 zł for the councillors' expenses for the Poznań exhibition, 20 thousand zł for medicines for poor sick people, 6 thousand zł each for the Jewish and the Christian "Dobroczynność" [charity societies], 500 zł for the Jewish society "Postęp", 200 zł for the "Muza", 100 zł for the Orthodox library, 1000 zł for a summer colony for Jewish children, 1000 zł for the gemilut-hesed (interest-free loan) fund, 500 zł for evening courses for Jewish artisans.
The salaries of the magistrate members were set: for the mayor (president) 7,621 zł, deputy — 2760 zł, the 2 ławnicy 4128 zł, and for the departmental ławnik Mr. Blum 5557 zł.
When the salary for the departmental ławnik was being set, a conflict arose between Mr. Majcherkiewicz [?] (Sanacja), who demanded that the post of departmental ławnik be struck out, and the Jews Wajslfisz [?] and Blum, who exposed his hypocrisy and ill will toward the only Jewish representative in the magistrate. By a large majority of votes the post was kept. From among the Jews, Wajslfisz, Czarniecki and Faluch [?] were elected to the school-building commission.
It is worth noting that in the building of the first public school for boys by the old town council not a single Jewish offer was accepted, and it is the duty of the Jewish representatives on the town council, the magistrate and the building commission to see by every possible means that Jewish craftsmen are admitted to work on the new school building.
—o—
From the court
[Olkusz — Court.] In the local court a case was heard that K. Szapel [?] brought against the teacher of the public school, Mrs. Wagner, for beating his 12-year-old boy with a wire and drawing blood during a lesson.
The court sentenced the teacher to a fine of 100 zł, alternatively 2 weeks' arrest, and court costs.
A. B.

Dąbrowa — A Swindler Posing as an Agent for Medical Instruments

[Dąbrowa — Local news.]
Dąbrowa
A swindler posing as an agent for medical instruments.
A certain man came to the local doctor M— Z. and introduced himself as an agent for medical instruments, and offered the doctor to buy a quartz lamp from him very cheaply.
The doctor made the transaction and signed an order form for the agent. The agent, however, insisted that the doctor should already give him bills of exchange for the purchase sum, to which the doctor did not agree, explaining that after receiving the purchased instrument he would settle the amount.
Meanwhile the doctor went into another room; the "agent" used the opportunity and, with the help of the doctor's stamp, forged 2 bills of exchange for 400 zł. each.
The "agent" discounted the bills "on the street" and vanished with the money.
Site for a "Beit ha-Chaim" — approved.
This Tuesday a commission, consisting of the Będzin starosta, the district (powiat) doctor, an architect, and representatives of the magistrate and the Jewish community, visited the site that was bought for a "Beit ha-Chaim" [cemetery].
The commission recognized the plot as suitable for the purpose.
From the city council.
At the city council meeting held last Saturday night the budget was approved in the third reading.
Of the budget, which amounts to about 2 million zł., the Jewish population — or rather the "Agudah" — receives a whole 15 hundred zł...
This "favour" the Sanacja councillors did after many requests and entreaties by the Jewish councillors...
During the vote on the Jewish subsidy the PPS and the Endeks left the meeting in protest.
Elections to the conference for Working Eretz Israel.
On Friday elections took place here to the conference for Working Eretz Israel. Three lists took part: "Hashomer Hatzair" (No. 1), "Poalei Zion" (No. 6), "Gordonia" (No. 7). 311 persons had the right to vote; 267 cast votes.
List 1 received 48 votes, 1 mandate: Yaakov Horowitz (Warsaw).
List 6 received 146 votes, 4 mandates: Mordechai Grossfeld (Dąbrowa), Nachman Beitner (Będzin), Noach Krempel and Pesach Siegreich (Dąbrowa).
List 7 received 73 votes, 2 mandates: Ozer Abzhanski[?] and Shmuel Patsagowski[?] (Łódź).
A farewell Sabbath of Cantor Żupowicz.
Because of his departure on a longer leave, Mr. Żupowicz will lead the prayers this Sabbath, and he promises to give the public "the last money" [i.e. his very best].
From the editors:
Because the staff of the editorial office and the printing shop has been reduced owing to holidays, this issue appears in only 6 pages.
Lidia Potocka and Julius Adler in Zagłębie
After a break of 2 years the famous Jewish artist Lidia Potocka is coming to Zagłębie again for several guest performances; she gives spiritual pleasure with her appearances on the stage.
Her partner is none other than the darling of the Yiddish theatre public, the long-time well-known artist Julius Adler, who returned a few weeks ago from America for a tour.
"A Woman of 30" will be played on Saturday night in Będzin and on Sunday evening in Sosnowiec.
Concert of School 4.
On Wednesday the school orchestra of Public School 4 in Będzin gave a concert at "Nowości".
The programme, consisting of the best musical works, such as Schulz, Meyerbeer, Chopin, was received by the large number of guests with stormy ovations.
The melodies from "The Dybbuk" had particular success.
A landlord's "advice".
In the house of Mr. Perlgricht in Mandzhev[?] lives the tenant Hershl Braner, whom the landlord is set on evicting; and being unable to carry out his will by legal means, he "honours" the tenant with... "one" [a blow; reading doubtful].
He 54 — she 24..
In Strzemieszyce lived a Christian couple. He is 54 years old and she 30 years younger. The temperamental little wife made her old man's years miserable, and also once gave his sides a good thrashing...
The heroic little wife stood these days before the Sosnowiec district court, which sentenced her to 2 weeks in prison

Suicide of a Christian merchant.
[Sosnowiec area — News.]
On Tuesday a Christian merchant in Piaski committed suicide by drinking a sizeable portion of vinegar essence.

Miss G. of Zawiercie sought ways to pass as a young lady. To that end she forged her civil identity card, which she "adjusted" by 4 years fewer...

The dishes got a "tikkun"...

The number of protested bills of exchange grows from day to day. The banks have no cash, and the economic situation of the merchants is simply disastrous.

Sosnowiec municipal budget before the plenum of the City Council.
On Wednesday evening the Sosnowiec City Council held a session. The main point of the session was the preliminary budget for 1929/30, which according to the announcement of the voivode must be approved this month.
The Endek [National Democrat] councillors propose that, since the councillors received the budget just before the session, there had been no possibility of studying the budget, and therefore it should be postponed to the next session.
Over this proposal a polemic arises between councillor Wolf and the president, and finally it is decided that the president shall deliver his exposé at today's session and the budget shall be dealt with only next Monday.
In the exposé the president stressed that, although the budget has been raised this year by 400 thousand zł., it is nevertheless more economical in that 25 per cent of the budget income is earmarked for repaying loan debts.

[Article — citizen and police.] Citizen, keep your nerves in check
when you come into contact with authority.
Quite often each of us happens to witness such embarrassing scenes:
On a pavement several acquaintances meet by chance and stop in the middle to have a little chat, or someone crosses the roadway without keeping to the line prescribed by the regulations.
Likewise, someone feels like smoking a cigarette (papirosa) right in the waiting hall of a cinema, a theatre or some other public place, or someone forgets to take off his hat in the corridors of a court, and the like.
Unnoticed, a policeman sidles up and catches them right at the hot moment of the offence committed.
True, these are all light, third-rank offences, but offences nonetheless, and punishable offences.
And that is precisely why, when that same policeman calls the guilty man or the guilty woman aside and fines them on the spot 1 or 2 zł., they make no long arguments, open their purses and submit at once to the verdict.
But not all people have such calm, peaceably tempered natures; one does come across hot heads, or stubborn people, who on no account want to pay the złotys demanded and also refuse to identify themselves — it must come to quarrels, insults, and the end is that the obstinate citizen is pushed and dragged to the commissariat (police station) and is brought to judicial responsibility under article 142, 154, 262 or 832[?] of the penal code.
In such cases the courts are merciless; no explanations or excuses help; the accused are sentenced to the highest penalties.
The same fate, with all the unpleasant consequences, can also befall any other chance passer-by who, being a witness to such or another embarrassing scene, cannot restrain himself but stops, tries to interfere in the action of this or that police functionary, or starts to intervene on behalf of the detained person.
Such trials take place in the courts by the tens and hundreds every day.
How much bad blood, grief, time and money such incidents cost — not only the direct victim, but also his family and relatives.
And all these troubles arise mostly from stubbornness, hot-headedness and hooliganism[?].
We therefore draw the attention of the broad public on this occasion to the need to keep one's nervous equilibrium everywhere in relation to the police authority.
In trying to calm the irritated tempers of certain nervous and obstinate citizens, we do not thereby mean to say that justice is always necessarily only on the side of authority.
There are certainly also individual functionaries who lack the necessary tact and do not understand how, in an urgent case, to safeguard the prestige of the state and of their office while at the same time sparing the human dignity of the citizen; they quite often let themselves be carried away, or are governed by ill-willed influences, and with their actions thereby bring about the most unpleasant misunderstandings and even injustices.
Whoever feels wronged by the action of this or that police functionary must on no account take it upon himself to react right away on the spot; he must immediately turn with an appropriate complaint to the police command, where a disciplinary inquiry will be opened against the guilty party, and he will then be duly punished for his deed.
J. Einfeld.
From Sport.

[Sport — football and cycling, Zagłębie.]
“Świt” — “Maccabi” 3:1 (1:1).
Great interest was aroused in sporting circles by the class “A” championship match between “Świt” and “Maccabi”. About a thousand spectators attended the match.
The course of play was interesting and was conducted at a fast tempo. “Maccabi” immediately takes over the initiative and becomes the only one setting the tone on the pitch. They bombard the opponents' goal, but without success. “Świt” exploits a mistake by the “Maccabi” defence and in the 38th minute scores the only goal. “Maccabi” makes a great effort and 5 minutes later Michel [?] equalises. The first half remains 1:1.
In the second half “Maccabi” dominates the pitch, and already in the 3rd minute Prachtzweig [?] shoots the ball from 20 metres and it is turned into a goal. “Świt” tries to break through [?] to the “Maccabi” goal, but without success. They begin to play very brutally. Thereupon [?] the referee is forced to send off a “Świt” player. Towards the end Samer [?] increases the score and it stays 3:1 [?] for “Maccabi”. Best on the pitch for “Maccabi”: Golanzka [?], Prachtzweig [?], Schlesinger. Referee Mr. Kazimacki [?] very good.
K.S. “Pogoń” (Katowice) — “Gwiazda” 1:5 (0:2).
On Saturday “Gwiazda” invited the reserve team of “Pogoń” to a friendly match. The course of the match was interesting at moments. In the first minutes of play the young players of “Gwiazda” hold up very well and lead very nice attacks, but without success, because everyone wants to score a goal on his own. Only in the 20th minute does “Pogoń” score the first goal. Right before the end of the half the referee awards an 11-metre kick [penalty] against “Gwiazda”, and the centre-forward of “Pogoń” converts [?] it into the second goal.
In the second half “Gwiazda” loses strength because of the guests' fast tempo, and already in the 8th minute “Pogoń” scores the 3rd and afterwards the 4th goal. “Gwiazda” gradually recovers and Władymirski scores the only goal for his club. “Pogoń”, however, soon retaliates, and the final result remains 1:5 for “Pogoń”.
“Giszowiec” — “Arie” 1:1 (0:0).
“Arie” played very nicely; especially distinguished was the goalkeeper Preiser, who saved his club from certain defeat. The first half ends goalless; only in the second half does the referee award an 11-metre kick against “Arie”, and the guests score a goal. Towards the end “Arie” equalises through Apelbaum, and the result is 1:1.
“Gwiazda” (Będzin) — “Samson” 1:3 (1:0).
A deserved victory for “Gwiazda”, which played much more nicely than “Samson”. Referee Mr. Kimelman good.

The Appearance of Julius Adler and Lida Potocka in Zagłębie.

[Theatre — guest performances, Będzin and Sosnowiec.]
The guest performances given in Będzin and in Sosnowiec by the two artists of the Yiddish stage in the drama “The Woman of 30” exceeded all expectations.
The God-blessed artist Lida Potocka showed here all her artistry. She embodied the eternal feminine in woman, and the stormy struggle that rages in a 30-year-old woman in the clash and wrestling between feelings of passionate love for her husband's colleague and the untearable attachment to home and husband — and how in the end the latter wins.
Julius Adler played his role as a highly intelligent and gentlemanly man with artistry, because every movement or conversation was so unforced, free and natural that one had the impression that it was not Adler playing on the stage, but that he was chatting with his wife really at home.
The impression this guest performance left on the large theatre audience will not be forgotten so quickly.
Letters to the Editor

[Dąbrowa — letters to the editor; Zionism; city council; medicine.]
I.
Esteemed Editors!
We ask you to publish in your esteemed newspaper the following open letter, which we consider extremely important for the Jewish population of Dąbrowa.
We take upon ourselves full responsibility for the content of this letter, and we thank you in advance.
At the general meeting of the local Zionist Organization, held on Sunday, Isru Chag (the day after) Shavuot, among other items on the agenda the activity of the Zionist councillors in the Dąbrowa city council was considered.
Although the councillors, who were asked and summoned twice, found it more important to stay sitting at home rather than come and report what they are doing in the city council in the name of the organization and in the name of their voters —
on the basis of the fact that a number of members, who had themselves attended sessions from the gallery, reported how our councillors behaved on general municipal and specifically Jewish questions, how from the very first minute they went into the old, mouldy "Mah Yafit" dance, surrendered themselves entirely to the Sanacja and got for it materially — a round zero; morally they brought it about that the Jewish population was constantly insulted and spat upon, and against all the wrongs and insults the voice of the Jewish councillor was not raised even once!
Therefore the following resolution, addressed to our councillors, was adopted unanimously:
"The general meeting of the Zionist Organization in Dąbrowa of 16 June of this year protests against the conduct of its councillors in the city council from the first day of their election, who do everything on their own judgment, unwilling to come into contact with the Zionist Organization, and this has caused them to offend the honour of the local Jewish population; and it declares that Messrs. Bernard Rechnitz[?] and Lipa Puterka (especially the latter, since he is the declared Zionist candidate) are not capable of representing the national Jewish public, our honour and our interests in the city council, and categorically demands of the councillor gentlemen that they immediately lay down their mandates in favour of others, who will indeed understand their tasks in the city council and fulfil them completely.
The Board of the Zionist Organization in Dąbrowa."
II.
Esteemed Mr. Editor!
Allow me to touch in your esteemed newspaper on the following painful matter: the attitude of some of the doctors toward the sick here in Dąbrowa.
When one night I turned to Doctors Gwa…ski[?] and Mitelman, and explained to them that my wife's condition was a dangerous one, the first doctor excused himself that he was weak, and the second refused altogether. Only thanks to the intervention of the police did Dr. Mitelman agree to answer that a droshky [cab] should be provided for him and that 150 złoty be paid to him in advance...
Respectfully,
Elimelech Zeldiger. Dąbrowa.

The Short Memory. (Understanding for Development and Commitment for Citizens.)

It all comes down in the end to talking about one and the same question, about one and the same interests, about one and the same duties toward the population, toward the broad strata of the popular masses.
These would seem to be questions that concern every town citizen, and yet the latter are not taken into account. We know that the town's citizens — that is, merchants, small traders and craftsmen — pour colossal sums into the state treasury; we know that they are the ones who pay taxes constantly and continually, without end, and as such — as citizens from whom the country and the state derive benefit — one ought to consult with them, one ought to come into contact with them and act as those whom the questions concern agree. Unfortunately we see none of this; unfortunately we see that nothing and nobody is taken into account.
It goes without saying that things would be entirely different if the citizens were indeed taken into account; the public institutions would have an entirely different face if the citizens reacted to undesirable phenomena.
We people of Będzin have in recent years been steadily going backwards. Although the town is growing, although various buildings are being put up and new streets are being cut, all this is nevertheless not taken into account, and what is due to us, what we deserve to have, is being taken away from us.
Before the war, for instance, we had a district court („Kreis-Gericht“) in Będzin; today we no longer have one. We know, after all, that when an important trial comes up, it is heard in the Sąd Okręgowy (regional court), which is in Sosnowiec, and the merchants of Będzin must in that case travel there.
It goes without saying that had the citizens of Będzin reacted in their time to such a measure, they would have achieved their aim. But here, after all, people are indifferent to everything and do not like to reconsider anything, so that things go on as they always have, and whatever is done to us is done and over with.
Further: Sosnowiec has a labour inspector, to whom one very often has to turn, employers as well as employees, and then Będzin again has to travel to Sosnowiec.
Now the labour courts have been founded; they were set up both in Sosnowiec and in Dąbrowa, so Będzin was bypassed altogether, and in this matter the people of Będzin must be wanderers. We are treated like stepchildren, as if there were nothing to be had from Będzin, and therefore we cannot demand anything of anyone.
They have begun to build a post-office building here; well, it goes without saying that the site for the post-office building was chosen precisely behind the town.
We understand that when one wants to enlarge a town, one builds various public buildings outside the town for two reasons: first, because the land is cheaper, and second, so that the new quarters become more popular. Yes, we understand this perfectly, but that was said of other institutions, and by no means when it comes to such a popular institution as a post office, to which all strata of the population are drawn, even several times a day. For who does not need to use a post office nowadays? Who does not have to send off and collect money there? To pay bills of exchange? To send registered letters, [and] dispatch parcels? The post is, after all, today the real living nerve among all strata of the population; therefore the whole town ought to have been interested in having the future post-office building located in the very centre of the town. And even if they wanted to put the building on a new street so that traffic there would become livelier, one could also have found a kind of middle point, so that it would not be too far from any side of the town.
But here nothing and nobody is taken into account, and that is why things look the way they do, so that nothing is done for the benefit of the citizens and their interests. Further, we do not have the institutions, the representative bodies, that would react when something is not done for the citizens' benefit. Otherwise one would have to react to every measure taken, and then one mistake after another would not have been made.
What more is needed: Będzin is, no evil eye, a town of merchants, and there is no one to defend the merchants. When declarations were read out in the town council a few weeks ago, every group solemnly announced that it would defend its interests, that it would look after its voters at every turn — and back then no one even knew that in Będzin there live such people called merchants; they had no defenders there, and indeed no one said that he would defend the interests of the merchants. Yet when something comes up — when money is needed, when a campaign must be carried out — the first people thought of are the merchants, those who stand in front of their shops and watch out for customers.
— Yes, this is the best proof that among us everything is still fragmented, that we are still far from understanding our duties. We only know that it hurts when we are beaten; but if the pain stops for a minute, we already forget that we have meanwhile lost a little strength and have grown weak...
And so, because we have such a short memory and never recall our weaknesses, what could be improved is not improved, and what could, with intensive activity, indeed be removed is never removed.
R. Let.
A Little Feuilleton.

[Satirical feuilleton — Poland; the student riots in Lwów, 1929.] (Project for a new pavilion.)
Until not long ago I was convinced that printing machines are not manufactured in Poland, to say nothing of rotary presses that throw out, at tremendous speed, finished newspapers of dozens of pages, folded and counted, and certainly not the rare linotypes with their wonderful construction, which ingeniously throw out finished cast lines.
I thought that our machine industry was still young, that it was not yet capable of producing such delicate parts, and so I was not surprised that at the grand Poznań exhibition [the Polish General National Exhibition, PeWuKa, 1929], where everything the country possesses is on display, where every branch of the economy shows us its development and progress in facts and figures — that at this Polish exhibition there is no pavilion of printing machines.
In the last few weeks I have become convinced that I was living in error. I found out that, on the contrary, in this field we have tremendous successes to record. The young academics in Lemberg [Lwów] have proved most clearly that my project is a logical one; they worked wonders in "processing" printing machines — and of the very newest construction at that. From this I foresaw bright prospects for the art of printing.
Having studied closely the course of their work, the speed and refinement with which they "finished off" the most delicate parts of the machines, I came to the conclusion that in the matter of printing machines we stand high enough, and that we can already, with satisfaction, set up a pavilion devoted to our latest achievements in printing, according to the following project.
The pavilion must be painted black; at the entrance one should show the first "printing machines" of the Middle Ages, from which today's Lemberg "masters" drew their sustenance.
The pictures with which the pavilion is to be hung must show, regarding the whole process of our modern "processing", in the simplest way, the complicated parts of rotary presses and linotypes.
One picture should show how a secret hand turns a knob and how, instantly, as if by magic, thousands of "student-mechanics" spring up with tools in hand, ready for work.
A second picture should clearly show the "stormy urge" to work. This can be illustrated by [?] staved-in [?] iron doors, broken doors, hacked windows and smashed [?] panes.
A third picture should show the "mechanics" at "work" — flushed faces, rolled-up sleeves, clenched fists, spades and axes, rods [?], irons and heavy hammers which strike with rare assurance at the most delicate parts of the wonderful linotypes and rotary machines.
A fourth picture — victims of the "work": split skulls, gouged-out eyes, people on "stretchers" ["noshilkes", Pol. nosze] on their way to the Jewish hospital.
And in the middle of the pavilion a finished "piece of work" — a heap of wheels and bars, screws, rollers and type, painted and splashed from above with red paint resembling blood...
And over it an inscription in red letters: "Ten minutes' work of the student youth in Lemberg in the year 1929".
What a wonderfully instructive picture that would have been for the tens of thousands of visitors to the Poznań exhibition; they would have left the exhibition with the firm conviction that a "happy" future awaits us: if young academics, not even "graduated" yet, could accomplish all this in only ten minutes — what heroic deeds will they show in the course of their whole lives, after they finish their studies!
Yaakov.
Our Panorama

Our Panorama. By Ben Amotz.
(A little town that ought to be immortalised. — A policeman as a stickler that Jews should pray with a minyan. — Hasidim who come to the rebbe get beaten. — A "gift" for sub-tenants. — The victory of the Liberals in England brings harm. — Gentiles slaughter and rabbinic judges write prohibitions.)
Czeladź is a little town that deserves to be immortalised in history, and especially in the present epoch, when deeds that ought not to be done are done just to get a "seat" somewhere — no matter where, even in the Chamber of Commerce...
And precisely in this field Czeladź is an exception. There people do not fight to grab a "seat" — on the contrary, they push the honour away from themselves; even chairs with such a "stanowisko" [post] as president and vice-president are tossed around like a burnt cholent...
The town council begs them for mercy — "don't shame us", don't throw a "stekl"[?] before the door, but the magistrate [municipality] argues "I do not want it", we don't want to, and "go stick yourselves in butter"...
But this is not what we are driving at. The "virtues" of Czeladź are such that they will no doubt arouse "the greatest joy" in every religious Jew; anyone who reads these lines will at once find a hint in it.
— "The sun also rises, and the sun goes down"...
Today's generation, which has strayed from the straight path, should draw a moral from it: that a policeman has the mission of "recruiting" Jews to pray in congregation...
And this is how it happened.
The Radomsko Hasidim in Czeladź suffer great troubles from their landlord; almost every quarter they get "thrown out", and they have no place of rest at all where they could practise Hasidism properly.
And it came to pass one day. It is established that wherever the word "vayehi" appears, it signals trouble. And here indeed was the trouble: the landlord hung a padlock on the door of the "shtibl" and so barricaded the way for the Hasidim.
Well? Where do Jews run in a time of trouble? Probably to the police commissariat — from where a policeman was indeed delegated, an "expert" in Hasidic matters, who made an inquiry and investigation on the spot and, after acquainting himself with the claims of both sides, ordered the padlock to be removed at once, so that the Hasidim could pray in congregation.
For greater force and vigour the policeman stood in the street, and as soon as he saw a Jew he struck up a conversation with him and asked him to go in and pray, so that it should be "in the multitude of people is the king's glory"...
The Hasidim inside[?] then prayed with all the more fervour, because the policeman standing outside kept sending in fresh "material"...
— Well? Doesn't such a place deserve to be immortalised? If only every town had such policemen — the "Agudah" [Agudat Israel] would have no reason to exist at all...
———
The police in Pilica had work during our "Season of the Giving of our Torah" [Shavuot]. They did not drive the local Jews to pray, because the Jews of Pilica — more precisely, the Ger Hasidim and all their congregation — are entirely occupied with "Jewish affairs": they wage a holy war like Chmielnicki in his day.
Last Shavuot the battle was fought "with thunder and lightning": the Hasidim who had come for the holiday to the Pilica rabbi were attacked in the same style in which the Lwów academics used to treat the "sinful Zhids".. and instead of greenery the visiting Hasidim received "gifts" decorated in red colours..
———
Since we have come to speak of "gifts", it is also worth mentioning the "gift" with which a Jewish tenant honoured the Rozprza[?] Hasidim in Będzin on Shavuot.
The tenant wants at all costs to be rid of his sub-tenant — the Rozprza Hasidim. And seeing that he would not carry out his plan by legal means, he hit upon such a "clever" idea:
When the Hasidim had gone home after prayers, a child went into the "shtibl" and did there...
When the Hasidim came back after the meal, their blood simply froze at the sight of the shameful desecration of the holy... and they had no choice but to clear it away...
— Woe to the wicked and woe to his neighbour..
———
The whole liberal world rejoices at the victory of the Labour Party in the last parliamentary elections in England, but for Dańdówka the victory is a great misfortune.
On the day the news arrived that the Liberals in England had won, a revolution broke out in the Dańdówka beit midrash, led by a left Poale Zionist...
The revolutionaries entered the beit midrash to the strains of the "Marseillaise", toppled the old gabbaim from the throne, occupied the beit midrash and took "captive" the Holy Ark, the prayer-stand and everything connected with liberalism..
The side[?] of "reaction" is trying to go on the defensive, but without success, and as our correspondent complains to us, the Sitra Achra has prevailed there, and as long as MacDonald "rides the horse" the Jews of Dańdówka will not have a peaceful Sabbath...
———
For the events in Modrzejów we can find no fitting name. The local "citizens" call it anarchy, and our correspondent writes that it is a "storm in a glass of water"..
Well? What to do? We have decided to hand the "matter" over to you, dear readers, and you must declare what reigns in Modrzejów:
— Anarchy or a "storm in a glass of water"?
The story goes like this:
In Modrzejów there is no mikveh; actually there is a mikveh, but it is in the same state as the Będzin mikveh. It needs repairing. Money was collected, and the money — also as in Będzin — disappeared...
And from this mikveh a "fire" broke out and seized the butchers and the shochtim. They[?], the shochtim, refuse to slaughter, and the butchers honour them with a "libation".. that is: instead of into the gutters, they take the filth and pour it as a libation over the shochtim...
For such an "honour" the shochtim refuse to slaughter all the more; so the police are brought in, who "order" ["rozkazywać"]:
— "Slaughter kosher-style!"...
And when the shochet is stubborn and says "no", there is a remedy for that too: they slaughter as treif and rule that "all may slaughter" — even a gentile.
In this jazz-band[?] orchestra the moreh tzedek [rabbinic judge] also takes part, writing prohibitions — "and to him who hears it shall be delight, and a good blessing shall come upon him"..
Ben Amotz.
This Is Not the Way Out

(A reply to Mr. R. Let [?] on his article "Bankruptcies and Lawlessness").

We have received the following article from a well-known Radom merchant, and we print it on the basis of free discussion. — The Editors.

Reading the so-called article "Bankruptcies and Lawlessness" in Zaglembier Tsaytung no. 20, in which the abnormal situation in the commercial world caused by malicious bankruptcies is discussed, one must stop for a while and ask the author: is he acquainted with the actual circumstances of today's merchants in general, and of the Jewish ones in particular?

To me, as a simple reader, all the author's assertions seem unfounded, and I am altogether doubtful whether his project of creating a committee to fight malicious bankruptcies is feasible, and whether this is the right way out to improve the situation.

In my opinion, the division of the merchant class into two categories, as the author formulates it, does not hold up. One gets the impression that the author would like to take under his protection the richer ones, the big firms, whose bankruptcies he considers a self-evident thing because of their large obligations, taxes, debts and running costs ["hanhage"]. The smaller ones, on the other hand, one may sooner suspect of malice. This classification is far from the truth. True, one can divide the merchant class into categories, but precisely in the opposite sense. For if it is a matter of real malice, it is altogether doubtful whether such cases actually exist. Let us take, for example, those whom the author regards as the most solid, that is, the big firms: if one of them goes bankrupt, it is in most cases done with a prior calculation, so that it can, and has the means to, settle at once and stay on its feet, and in such a case at most [literally "least of all"] its commercial reputation suffers. He may even be a serious [?] person, and nobody will suspect him of malice here. Quite different is a similar case of bankruptcy of a smaller, hard-pressed merchant, who calculates none of this in advance; his economic collapse comes elementally, all at once, and in the economic crash he is left completely broken and ruined. Moreover, his situation is all the more catastrophic in that every creditor presses him, and "zajęcia" [seizures] and "klauzule" [enforcement writs] pour down on him from all sides. They sell off his last possessions, since he has nothing to settle with, and in everyone's eyes he is called a bankrupt — and a malicious bankrupt at that.

Let us take a merchant who goes bankrupt for 150 thousand zł. and a merchant who goes bankrupt for 10 thousand zł. How does the author imagine the repressions on the part of the creditors against both of the said parties would look? Whom can the author in this case call the more malicious bankrupt?

It would already be high time to unmask ourselves [printed "remaskirn", a misprint for "demaskirn"] and tell ourselves the truth, however sad it may be.

Nor do I see in the author's project, in which he proposes to create a committee to fight malicious bankruptcies, any radical means of changing the situation. Times are bad for everyone, and I very much doubt whether such a committee could be put together from the Zagłębie merchants that would be capable of judging the difference between malice and non-malice; for if [people] become judges of others' honesty and solidity, I do not know whether, in today's abnormal times, the judges themselves would not already have stumbled too.

As a simple man, I see another way out, namely: first of all one must demand what is honestly due to us. Many of the merchants of the second category would wish to liquidate their businesses if everyone had the possibility of obtaining work according to his abilities. The conclusion from this is "alia" [?]: as long as Jews are not admitted to various government posts, and as long as a "numerus clausus" still exists in every enterprise in the country and free emigration is not introduced, all these committees are a pity — they will only bore everyone.

In my opinion it would be desirable for other merchants, too, to voice their opinion on this question.

M. B—r.
In What Light Zagłębie Is Seen

[Zagłębie — economy and trade; series, part V.]
Through the eyes of foreign visitors.
V.
When wages are paid out normally (on the 1st and the 15th of every month), everything is alive, trade bustles, the mood throughout Zagłębie is hopeful [?], and the wheel turns round and round. But when the workers get only "zaliczki" [advances], or the working hours are cut back altogether, it echoes at once in every nook and corner — across the whole region.
Invisible threads run from the underground infernos to the smart shops, cafés and places of entertainment.
Here coal does not only directly heat the stoves and factory boilers; it is also the accumulator for the motor of all economic and social life, and the driving force of commercial momentum...
Here coal regulates not only the temperature and the heating system but the whole economic system in general...
One should be here after a "normal payday" in the coal mines. Zagłębie is black with crowds of people. It is a real "migration of nations" then. Transport is good, cheap and runs in many directions. Every half hour the trams, buses and trains from Katowice and from the neighbouring towns and townlets disgorge thousands upon thousands of arriving "Ślązaks" [Silesians], who spread through the town, buy up all kinds of goods, swallow up everything and, laden with bundles and baskets, return to Upper Silesia across the non-existent border.
Zagłębie lives with and off the "Ślązak". He is the key to the economic problem here on the spot and far beyond the local trading points. When the "Ślązak" comes there is a livelihood; when he does not come it is dead...
Everyone throws himself at the "Ślązak", everything revolves [?] around him. And he, the best consumer, although he is incessantly incited and stirred up against the Jews by the Jew-haters and their organ "Do Czynu" (a publication similar to the sadly notorious Bydgoszcz "Szabas-Kurier") — buys, for the most part, precisely from Jews, whom he trusts and from whom he does indeed get the necessary articles at much cheaper prices...
The merchant has already caught on. He knows what the "Ślązak" needs and what sells with him. He makes an effort to make the goods cheaper and nicer. Even the shop windows are adapted to the taste of the Upper Silesian customer. One no longer sees on Modrzejowska Street the old-fashioned "wystawas" [shop displays] of former days. Doors and windows are knocked into the shops; people adapt to the taste of the Upper Silesians — wide, bright, attractive shop windows, modern, elegant, especially to please the "Ślązak" so as to take in money from him...
Until a year ago — I am told — business here was booming. Now it is a little weaker...
The general depressed situation in Poland can be felt here too. If not directly, then indirectly. The declassed and economically worn-out Jews of Łódź take off the cap of shame, buy a bit of merchandise on credit and travel with their bundles straight to Katowice, to Königshütte [Chorzów] and so on. Thus a new Jewish branch of livelihood is growing up there — peddlers; new Jewish settlements are being built up there. But that is a chapter in itself.
* * *
When one observes the local trade and sees the dominant role the "Ślązak" plays in local commerce, Upper Silesia grows in one's imagination into some monster-creature, incomprehensible and extremely mysterious. Upper Silesia looks like an abyss, without end and without limit. It is insatiable and unappeased in its needs; it swallows everything, digests and boils it in its enormous stomach, and with its juices feeds tens of thousands of local and foreign shopkeepers, peddlers and "instalment" (avcug) merchants, strengthens them and gives them new energy, new capital...
Where does this come from? What kind of rare creature is the Upper Silesian?
It is an interesting study, and many things became clear and understandable to me while visiting Upper Silesia — things that at first had looked so strange, wondrous and incomprehensible to me...
Katowice is an important, seething centre, but a small, though thoroughly European, city; and its notions, though of great commercial scope and mighty industrial momentum, are also very small-townish here. In this respect Katowice is genuinely Polish.
In Poland people love winged words. The "strong" epithet impresses. The people of Katowice too warm themselves with pleasure in the illusory downy feathers of a French metropolis in miniature, although the warmth of the "black diamonds" is far stronger here and far more natural...
Katowice — "the Polish Paris"; the nickname has a fine ring. But not without a curiosity. For precisely this city has a pronounced character of its own.
Katowice, the capital of eastern Upper Silesia, concentrates and centralises Polish heavy industry. Here are the managing bodies of the more than 100 large mines of the whole coal and smelting district; from here they are all controlled, here production policy is defined. Here the prices are dictated for internal Polish consumption, as well as for coal exports to the countries on the other side of the Baltic Sea.
Katowice is materialistic through and through. Politics here is materialistic, the spirit is materialistic, and culture too, in its progress, has the characteristic tinge of a modern large industrial place that lives out its life in the rhythm and poetry of the machines' clatter [?]...
Concentrated creative work, purposeful energy, a materialistic spirit — these are the characteristic features of this somewhat remarkable "Polish Paris". Every stone of its well-paved streets, every brick of its tall, architecturally handsome houses breathes the tremendous energy and joy of work.
Dr. A. Weissman — The Seduced Girl

"Nothing," the Sister reassured Mania. "All the Sisters, seeing you so early at the prayer-singing, have grown fond of you and would like you to stay with them; they are afraid you will not want to." And she glanced at the Sisters, who were dispersing [?] one by one.

———
Towards evening, when the sun had only just begun to set, Mania found herself alone in the room for the first time.
"Alone at last," she said to herself, gathering her thoughts by herself. "God! How does one live through the night, so that I may be freed from here at last?"
Not for a minute did the hope leave her that the door would open and in would come her father, her mother or her beloved, Chaim.
"Why, he loves me so, and I exchanged him for that Ludwig."
With the word "that" she meant to express all her anger, her disgust for him. And before her rose the terrible picture of the past night, when he had led her, in a faint, somewhere to a village cottage, and late at night, when out of weariness she had leant against a bed, Ludwig came in — he whom she had loved so much before and whose words she had always believed — and now threw himself on her like a wild beast; with all her strength she pushed him away from her and raised an outcry, so that everyone in the house came running; and if not for Jan, who rescued her from Ludwig's hands, who knows what would have become of her?
And afterwards, when Jan stayed alone with her, he proposed that she write a few words to her parents, and he would deliver it to them. She did so, and she waits and believes that her parents will find her.
She remembers that when she asked Jan to take her home, he answered:
"That I cannot do; I can only pass the little letter to your parents in the deepest secrecy."
And when she asked him:
"Where am I? I want to write to my parents so they will know where to look for me," Jan answered:
"That I cannot say." And she wrote to her parents that she was in a locked room and begged them to rescue her.
She began to walk about the room, holding her head in both hands.
"I understand nothing! I understand nothing!"
Mania was very glad that she had been left alone. Her whole life, her whole past appeared before her like a panorama.
She remembers how, still a child, she used to run about near the mill, splashing her little feet at the riverbank. Everyone in the village loved her and fussed over her; her father was rarely at home, he travelled about the villages buying grain. Her mother and grandmother were always cross, sighing and groaning; she never saw a smile from them, a kind word she seldom heard from them. Over there opposite, by contrast, in the white house, it was always bright, it was always merry there — they sang and laughed.
More than once, when all the windows were shining so brightly, Mania would run across the little bridge over the stream, stand on tiptoe and peep into the window: it was so beautiful there, so good, a delight — healthy [?], strong people, lots of guests...
She would stand at the window until her mother or an older sister came running and dragged her home by her braids.
And Mania would come home, where it is so dark — the whole room lit by one small lamp, and big black shadows covering the walls.
Father eats supper and sighs over every bite, mother complains that something hurts her, grandmother sits in a corner and looks with frightened eyes at the frightful room...
(To be continued.)
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Budget Adopted in the Third Reading

[Head of the local page; Będzin — City council.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 20 Sivan 5689 — Piątek 28 czerwca 1929 [Friday, 28 June 1929].)
Będzin
The budget adopted in the third reading.
On Thursday a meeting [of the city council] took place under the chairmanship of Vice-President Mr. Ehrlich, at which the budget was adopted in the third reading.
The ordinary budget thus fixed, which amounts to no less than close to 2 million zł., was adopted "on one foot" (in a hurry) and in a very merry mood; some of the Jewish councillors raised their hands like automatons.
At the meeting councillor Mrs. Ratner made a statement that, because almost all the proposals adopted at the second reading — such as increasing the subsidy for poor women in childbirth, for the Jewish schools, for the orphans, etc. — had been struck out again, she would take no part in the budget vote.
———
At Tuesday's meeting, chaired by President Mr. Fürstenberg, the investment tax, amounting to a sum of 120 thousand zł., was adopted in the third reading.
The councillors of the Sanacja did not come to the meeting.
Before the vote on the investment tax councillor Mrs. Ratner took the floor and declared: since the citizens of the town, and especially merchants and small traders, are now going through a terrible crisis, the magistrat (municipal government) ought not to burden the population with new tax burdens. If the magistrat wants to build a water supply system, this can be done out of the large number of unnecessary expenditures in the budget. For that reason — declared Mrs. Ratner — she will not vote for the tax.
The President and the Vice-President replied to the statement that the tax would benefit the population in that a water supply system would be built in the town from this revenue. As regards the tax burden, the Vice-President declared that, as representative of the "Merchants' Association" (Sokhrim Fareyn) and of the house-owners, he had conferred with them and all had agreed that the tax should be adopted, so that the water supply could be built as quickly as possible.
After these statements all the councillors, even the merchants' councillors who had voted against at the second reading, this time voted in favour, and the tax statute was adopted.
Then the following questions were put to the magistrat: 1) from Director Blaujewicz [?], that the magistrat should intervene so that the work on the post-office building should not be interrupted; 2) from Mr. Ehrlich, why Dr. Rechtszaft had refused to examine the girl pupils of "Beis Yaakov"; and 3) from Mr. Jakubowicz, whether the magistrat knows that Dr. Rechtszaft demanded payment for examining "Mizrachi" pupils before they left for the summer camp.
To all these questions the magistrat answered that they have no knowledge of it whatsoever.
Characteristic was the discussion about the petition of the hairdressers' guild, which asks that when two days of a holiday fall, the barbershops [?] may be open on the second day from 8 to 11 in the morning.
The petition was supported by councillors Klejnman, Jakubowicz and the alderman (ławnik) Goldsztajn. The non-Jewish councillors, headed by the "Agudah"-alderman Hetmańczyk, seeing in the petition a "Jewish power", opened their mouths and spoke against…
The upshot: Hetmańczyk's proposal was adopted that the question be referred to the committee for general affairs.
At the meeting the magistrat's proposal was adopted that the city council should give it power of attorney to issue bills of exchange for 250 thousand zł.
The first group of children leaves for summer camp.
Next Sunday the first group of Jewish schoolboys leaves for the summer camp „Zagłębianka“.
An arbitration court elected.

This week a new arbitration court was elected, whose task is to settle disputes between landlords and tenants.
The arbitration court consists of 6 members, 4 Christians and 2 Jews (in a town with 50 per cent Jewish inhabitants).
On the Jewish side, councillor Kleinman and Hirsz (an artisan) were elected.
Elections to the 16th Congress.

Next Sunday the elections to the 16th Zionist Congress take place.
All Zionist groupings are conducting a vigorous election campaign.
The kehilla will finally have a president.
With the consent of the starosta, a president of the local Jewish community (kehilla) will be elected on Sunday.
The Chevra Kadisha wardens are “democrats”...
The Chevra Kadisha (burial society) has bought a very fine hearse for 3 thousand złoty. The hearse was inaugurated by a respectable Jew and also by a poor man...
The birth pangs of the Jewish “club”.

On Sunday, on the initiative of councillor Jakubowicz, a meeting of the Jewish city councillors was called in order to form a Jewish councillors' “club” (caucus).
No more than 7 councillors came, and instead of a “klub” what grew was the “klog” (lament)...
Cantor Badasz leads the prayers this Sabbath.

The Częstochowa town cantor, Mr. Józef Badasz, will lead the prayers with an enlarged choir this Sabbath in the synagogue of the Ashkenazim.
Mr. Badasz possesses a lyrical voice and his praying arouses enthusiasm.
Enrol your children in the public schools.

Until the 30th of this month is the time to enrol new pupils, boys and girls, in the public elementary schools.
In particular, parents are obliged to register children born in the year 1922.
Saved from an Accident.

On Wednesday a Jewish woman, while getting off the tram on Kołłątaja Street, fell onto the tram line.
Fortunately the tram was stopped at once, and thus the woman was saved from a certain accident.
Sosnowiec — Stormy Debate at the Meeting of the Bank for Artisans and Small Traders.

On Sunday the annual general meeting of the members of the „Bank for Artisans and Small Traders“ took place in the hall of the „Hotel Polski“.
The meeting was a very stormy one. Two camps fought: the „satisfied“ and the dissatisfied. On the „green table“ lay the bank, which is weaker compared with last year, and the speakers of both sides, like experienced professors, „experts“, made the diagnosis of who is the culprit who caused the institution to sink somewhat in the moral sense.
And where there are sides, there is interest. About 300 members came. The mood was chaotic, the discussions were „adorned“ with market-place curses, and the chairmen, Messrs. dentist Rotsztajn and B. Rozman, were forced to conduct the meeting standing (on benches).
———
At the beginning the meeting is conducted under the chairmanship of dentist Rotsztajn. After the reading of the minutes of the last general meeting the official reports begin:
The report of the supervisory board is given by the chairman [printed „priezes“] Mr. Fürstenberg, who points out that the damage to the bank was caused by the politics which were brought into the institution.
The report of the management is given by Dr. Herzman. There are — he says — various reasons that caused the bank not to develop as it should. The main reasons are that on Targowa Street there are no fewer than 4 Jewish banks, and that in a purely economic institution political machinations are conducted.
The bank manager Mr. Buksbaum delivers the balance-sheet report. From the report we learn, unfortunately, that in the year 1928 142 members left the bank (today the bank still counts 762 members) and the profit is 976 zł. and 11 groszy...
Mr. Buksbaum also reads the report of the Auditing Union, in which the management and council are censured for their negligence in collecting outstanding debts, and in particular that the bank is not careful in granting credits, which are given in such amounts that the majority of members are thereby [?] left out [?].
After the reports the discussion began. Because of the large number of registered speakers the speaking time was limited to 5 minutes, but when Messrs. Feldman, Rinski [?], Grinfeld and others spoke, relating facts about the activity of Mr. Nachemja in the bank, the audience „enjoyed it“ and the speakers' time was extended.
In the discussion, which often reached stormy moments and personal abuse and curses between both sides, Messrs. Barankiewicz [?], Roter, Suszycki, Feldman, Rinski, Ekstein, Grinfeld, Pasłuszny, Jaskierowicz and Piekarski took part, who criticized Mr. Nachemja in a very sharp manner for his activity in the bank. The main sin is that Mr. Nachemja supported certain people with larger loans and also brought politics into the bank.
A reply to the accusations was given by the auditor Mr. Szmojsz (Warsaw), who illuminated the situation that had arisen from all sides and pointed out that the culprit is not Mr. Nachemja, who has achieved a great deal for the institution, and the crisis in the bank is only thanks to the internal frictions, the constant tearing-apart among the artisans, into which the bank too was innocently drawn into the struggle.
In the end a resolution was adopted to turn to Mr. Nachemja that he should submit his resignation. If the resignation does not take place within 4 weeks, an extraordinary meeting shall then be called, at which a new management shall be elected.
In place of those drawn out by lot, the following were elected: Messrs. Dr. Herzberg, Józef Kafer, J. Zaks, J. Goldkorn, Izydor Firstenberg, Lewi, Balzam, Kuczyński, Eliner, Rozman, Rejngold.
The members of the artisans' guilds took no part in the elections and demonstratively left the hall.
It is to be hoped that the new management will find sympathy among the Jewish masses and the bank will return to its former level.

Mishap on a Motorcyclists' Outing. / The Jewish Community Remains No More Than a „House of the Dead“.. / 572 Poor Families Exempted from Housing Tax. Session of the City Council. / A Bandit Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison. / In the Church She Doused Her Former Bridegroom with Acid. / Interruption of the Tram.

[Sosnowiec — accident; followed by five short news items from Sosnowiec and the area (left column).]
On Sunday a group of motorcyclists organized an outing from Sosnowiec to Kraków on motorcycles. On the road beyond Chrzanów a collision occurred between two motorcycles. The result was that the wife of an official in Grojca [?] (possibly Grodziec) was seriously injured, and she was taken to hospital in a dangerous condition.
—o—
The Jewish Community Remains No More Than a „House of the Dead“..
A few weeks ago an inspection [„lustration“] by the starosta took place in the office of the local Jewish community.
This week the starosta sent various technical instructions for the office. At the same time the starosta announces that 1) the moral-conduct and property certificates hitherto issued by the community shall no longer be issued, and 2) the budget is to be collected in a strict manner, and from the „monies“ received the pensions of the officials are to be settled first of all.
—o—
572 Poor Families Exempted from Housing Tax. Session of the City Council.
At the Monday session of the local City Council, on the motion of the Magistrate, 572 poor families were exempted from paying housing tax for 1928.
At the session the PPS „club“ submitted an interpellation about the fact that the power station in Małobądz does not indicate on the bills for electricity how many kilowatts the consumer has used.
Because the session began an hour and a half late, the Endek councillors left the session.
—o—
A Bandit Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison.
In the local District Court the trial took place against a bandit who murdered the forest guard in a forest beyond Łazy.
The bandit was sentenced to 15 years in prison.
—o—
In the Church She Doused Her Former Bridegroom with Acid.
In Niwka the following act of revenge occurred. In the local church a „ślub“ (wedding) was to take place. The bridegroom, however, had a few years ago had a fiancée whom he had promised to marry. Having no work in Zagłębie he went off to France, where he forgot his former fiancée.
A few weeks ago the bridegroom came back and got engaged to a second bride, with whom he went to church on Sunday to take the „ślub“.
When the first fiancée found out about it she decided to take revenge on her betrayer.
She took up a position at the side of the church door, and when the bridegroom entered with the second bride, she sprang at him and doused him with vinegar essence.
After the „ślub“ the bridegroom had to go off to the outpatient clinic...
—o—
Interruption of the Tram.
Because of the Catholic Congress the tram will not run on Sunday the 30th from the Nowa Pogońska [?] station to Sosnowiec from 8.30 in the morning until 1 at midday.

Strict Ordinances of the Sosnowiec Magistrate
In connection with the priests' congress that will take place on the 28th, 29th and 30th of this month, the Magistrate has issued the following ordinances: the pavements and the streets must be sprinkled with water twice a day, and the gutters (rynsztok) limewashed.
To protect the inhabitants and the visitors from usurious prices, the Magistrate warns that all those who allow themselves to charge high prices for foodstuffs will be arrested and their shops will be closed.
A large number of inspectors will be active for this purpose.
The sanitary commission is also active on this account, and several bakeries and beer-houses have been closed.
Olkusz. — Elections to the Sick Fund

[Olkusz — Sick Fund.]
In connection with the announcement of the elections to the county (powiat) Sick Fund, on the initiative of S. Stark, Yenkl Briks and others, a meeting of Jewish workers, members of the Sick Fund, took place on Sunday evening in the premises of the “Muze”[?]; it was resolved to found an election committee for the whole powiat, which has already notified Wolbrom, Pilica, Skała and Żarnowiec to send delegates to the next meeting. It is worth noting that ever since the Fund has existed, the Jews — employers and employees alike — have not considered it necessary to take part in the elections, and therefore the administration and staff of the Fund have been[?] “Jew-free”[?]. And since among us[?] there reigns no party antagonism, it is possible that with an active participation of Jews in the elections, Jews could obtain a sizeable representation on both sides.

All May Slaughter...
For a long time the dozór members (the community board) had been struck by the fact that ever less income was flowing into the gmina (community) treasury from the slaughter of poultry, and after a careful check they established that many poultry dealers, as well as private housewives, had not bought any slaughter tickets at the gmina treasury, but [went] only to the shochtim. A. B.

From the Chess Tournament.
The second tournament, which began last Sunday, has already clarified the situation a little. Mr. Cukier, who had been undefeated[?], lost to Fajger, who is a “specialist” at snatching points from the leaders. Mr. Merin started nicely at the beginning and then lost his footing entirely, losing as many as 5 games. The present standing is as follows: Kimelman 5½ points, Cukier 5 points, Redlich 4 points, Szwajcer 3½ points, Merin 3 points, Eng. Filips, Dr. Grodzinski[?], Zylberberg and Fajger 2 points each.

A Jew as Investigating Judge.
The magister Mr. Maurycy Lejbowicz of Sosnowiec has been appointed investigating judge for special important cases at the Sosnowiec District Court.

A Tram Ticket from Czeladź to 3 Maja — 35 Gr.
As is known, a tram ticket from Będzin to Czeladź costs 50 gr. If the passenger rode only as far as the Sercarush[?] brewery, he paid only 35 gr.
Therefore, on the intervention of the Będzin Merchants' Association, the Magistrate applied to the tram management with a request that the tram fare-stage be at the New Market, i.e. that from that place to Czeladź [the fare] should cost 35 gr.
Yesterday the Magistrate received a reply from the tram management, which announces that from 1 July the tram fare-stage will be at the Old Market, i.e. from that day[?] on a ticket from the Old Market to Czeladź and back will cost 35 gr.

Conscious Calculation — Prepare Now for Winter (article)

Conscious calculation. The hard reckoning is preparing now, in summer, for the winter.

Economic conditions, the method of thrift, reckoning and calculation — these have no place at all among us in the public sense. We have no authority to instruct us on the necessary steps in such a case. To this day we live, sadly, for the most part under the psychosis of the war and the years of hatred, when money was like [ashes] — and however terrible and depressing it was, it has been forgotten in a deep oblivion. This is not taken into account, and people do not want to remember that we have long been living in other times, and that life and the whole system must be arranged on a different basis. We were schooled in war, and we did not occupy ourselves with thrift and economy — even after the war no one tried to take up the matter; so that none of us went through the 'routine' or the 'training,' and it is no wonder that we remained thus, neither on this side nor on that; harder times befell the Jews at intervals, until [uncertainty] set in among us — people did not know how to reckon. The far-sighted view was lost entirely, and people began to live without any system and without any conscious calculation; and to this were added enormous burdens of taxes, which drove wholly respectable households to catastrophe — once they lost their balance they fell from the [arena] and lost their connection to economic existence.

Clearly, had we undergone economic training that would teach us the proper guidance, we would not have 'slipped' in the event of a catastrophe: we would have reacted in good time, and the situation would have been saved on the spot. But now, given such a state of affairs, we must not go on behaving this way, and life must be arranged differently — to live by reckoning, to be economically aware and to be well oriented on the ground.

In government circles too people are beginning to regard economic reckoning as a first-rate matter. Not long ago we received a circular (cyrkularz) from the Voivode in Kielce, appealing to us to devote a few articles to the question of the necessity of stocking coal for winter during the summer months. At first glance one might laugh — that we, the residents of Zagłębie, should now stock up on coal for winter — after all we are surrounded by it all year round. But when one considers the question seriously, one arrives at the conclusion that we too must lay in coal for winter in these months. There is no need to look far: last winter there was a frost, and then we received no coal from any part of Poland; merchants paid for coal day by day and received it in railway cars, whereas we here in Zagłębie could not obtain coal, since it was more convenient for the coal merchant to sell his coal to the outside dealer than to bring it into town; and at that moment a slice of coal could not be had at any price — even though we are steeped in this commodity at all times. This proof shows how much we too here in Zagłębie need to lay in coal for winter in the present months.

Of course we are not saying that it is easy to stock coal in summer for winter when it is hard to get through the day and one cannot cover current income; of course the situation is very bad — but this is not said of everyone: there are people with good reckoning and precise calculation who [can] save and prepare a stock now for winter, and they must do so by every possible means. For from this both those who can prepare a stock will profit — since they will have goods ready at a cheaper price — and, later on, those who had no possibility of preparing a stock, since in the great frosts there will be fewer private [speculators] among us, and the small buyer will have a chance to obtain a slice of coal. We must live by reckoning; we must know how to calculate both in commerce and in private family use; and therefore now is the right moment to lay in coal for winter. Conscious calculation must now embrace the important positions in the Jewish middle class.

R. Let.
'Am-ha'aretz, Carry Me!' (an article on the burden of charity)

Am-ha'aretz, trog mikh (common man, carry me).

Będzin is a town of several thousand fine Jewish souls; and even today, when the situation is bad and times are hard and Jews have nothing to eat — there are still hundreds of Jews who, thank God, have a livelihood, and indeed 'bread.' And here before me lies the report of 'Ezrat Yetomim' (Orphans' Aid), an institution we tend so much and which dozens have understood to support. And who are these dozens? The same ones whose names one meets, and whose money is consumed by other institutions — philanthropic as well as cultural — for 'Jawne,' for 'Talmud Torah,' for 'Keren Hajesod' and for 'matzot.'

But the 'others' — a whole and [teeming] number of the names of these 'others,' men of [titles] — may it be said of every Jew — them one does not see here, neither here nor there; they shut themselves up in their homes, sunk in their heavy interest accounts, swallowed up in their new mortgage bonds — for still better days, still more sun-drenched for them, in which they will amass still more money, in which they will be still richer, still stingier, still more money-loving. And let it be said openly! — most of the names of these 'others,' who consider themselves exempt from every obligation toward the Jewish community, all belong to the same stratum: the esteemed 'fine Jews' (sheyne yidn).

Claims upon the Jewish public they have a sackful — but when it comes to the 'zetl' (the donation slip) — halt! The fist does not budge. It can only be that we have here a matter of a special psychology. The meaning of the 'Hasid' of old was 'first of all' [devotion]; the 'Hasid' of today, of whom the 'Agudah' party is forever boasting — he has the [smell] of the 'knobl' (garlic) and the [standing], and the 'shtoysl' (position of power) — and thanks to this the [world] is not destroyed, God forbid. He stands in his grandeur, an 'esteemed Jew,' an old man; who even speaks any longer of the fact that he has the pennies in his pocket, that he is warm under his [fur], and looks down on the world from above. And from [those] 'fine Jews' rises a single cry: 'Am-ha'aretz, trog mikh!' (common man, carry me!).
